lessons.title: Multiple Choice Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Air flows in the order pharynx, larynx, trachea, bronchi and bronchioles.
  • The epiglottis guards the glottis and stops food entering the larynx.
  • Oxygen enters the blood from the lungs by diffusion.
  • The trachea is the windpipe and the diaphragm separates chest and abdominal cavities.
  • Emphysema breaks alveolar walls; pneumonia fills alveoli and causes fever with sputum.
  • Chemotherapy is used as a treatment for lung cancer.

Solved Exercises

Exercise A: Select the correct answer

Q: 1. The correct order of the structures involved in the flow of air in the human body is:

Options: (a) Pharynx — Trachea — Larynx — Bronchi — Bronchioles (b) Larynx — Pharynx — Trachea — Bronchioles — Bronchi (c) Trachea — Pharynx — Larynx — Bronchi — Bronchioles (d) Pharynx — Larynx — Trachea — Bronchi — Bronchioles

Correct answer: Pharynx — Larynx — Trachea — Bronchi — Bronchioles

Q: 2. Food is prevented from entering into the Larynx by:

Options: (a) Glottis (b) Epiglottis (c) Vocal cards (d) Internal nostrils

Correct answer: Epiglottis

Q: 3. Oxygen from the lungs enter into the blood due to:

Options: (a) Diffusion (b) Less affinity of O₂ for air (c) Higher affinity of CO₂ for air (d) Osmosis

Correct answer: Diffusion

Q: 4. Which part of the air passageway is also called the windpipe?

Options: (a) Bronchus (b) Alveolus (c) Larynx (d) Trachea

Correct answer: Trachea

Q: 5. In which disease are the walls of the alveoli are broken?

Options: (a) Pneumonia (b) Bronchitis (c) Emphysema (d) Asthma

Correct answer: Emphysema

Q: 6. The diaphragm is flat, the ribs move out; this occurs during:

Options: (a) Expiration (b) Inspiration (c) Lungs expansion (d) Breathing

Correct answer: Inspiration

Q: 7. The chest cavity is separated from the abdominal cavity by a muscle called:

Options: (a) Larynx (b) Trachea (c) Bronchus (d) Diaphragm

Correct answer: Diaphragm

Q: 8. Respiration at cellular level is known as:

Options: (a) Breathing (b) Ventilation (c) Oxidation (d) Inhalation

Correct answer: Oxidation

Q: 9. High fever, cold and cough with sputum production are symptoms of:

Options: (a) Emphysema (b) Asthma (c) Pneumonia (d) Bronchitis

Correct answer: Pneumonia

Q: 10. Chemotherapy is a treatment of:

Options: (a) Emphysema (b) Bronchitis (c) Asthma (d) Lung cancer

Correct answer: Lung cancer

mcqs.q: 1. The correct order of the structures involved in the flow of air in the human body is:
mcqs.why: Air passes from the pharynx into the larynx, then into the trachea, which divides into bronchi and then bronchioles, exactly in this order as described for the air passageway.

mcqs.q: 2. Food is prevented from entering into the Larynx by:
mcqs.why: The glottis is guarded by a lid-like structure called the epiglottis, which prevents food from entering the larynx and trachea; the glottis itself is only the opening.

mcqs.q: 3. Oxygen from the lungs enter into the blood due to:
options: Less affinity of O₂ for air
Higher affinity of CO₂ for air
mcqs.why: Gaseous exchange in the lungs occurs by diffusion across the thin walls of the alveoli into the surrounding blood capillaries, not by osmosis or by affinity effects.

mcqs.q: 4. Which part of the air passageway is also called the windpipe?
mcqs.why: The larynx opens into the trachea, which is also called the wind pipe; it is the long tube running down the neck into the chest cavity.

mcqs.q: 5. In which disease are the walls of the alveoli are broken?
mcqs.why: In emphysema the walls of the alveoli are broken down, reducing the surface for gaseous exchange, whereas pneumonia fills the alveoli with pus and bronchitis inflames the bronchi.

mcqs.q: 6. The diaphragm is flat, the ribs move out; this occurs during:
mcqs.why: During inspiration the diaphragm contracts and becomes flat and the ribcage expands, so chest volume increases and air rushes in; during expiration the diaphragm relaxes and becomes dome-shaped.

mcqs.q: 7. The chest cavity is separated from the abdominal cavity by a muscle called:
mcqs.why: The diaphragm is the thick dome-shaped muscular sheet below the lungs that forms the floor of the chest cavity and separates it from the abdominal cavity.

mcqs.q: 8. Respiration at cellular level is known as:
mcqs.why: Respiration is the cellular process in which food molecules such as glucose are oxidised to release energy, so cellular respiration is known as oxidation, while breathing is only the movement of air.

mcqs.q: 9. High fever, cold and cough with sputum production are symptoms of:
mcqs.why: Pneumonia is an inflammation of the lungs due to infection in the alveoli, which fill with pus, and it presents with high fever, cold and cough with sputum production.

mcqs.q: 10. Chemotherapy is a treatment of:
mcqs.why: Chemotherapy uses anti-cancer chemicals and is a treatment for lung cancer; bronchitis, emphysema and asthma are managed by other means, not by chemotherapy.

lessons.title: Short Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Plants exchange gases through the epidermis, stomata in leaves and lenticels in bark.
  • Respiration is cellular breakdown of food; breathing is movement of air at the lungs.
  • Large surface area of leaves and of the many thin-walled alveoli speeds up diffusion.
  • The trachea has 16 to 20 C-shaped cartilage rings that keep the airway open.
  • In inspiration the diaphragm contracts and flattens, increasing chest volume.
  • Inhaled air has 21% oxygen and 0.04% carbon dioxide; exhaled air has 16% oxygen and 4% carbon dioxide.
  • Tobacco smoke has over 4,000 chemicals including more than 69 known carcinogens.

Solved Exercises

Exercise B: Write short answers to the following questions

Q: 1. Why do plants not need a specialised respiratory system?

Ans: In plants, gaseous exchange between the body and the environment occurs through the general surface of the plant. The outer surface of the root, stem and leaves, called the epidermis, allows the exchange of gases between the inner cells and the environment. In leaves and young stems the epidermis has small pores called stomata through which air moves in and out, and in woody stems the bark contains special pores called lenticels for the same purpose. Inside the body, gaseous exchange occurs directly between the cells and the air, and in the daytime the carbon dioxide produced in respiration is used in photosynthesis while the oxygen produced in photosynthesis is used in respiration. So every part of the plant can exchange gases on its own and no specialised respiratory system is needed.

Q: 2. Differentiate between the terms “respiration” and “breathing”.

Ans: Respiration is an energy releasing process at the cellular level. In this process, food molecules (e.g. glucose) are broken down into simpler compounds like carbon dioxide and water with the release of energy; for aerobic respiration, oxygen is required for the complete oxidation of food molecules while carbon dioxide is released as a by product. Breathing, on the other hand, is the physical process in which animals move air into and out of their body. It is done to get oxygen from air and to release carbon dioxide in it, and in breathing fresh air is made available to the respiratory surface of the lung for gaseous exchange. So respiration takes place inside the cells, while breathing is the movement of air at the level of the lungs.

Q: 3. How are the surface area of leaves and lungs important for gaseous exchange?

Ans: Gaseous exchange occurs by diffusion, so it can only take place properly if a large surface is available for the gases to cross. A leaf has a broad surface covered by the epidermis, which has small pores called stomata; air moves in and out through the stomata and, inside the leaf, gaseous exchange occurs between the cells and the air. In the lungs, each bronchiole ends in a duct which opens in a cluster of pouches called alveoli, so the lungs contain a very large number of alveoli. The alveoli are thin-walled and provide the surface for gaseous exchange, and their walls are covered with a network of blood capillaries where gaseous exchange occurs. The large surface area of the leaves and of the alveoli therefore allows oxygen and carbon dioxide to diffuse rapidly and in sufficient amounts.

Q: 4. What is the function of the cartilage present in the walls of the trachea and bronchi?

Ans: The trachea has 16 to 20 C-shaped cartilaginous rings. These rings prevent the trachea from collapsing and keep the passage of air open. The bronchi also possess cartilaginous rings, but smaller than those of the trachea, and they do the same job in the bronchi. In this way the cartilage keeps the air passageway permanently open so that air can flow freely to and from the lungs during breathing.

Q: 5. What is a diaphragm and what is its role in breathing?

Ans: The diaphragm is a thick muscular structure present below the lungs; it is a dome-shaped sheet of skeletal muscles at the base of the chest cavity. It plays the central role in breathing. During inspiration, the muscles of the diaphragm contract, so it becomes flat instead of its domed position; the volume of the chest cavity increases, the pressure in the lungs decreases and atmospheric air rushes in. During expiration, the diaphragm relaxes and becomes dome-shaped again; the volume of the chest cavity decreases, the pressure on the lungs increases and the air is expelled out.

Q: 6. What are carcinogens? Name any two carcinogens present in tobacco.

Ans: Carcinogens are cancer causing chemicals. Tobacco smoke contains over 4,000 different chemicals, out of which there are more than 69 known carcinogens. Two carcinogens present in tobacco are benzene, which is a major component of cigarettes and causes blood cancer (leukaemia), and formaldehyde, which causes cancers and respiratory, skin and gastrointestinal problems. Tar present in tobacco smoke also contains many carcinogens.

Q: 7. Compare the composition of inhaled and exhaled air.

Ans: Inhaled (inspired) air contains 21% oxygen and only 0.04% carbon dioxide, while its water vapours and temperature are variable. Exhaled (expired) air contains less oxygen, 16%, and much more carbon dioxide, 4%; it is saturated with water vapours and its temperature is 38 °C. The difference arises because the body uses oxygen for respiration and produces carbon dioxide, so the air leaving the lungs has lost oxygen and gained carbon dioxide and water vapours.

mcqs.q: Why do plants not need a specialised respiratory system?
options: Because every part can exchange gases through its own surface
Because plants do not carry out respiration at any time
Because plants take in air only through their roots
Because gases enter plants only through the flowers
mcqs.why: The epidermis of root, stem and leaves allows exchange between inner cells and the environment through stomata and lenticels, so each part exchanges gases on its own and no specialised system is needed.

mcqs.q: Through which pores does air move in and out in leaves and young stems?
mcqs.why: In leaves and young stems the epidermis has small pores called stomata through which air moves in and out; lenticels are the special pores found in the bark of woody stems instead.

mcqs.q: Through which pores does gaseous exchange occur in woody stems covered by bark?
mcqs.why: Gaseous exchange cannot occur through bark, so the bark of woody stems contains special pores called lenticels which allow gaseous exchange with the environment.

mcqs.q: What is the correct difference between respiration and breathing?
options: Respiration moves air at the lungs, while breathing occurs inside cells
Respiration occurs inside cells, while breathing moves air at the lungs
Both respiration and breathing occur only inside the mitochondria
Breathing releases energy from glucose, while respiration moves air
mcqs.why: Respiration is the cellular energy-releasing breakdown of food molecules, while breathing is the physical movement of air into and out of the body at the level of the lungs.

mcqs.q: How do the alveoli provide an effective surface for gaseous exchange in the lungs?
options: They are thick-walled sacs with very few capillaries around them
They are present in small numbers at the end of the trachea only
They are thin-walled and present in very large numbers with capillary networks
They store air so that exchange can happen once a day
mcqs.why: Each bronchiole ends in a cluster of thin-walled alveoli, and the lungs contain a very large number of them whose walls are covered with blood capillaries, giving a huge surface for diffusion.

mcqs.q: How many C-shaped cartilaginous rings are present in the trachea?
mcqs.why: The trachea has 16 to 20 C-shaped cartilaginous rings; the bronchi also possess cartilaginous rings, but they are smaller than those of the trachea.

mcqs.q: What is the function of the cartilage in the walls of the trachea and bronchi?
options: It produces mucus to trap dust particles in the air
It contracts to pump air into and out of the lungs
It prevents collapse and keeps the air passage open
It warms the incoming air before it reaches the lungs
mcqs.why: The cartilaginous rings prevent the trachea and bronchi from collapsing and keep the passage of air permanently open so air can flow freely during breathing.

mcqs.q: What happens to the diaphragm and chest cavity during inspiration?
options: The diaphragm relaxes, becomes dome-shaped and chest volume decreases
The diaphragm contracts, becomes flat and chest volume increases
The diaphragm stays dome-shaped and chest pressure increases
The diaphragm contracts and chest volume decreases so air is expelled
mcqs.why: During inspiration the diaphragm muscles contract so it becomes flat, the volume of the chest cavity increases, pressure in the lungs decreases and atmospheric air rushes in.

mcqs.q: Tobacco smoke contains more than how many known carcinogens?
mcqs.why: Tobacco smoke contains over 4,000 different chemicals, out of which there are more than 69 known carcinogens, including benzene and formaldehyde, and tar also contains many carcinogens.

mcqs.q: What is the percentage of carbon dioxide in exhaled air compared with inhaled air?
options: Exhaled air has 0.04% and inhaled air has 4% carbon dioxide
Both inhaled and exhaled air have 0.04% carbon dioxide
Inhaled air has 21% and exhaled air has 16% carbon dioxide
Inhaled air has 0.04% and exhaled air has 4% carbon dioxide
mcqs.why: Inhaled air contains 21% oxygen and only 0.04% carbon dioxide, while exhaled air contains 16% oxygen and 4% carbon dioxide, because the body uses oxygen and produces carbon dioxide in respiration.

lessons.title: Detailed Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • In daytime leaves take in carbon dioxide and release oxygen; at night the exchange reverses.
  • Inspiration: diaphragm flattens and ribcage expands, so lung pressure falls and air rushes in.
  • Expiration: muscles relax, diaphragm domes up, chest volume falls and air is expelled.
  • Nasal cavity warms, moistens and dust-frees air; pharynx tonsils trap microorganisms.
  • Bronchioles are one millimetre or less, lack cartilage and end in alveoli with capillaries.
  • Bronchitis inflames bronchi; pneumonia infects alveoli; smoking is the main cause of lung cancer.

Solved Exercises

Exercise C: Write detailed answers to the following questions

Q: 1. The gaseous exchange in plants is important for photosynthesis and respiration. Explain the types of gases exchanged and its mechanism.

Ans: All plant cells carry out respiration all the time, while the green parts (leaves) of plants also carry out photosynthesis during the daytime. The two gases exchanged are oxygen and carbon dioxide, and each process uses the gas produced by the other. During the daytime, for photosynthesis the leaves use carbon dioxide which is produced during respiration, and they also take carbon dioxide from the environment. For respiration, the leaves use oxygen which is produced during photosynthesis, and during respiration they release carbon dioxide which is used in photosynthesis. So, during daytime leaves are taking carbon dioxide from the environment and releasing oxygen in it. During the night, all cells are carrying out respiration while there is no photosynthesis, so the cells get oxygen from the environment and release carbon dioxide in it. As far as the mechanism is concerned, in plants the gaseous exchange between the body and the environment occurs through the surface. The outer surface of the root, stem and leaves is called the epidermis, and this layer allows the exchange of gases between the inner cells and the environment; at some parts a thick cuticle present over the epidermis also allows the exchange of gases. In leaves and young stems, the epidermis has small pores called stomata, and in these parts the air moves in and out through the stomata; inside the body, gaseous exchange occurs between the cells and air. In woody stems, the entire surface is covered by bark and gaseous exchange cannot occur through bark, so the bark contains special pores called lenticels, which allow the gaseous exchange with the environment.

Q: 2. Describe the mechanism of breathing in human beings.

Ans: Breathing consists of two phases, the taking in of air called inspiration and letting out of air called expiration, and these two phases take place continuously one after the other. Air moves in when the air pressure in the lungs is lower than the pressure outside the body, and it moves out when the pressure in the lungs is greater than the atmospheric pressure. a) Inspiration: During inspiration, the volume of the chest cavity increases and the pressure in the lungs decreases. It happens due to two reasons. The muscles of the diaphragm contract, so it becomes flat instead of its domed position; and the intercostal muscles present between the ribs contract, due to which the ribcage expands. Due to these movements the volume of the chest cavity increases and so pressure on the lungs decreases, and as a result the atmospheric air rushes in to the lungs through the air passageway. b) Expiration: During this process, the muscles of the ribs and the diaphragm relax. The ribcage goes down to its original position whereas the diaphragm becomes dome-shaped. The volume of the chest cavity is decreased, which increases the pressure on the lungs and expels the air out.

Q: 3. Draw a diagram of the air passage in the human body and describe the role of different parts in the flow of air through it.

Ans: Diagram (in words): The figure shows the head and chest of a human from the side and front. At the front of the face are the two openings, the Nostrils, leading into the Nasal cavity inside the head. Behind the nasal cavity, at the back of the throat, lies the Pharynx, and just below it the small lid-like Epiglottis. Below the pharynx the passage continues into the Larynx, from which the long tube of the Trachea runs down the centre of the neck into the chest. In the chest the trachea divides into a Bronchus going to each side. The two lungs fill the chest: the Right lung on one side and the Left lung on the other, each surrounded by the Pleural cavity. Below the lungs, forming the floor of the chest, is the curved sheet of the Diaphragm. Role of each part in the flow of air: Nostril — the two external nostrils lie on the ventral side of the head and allow the air from the outside into the two nasal cavities. Nasal cavity — here the air is warmed, moistened and dust freed by the hairs and the mucous membrane of the nasal cavity. Pharynx — the nasal cavities lead into the pharynx, which is about a 4.5 inches long muscular passage also lined by the mucous membrane; it contains tonsils and adenoids, organs of lymphatic tissue used to trap and filter microorganisms, and it passes the air onwards to the larynx. Epiglottis — at the back of the pharynx one passage opens through the glottis into the trachea, and the glottis is guarded by a lid like structure called the epiglottis, which prevents food from entering the larynx and trachea. Larynx — the air moves from the pharynx into the larynx or voice box, which surrounds the upper part of the trachea and whose cavity is also lined by the mucous membrane. Trachea — the larynx opens into the trachea or wind pipe, a tubular structure lying ventral to the esophagus and extending to the chest cavity; its inner surface is ciliated and secretes mucus, which helps to filter, moisten and warm the incoming air, and its 16 to 20 C-shaped cartilaginous rings prevent it from collapsing and keep the passage of air open. Bronchus — inside the thorax the trachea divides into two branches called bronchi; each bronchus enters the lung on its own side and, on entering the lungs, divides and sub-divides progressively into smaller bronchi and finally into bronchioles of one millimeter or less, which have no cartilage; each bronchiole ends in a duct opening in a cluster of thin-walled alveoli, whose walls are covered with a network of blood capillaries where gaseous exchange occurs. Pleural cavity — each lung is enclosed in a double membrane called pleura, which contains a pleural fluid; this fluid makes the movements of the lungs (expansion and contraction) easy. Right lung and Left lung — the lungs are placed in the chest cavity, enclosed from above and sides by the chest wall, and they receive the air through the bronchi for gaseous exchange in the alveoli. Diaphragm — the thick muscular, dome-shaped sheet below the lungs; by contracting and relaxing it changes the volume of the chest cavity and so drives air into and out of the lungs during breathing.

Q: 4. What are the causes of respiratory disorders such as bronchitis, pneumonia and lung cancer?

Ans: Bronchitis: When the lining of the bronchi or bronchioles becomes inflamed or infected, this condition is called bronchitis. It is caused by viruses, bacteria, and their particles that irritate the bronchial tubes. Bronchitis reduces the amount of air that can flow and causes formation of mucus in the airways. Pneumonia: Pneumonia is an inflammation in the lungs, due to infection in the alveoli, and the alveoli are filled with pus. It is caused by bacteria, viruses or fungi. It can also be transmitted by breathing in air with small droplets, which get into the air when an infected person (having these germs) coughs or sneezes. Lung cancer: Lung cancer is a respiratory disease which is more common in men than in women. The most common causes are smoking, industrial carcinogens and air pollution. The main causes of any cancer are carcinogens (such as those in tobacco smoke), ionising radiation and viral infection. Smoking is the main contributor to lung cancer, and cigarette smoke contains over 69 known carcinogens (cancer causing chemicals). Breathing in the exhausts of fossil fuels, which contain harmful compounds like carbon monoxide, nitrogen oxide, carbon dioxide, formaldehyde and soot, also increases the risk of lung cancer.

mcqs.q: What is the net gaseous exchange of leaves during the daytime?
options: Leaves take carbon dioxide from the environment and release oxygen into it
Leaves take oxygen from the environment and release carbon dioxide into it
Leaves take in both oxygen and carbon dioxide and release neither gas
Leaves release both oxygen and carbon dioxide and take in neither gas
mcqs.why: During daytime the carbon dioxide from respiration is used in photosynthesis and extra carbon dioxide is taken from the environment, while oxygen from photosynthesis exceeds respiratory use, so leaves release oxygen.

mcqs.q: What is the gaseous exchange of plant cells during the night?
options: Cells carry out photosynthesis and release oxygen to the environment
Cells use carbon dioxide from the environment for photosynthesis only
Cells get oxygen from the environment and release carbon dioxide into it
Cells stop both respiration and gaseous exchange during the night
mcqs.why: At night there is no photosynthesis while respiration continues in every cell, so the cells get oxygen from the environment and release carbon dioxide into it.

mcqs.q: How do the intercostal muscles help during inspiration?
options: They relax so that the ribcage goes down to its original position
They contract so that the ribcage expands and chest volume increases
They relax so that pressure on the lungs increases and air leaves
They contract to make the diaphragm dome-shaped again
mcqs.why: During inspiration the intercostal muscles between the ribs contract and the ribcage expands; together with the flattening diaphragm this increases chest volume, lowers lung pressure and draws air in.

mcqs.q: What happens during expiration?
options: Rib and diaphragm muscles relax, chest volume decreases and air is expelled
Rib and diaphragm muscles contract, chest volume increases and air rushes in
The diaphragm becomes flat and the ribcage expands to expel air
Chest volume increases so pressure on the lungs falls and air leaves
mcqs.why: During expiration the muscles of the ribs and diaphragm relax, the ribcage goes down, the diaphragm becomes dome-shaped, chest volume decreases and the increased pressure expels the air out.

mcqs.q: What happens to air inside the nasal cavity?
options: It is cooled and dried by the mucous membrane of the cavity
It is filtered by the tonsils and adenoids present there
It is warmed, moistened and freed of dust by hairs and mucous membrane
It undergoes gaseous exchange with blood capillaries there
mcqs.why: In the nasal cavity the air is warmed, moistened and dust freed by the hairs and the mucous membrane before it passes onwards to the pharynx.

mcqs.q: What is the role of the tonsils and adenoids in the pharynx?
options: They trap and filter microorganisms entering with the air
They prevent food from entering the larynx during swallowing
They produce the voice as air passes through the pharynx
They secrete mucus that warms and moistens the incoming air
mcqs.why: The pharynx, a muscular passage about 4.5 inches long, contains tonsils and adenoids, which are lymphatic tissue organs used to trap and filter microorganisms.

mcqs.q: Which statement about bronchioles is correct?
options: They are wider than the bronchi and contain large cartilage rings
They are one millimetre or less in size and have no cartilage
They open directly into the trachea without joining bronchi
Each bronchiole ends in a single thick-walled air sac
mcqs.why: Bronchi divide and sub-divide into smaller bronchi and finally into bronchioles of one millimetre or less, which have no cartilage, and each bronchiole ends in a duct opening into alveoli.

mcqs.q: What is the function of the pleural fluid around the lungs?
options: It carries oxygen from the alveoli into the blood
It prevents the trachea and bronchi from collapsing
It makes the expansion and contraction movements of the lungs easy
It filters and warms the air before gaseous exchange occurs
mcqs.why: Each lung is enclosed in a double membrane called pleura containing pleural fluid, and this fluid makes the movements of the lungs, expansion and contraction, easy.

mcqs.q: How can pneumonia spread from an infected person to others?
options: By breathing in air carrying droplets coughed or sneezed out by the patient
By drinking water that was used by an infected person
By touching the skin of a person suffering from pneumonia
By inhaling cigarette smoke produced near an infected person
mcqs.why: Pneumonia is caused by bacteria, viruses or fungi infecting the alveoli, and it can be transmitted by breathing in air with small droplets released when an infected person coughs or sneezes.

mcqs.q: Which factor is the main contributor to lung cancer?
options: Breathing air in rooms with poor ventilation
Smoking, because cigarette smoke contains many carcinogens
Infection of the alveoli by bacteria, viruses or fungi
Inflammation of the lining of the bronchi and bronchioles
mcqs.why: Smoking is the main contributor to lung cancer and cigarette smoke contains over 69 known carcinogens; industrial carcinogens and air pollution, including fossil fuel exhausts, also increase the risk.

lessons.title: Activities
lessons.notes_html:
Solved Exercises

Activities

Q: 1. Investigate the effect of light on the net gaseous exchange from a leaf, by using bicarbonate as the indicator.

Ans: This activity investigates whether a leaf takes in or gives out carbon dioxide on the whole (net gaseous exchange) in light and in darkness. A leaf is placed in a tube of bicarbonate indicator, which changes according to the amount of carbon dioxide around the leaf; one tube is kept in bright light and another in darkness, and the indicator in the two tubes is compared. Expected observation: in bright light the indicator shows that the carbon dioxide around the leaf has decreased, because in the daytime the leaf carries out photosynthesis as well as respiration, takes carbon dioxide from the environment and releases oxygen in it. In darkness the indicator shows that the carbon dioxide has increased, because there is no photosynthesis and all cells only carry out respiration, taking oxygen from the environment and releasing carbon dioxide. Conclusion: light reverses the net gaseous exchange of a leaf — in light the net exchange is an uptake of carbon dioxide and release of oxygen, while in darkness it is an uptake of oxygen and release of carbon dioxide.

Q: 2. Investigate the breathing rate at rest and after exercise.

Ans: This activity investigates how exercise affects the rate of breathing. The number of breaths taken in one minute is counted while a person is sitting at rest, and then counted again in one minute immediately after exercise such as running or jogging. Expected observation: under resting condition the rate of breathing is 15-20 times per minute, while during and after exercise this rate increases instantly, up to 30-40 times per minute. Conclusion: during exercise more oxygen is required for the oxidation of glucose molecules to get more energy, and as a result more carbon dioxide is produced which accumulates in the blood; when this blood reaches the brain, the medulla (breathing centre) detects more carbon dioxide in the blood and sends nerve impulses to the diaphragm and rib muscles at greater speed, so the speed of contraction and relaxation of these muscles increases and the rate and depth of breathing increase.

Q: 3. Find out how much air a person can take into his lungs.

Ans: This activity measures the volume of air the lungs of a person can hold. A large bottle or jar is filled completely with water and inverted over a trough of water. The person takes the deepest possible breath in, and then breathes out all the air through a tube into the inverted bottle. Expected observation: the exhaled air collects at the top of the bottle and pushes the water down, and the volume of water displaced, read from the markings on the bottle, equals the volume of air the person took into his lungs in the deep breath. Conclusion: the lungs can take in a large, measurable volume of air in one deep breath, and this volume differs from person to person, because the size of the lungs of any organism is related to the activities and body form of that organism.

Q: 4. Demonstrate through experiment, that carbon dioxide is exhaled during respiration.

Ans: This activity demonstrates that the air breathed out contains carbon dioxide. Exhaled air is blown through a tube into a test tube of clear limewater, while ordinary air is pumped through a second tube of limewater as a control. Expected observation: the limewater through which exhaled air is blown turns milky (cloudy) quickly, while the limewater receiving ordinary air stays clear or turns milky only very slowly. Conclusion: exhaled air contains much more carbon dioxide than inhaled air, which the book's table of the composition of inspired and expired air confirms — inspired air has only 0.04% carbon dioxide while expired air has 4% carbon dioxide. This carbon dioxide is the gas produced in respiration and expelled by breathing, so carbon dioxide is exhaled during respiration.

lessons.title: Multiple Choice Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Homeostasis works through osmoregulation, excretion and thermoregulation together.
  • Xerophytes have thick cuticle, sunken stomata and deep roots, but very few stomata.
  • Loss of water as small droplets from plants is called guttation.
  • The ureter joins kidney to bladder; kidneys excrete urea, water and salts.
  • Blood cells do not enter the filtrate in the Bowman's capsule.
  • The liver makes urea from ammonia, and sweat both cools the body and removes wastes.

Solved Exercises

Exercise A: Select the correct answer.

Q: 1. Organisms have the ability to change and modify their internal conditions according to the environment through:

Options: (a) Osmoregulation (b) Excretion (c) Thermoregulation (d) All of the above

Correct answer: All of the above

Q: 2. All of the following are the adaptation of xerophytes except:

Options: (a) Thick cuticle (b) Large number of stomata (c) Sunken stomata (d) Deep root system

Correct answer: Large number of stomata

Q: 3. The loss of water from the plants in the form of small droplets is:

Options: (a) Stomatal transpiration (b) Cuticular transpiration (c) Lenticular transpiration (d) Guttation

Correct answer: Guttation

Q: 4. From a nephron, wastes enter into the

Options: (a) Collecting tubules (b) Ureter (c) Convoluted tubules (d) Medulla

Correct answer: Collecting tubules

Q: 5. The tube between the kidney and urinary bladder is the:

Options: (a) Ureter (b) Urethra (c) Renal tubule (d) Nephron

Correct answer: Ureter

Q: 6. Waste products excreted by the kidneys are:

Options: (a) Urea, water and salts (b) Salts, water and carbon dioxide (c) Urea and water (d) Urea and salts

Correct answer: Urea, water and salts

lessons.title: Short Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Homeostasis keeps the internal environment constant; osmoregulation balances water and solutes.
  • Hydrophytes shed water through many stomata on broad floating leaves.
  • Xerophytes conserve water with deep roots, few stomata and a thick waxy cuticle.
  • Kidneys make more urine when blood has excess water and retain water when solutes are high.
  • Calcium oxalate stones form 70% of kidney stones; lithotripsy breaks stones with shock waves.
  • In cold, raised hairs and goose bumps trap warm air; renal failure destroys nephrons.

Solved Exercises

Exercise B: Write short answers to the following questions.

Q: 1. Define homeostasis and osmoregulation.

Ans: Homeostasis is the ability to maintain the internal environment constant. Organisms make adjustments in their internal environment to overcome the effects of changes in the external environment, and in this way they try to maintain their internal environment in a constant state. The most important components of the internal environment which are readily affected are water, solutes and temperature. Osmoregulation is the process by which the amount of water and solutes are maintained in the body, i.e. the regulation of the amount of water in the body fluids (the water-solute balance, commonly called the water-salt balance).

Q: 2. Differentiate between the adaptations of hydrophytes and xerophytes for osmoregulation.

Ans: Hydrophytes are the plants which live in freshwater (ponds, rivers, streams, lakes etc.) or in wet soil, so water keeps on entering their bodies through their whole surface. They remove this extra water in different ways; for example, many hydrophytes have broad leaves which float on the surface of the water and have a large number of stomata on their upper surfaces, through which water moves out of their bodies, e.g. the water lily. Xerophytes live in dry environments (e.g. deserts), so their problem is to conserve water. They have deep roots to absorb water from almost dry soil, their body surface has very few stomata and is covered with a thick waxy cuticle to reduce the loss of water, and some xerophytes, e.g. cacti, store water in their specialised stems or roots, which are soft and juicy and are called succulent organs.

Q: 3. Briefly describe how kidneys control the composition of blood.

Ans: Kidneys filter the nitrogenous wastes from the blood and excrete them from the body. In addition to this, kidneys also control the water-solute balance of the blood. If there are more solutes in the blood, kidneys excrete them and retain water in the body. But if there is more water, kidneys produce more urine to remove excess water from the body. In this way, kidneys perform osmoregulation and keep the composition of the blood constant.

Q: 4. Enlist materials in our diet which are more likely to cause kidney stones?

Ans: The presence of more calcium oxalate, calcium and ammonium phosphates in a person's diet (green vegetables, fats, dairy products) is the major cause of kidney stones. Oxalates are present in green vegetables and tomatoes, so eating green leafy vegetables and tomatoes may form oxalate stones, and calcium oxalate type stones are 70% of all the kidney stones. Extra amounts of vitamins C and D in a diet may also cause stones. The other causes of kidney stones are reduced water intake, excess uric acid in the blood, urinary tract infections, and alcohol consumption.

Q: 5. Define lithotripsy?

Ans: Lithotripsy is the most recent method of removing kidney stones, and it is the non-surgical removal of kidney stones. This technique is used to break up stones present in the kidney, ureter or urinary bladder. In this method, the stone inside the kidney is targeted by shock-waves, and the shock waves break the stone into tiny pieces, which are passed out of the body in the urine. Lithotripsy works best with stones between 4 mm to 2 cm in diameter that are still located in the kidney.

Q: 6. What is the role of the skin in thermoregulation?

Ans: The skin of human beings and other mammals has been adapted as the organ for thermoregulation. There is a thin layer of fat cells beneath the epidermis of the skin, which does not allow heat to enter or leave the body. In cold conditions, the muscles attached at the base of the hair on the skin contract, so the hairs on the skin stand up and goose bumps are formed on the skin; these goose bumps and hair make a blanket of warm air which does not allow the body's heat to go out. In warm conditions, the skin provides a cooling effect when sweat is produced by the sweat glands, and excess body heat escapes through evaporation. Sweating also helps in the removal of some amounts of extra water, salts, and nitrogenous wastes from the body.

Q: 7. Which term is used for the disease where one or both kidneys do not perform their function?

Ans: The term used is kidney failure, also called renal failure. Due to various reasons, the nephrons are progressively destroyed and stop functioning, and this condition is termed as renal failure or kidney failure. In renal failure, nephrons are not able to filter the blood properly, therefore the level of urea and other nitrogenous wastes in the blood increases. The most common causes are long-term diabetes mellitus and hypertension, and severe infections in the kidney and the overuse of medicine (aspirin, ibuprofen, cocaine and acetaminophen) can also cause kidney failure.

options: The ability to maintain the internal environment constant
The removal of urine from the body through the urethra
The production of sweat to cool the surface of the skin
The breakdown of food molecules to release energy in cells

mcqs.q: What is osmoregulation?

The filtration of nitrogenous wastes from the blood by nephrons
The process by which the amount of water and solutes is maintained in the body
The removal of extra water from plants in the form of droplets

Through broad floating leaves with many stomata on the upper surface
Through deep roots that absorb water from almost dry soil
Through succulent stems and roots that store the extra water

They have thin cuticles so that water can leave the body easily
They have deep roots, very few stomata and a thick waxy cuticle

They produce more urine to remove the excess water
They stop producing urine until the balance is restored
They store the excess water inside the nephrons
mcqs.why: Kidneys control the water-solute balance of the blood: if there is more water they produce more urine to remove the excess, and if there are more solutes they excrete the solutes and retain water.

mcqs.q: What percentage of kidney stones are of the calcium oxalate type?
mcqs.why: Oxalates present in green vegetables and tomatoes can form oxalate stones, and calcium oxalate type stones are 70% of kidney stones, the most common type.

mcqs.q: How does lithotripsy remove kidney stones without surgery?
options: By dissolving the stones with dialysis fluid inside the kidney
By filtering the blood so that stones cannot reach the kidney
By targeting the stone with shock waves that break it into tiny pieces
By cutting open the kidney, ureter or bladder to take stones out

Stones larger than 5 cm in diameter located in the bladder

Muscles at the hair base contract, hairs stand up and trap a blanket of warm air
The fat layer under the skin melts and releases heat to the body
Blood vessels in the skin widen so more heat reaches the surface

options: Kidney stones block the ureter and urine cannot leave the bladder
Nephrons are progressively destroyed and cannot filter the blood properly
The kidneys produce too much urine and the body loses excess water

lessons.title: Detailed Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Each kidney is about 10 by 5 by 4 cm; the right kidney is slightly lower and smaller.
  • The hilus lets the renal artery in and the renal vein and ureter out.
  • The cortex is outer and the medulla inner, with pyramids pointing to the renal pelvis.
  • Each kidney has more than one million nephrons, each with a corpuscle and a tubule.
  • Plants excrete gases through stomata, extra water by transpiration and guttation, and latex, gums and resins through pores.
  • A dialyzer cleans blood across semi-permeable tubes, doing the filtering work of a failed kidney.

Solved Exercises

Exercise C: Write detailed answers to the following questions.

Q: 1. Describe the structure of kidneys in human beings.

Ans: Human beings possess a pair of kidneys. They are present below the diaphragm in the abdominal cavity, on the sides of the vertebral column, and are attached to the dorsal body wall. The right kidney is slightly lower and smaller than the left one. The kidney is a dark brown and bean shaped organ (having a concave and a convex side); the concave side of each kidney is towards the vertebral column. Each kidney is about 10 cm long, 5 cm wide and 4 cm thick. The kidney is enclosed in a tissue called the renal capsule. On the concave side of the kidney, there is a depression called the hilus; it is the point where the renal artery enters the kidney and where the renal vein and ureter leave the kidney. A longitudinal section of the kidney shows that it consists of two regions: the outer region is called the renal cortex, whereas the inner region is called the renal medulla. There are many cone-shaped areas in the renal medulla called the renal pyramids; the base of each pyramid faces the renal cortex while its tip is in a cavity called the renal pelvis, and the pelvis extends to the outside of the kidney and forms the ureter. The functional units of the kidneys are called nephrons, and there are more than one million nephrons in each kidney. A nephron consists of two parts, i.e. the renal corpuscle and the renal tubule. Diagram (in words): Fig. 11.9 'Structure of the Kidney' shows a bean-shaped kidney cut lengthwise; on the outside is the Renal capsule, the outer region is labelled Renal Cortex and the inner region Renal Medulla, containing the cone-shaped Renal Pyramid; at the concave side the Renal artery enters and the Renal vein leaves, the Renal pelvis collects the urine in the middle and continues downwards as the Ureter.

Q: 2. Why do plants excrete? What are the different mechanisms through which plants excrete different substances?

Ans: Plants do not possess any special organs for excretion. They get rid of different wastes in different ways, to maintain their internal environment. The materials which plants require to excrete are carbon dioxide produced during respiration, oxygen and water released as a by product of photosynthesis, and some metabolic products like latex, resins and gums. Excretion of carbon dioxide and oxygen: during the day time, when active photosynthesis is going on, CO2 is retained in the leaves of plants and is used for photosynthesis, and at night, when there is no photosynthesis, it is excreted through the open stomata of the leaves; during the day, the oxygen produced during photosynthesis is utilised in cellular respiration, and the extra oxygen is released out through the stomata. Excretion of extra water: plants store large amounts of water in the vacuoles of their cells, which results in turgor, but if plants have extra amounts of water they remove it in two ways: (1) Transpiration — during the day, plants remove their extra water by transpiration, and there are three types of transpiration, i.e. through the stomata (stomatal transpiration), cuticle (cuticular transpiration) and through lenticels (lenticular transpiration); (2) Guttation — transpiration does not occur at night, so some plants such as grasses use a special method to remove extra water at night through small pores at the tips or edges of their leaves, and this water comes out in the form of little drops. Excretion of other wastes: some plants store wastes in their bodies (stems, leaves or roots) in the form of harmless crystals, and some plants store their wastes in their leaves, so when their leaves fall the plant body also gets rid of these wastes. Some plants excrete their wastes through special pores by applying force; for example, the rubber plant excretes latex, the Acacia tree excretes gums, coniferous trees excrete resins, and the ladyfinger excretes mucilage. Resins, gums and latex are economically very important plant products and are used in many industrial products.

Q: 3. What are kidney stones and how are they formed? Suggest ways in which these stones can be removed from the body.

Ans: Kidneys filter harmful substances from the blood. Sometimes, the filtered harmful substances (e.g. calcium oxalate, calcium and ammonium phosphate, uric acid etc.) gather in the kidneys and make larger objects; such objects cannot pass in the urine and are called kidney stones. Some stones may leave the kidneys and get trapped in the ureter or urinary bladder, and these can then cause obstruction in the urinary tract. They are formed mainly when the diet contains more calcium oxalate, calcium and ammonium phosphates (green vegetables, fats, dairy products); extra amounts of vitamins C and D in a diet may also cause stones, and the other causes are reduced water intake, excess uric acid in the blood, urinary tract infections, and alcohol consumption. Patients of kidney stones feel severe pain in the kidney or lower abdomen, and other symptoms include nausea, vomiting, burning in urethra, frequent urination, foul-smelling urine, blood and pus in the urine and bloating. Removal: if kidney stones are small in size, the patient is advised to drink plenty of water so that stones can pass through the urine. If stones are large and cannot pass easily, the patient has to undergo surgery, in which the patient's kidney, ureter or urinary bladder is opened and stones are removed. The most recent method is lithotripsy, the non-surgical removal of kidney stones, in which the stone inside the kidney is targeted by shock-waves and the shock waves break the stone into tiny pieces, which are passed out of the body in the urine.

Q: 4. Define haemodialysis. How is it performed?

Ans: Dialysis is the cleaning of the blood of a patient suffering from renal failure (by using artificial methods). In dialysis, the blood and a dialysis fluid are kept on opposite sides of a membrane; the nitrogenous wastes of blood pass through the membrane and enter the dialysis fluid, and in this way the blood is purified. Haemodialysis is one of the two methods of dialysis. In this method, blood is passed through a machine called a dialyzer. The dialyzer contains tubes, the walls of which are made of semi-permeable membranes. Blood flows inside the tubes while the dialysis fluid flows outside. Extra water and wastes diffuse from the blood into the dialysis fluid. The purified blood is then returned back to the body. Diagram (in words): Fig. 11.14 'Haemodialysis' shows the patient lying down, with blood taken 'From artery to pump' into a 'Tube system made of a selectively permeable membrane', with 'Fresh dialysing solution' entering the dialyzer and 'Used dialysing solution (with urea and excess salt)' leaving it, and the cleaned blood returning 'From apparatus to vein'.

Q: 5. How does a dialyzer work? Relate the function of a dialyzer with that of the kidney.

Ans: A dialyzer is the machine used in haemodialysis. It contains tubes, the walls of which are made of semi-permeable membranes. The patient's blood is passed through the dialyzer and flows inside the tubes, while the dialysis fluid flows outside the tubes. Extra water and wastes diffuse from the blood, across the semi-permeable walls of the tubes, into the dialysis fluid, and the purified blood is then returned back to the body. Relation with the kidney: the dialyzer does artificially the same cleaning work that the kidney does naturally. The kidneys are the most important organs of homeostasis; they filter the nitrogenous wastes from the blood and excrete them from the body, and they also control the water-solute balance, excreting more solutes and retaining water when there are more solutes in the blood, and producing more urine when there is more water. When the kidneys fail (renal failure), nephrons are not able to filter the blood properly and the level of urea and other nitrogenous wastes in the blood increases, so the dialyzer takes over this filtering function: like the nephrons of the kidney, it removes nitrogenous wastes and extra water from the blood and returns the purified blood to the body.

options: About one thousand nephrons, each with a capsule and a pelvis
More than one lakh nephrons, each with a cortex and a medulla

mcqs.q: How do plants excrete carbon dioxide at night?
options: It is retained in the leaves and used for photosynthesis at night
It is excreted through the open stomata of the leaves

mcqs.q: What is guttation and when does it occur in plants such as grasses?
options: Loss of water as vapour through stomata during the daytime
Removal of extra water as drops through pores at leaf tips or edges at night

options: The rubber plant excretes gums and the Acacia tree excretes latex
Coniferous trees excrete mucilage and ladyfinger excretes resins
The Acacia tree excretes gums and coniferous trees excrete resins
The ladyfinger excretes latex and the rubber plant excretes mucilage

options: Urea, sweat and excess water filtered from the blood

mcqs.q: How does a dialyzer clean the blood during haemodialysis?

Solved Exercises

Activities

Q: 1. Examine the structure of a kidney (sheep or goat kidney / model).

Ans: Model answer: Take a sheep or goat kidney (or a model of a kidney) and examine it from the outside first. It is a dark brown, bean shaped organ, about 10 cm long, 5 cm wide and 4 cm thick, enclosed in a tissue called the renal capsule, with a concave side and a convex side. On the concave side there is a depression called the hilus, the point where the renal artery enters the kidney and where the renal vein and ureter leave the kidney. Now cut the kidney lengthwise (longitudinal section) or open the model: it consists of two regions, the outer renal cortex and the inner renal medulla. In the renal medulla there are many cone-shaped areas called the renal pyramids, whose bases face the renal cortex and whose tips lie in the cavity called the renal pelvis, which extends to the outside of the kidney and forms the ureter. The functional units working inside this structure are the nephrons, more than one million in each kidney, each made of a renal corpuscle (glomerulus and Bowman's capsule) and a renal tubule.

Q: 2. Trace the movement of a molecule of urea from the blood to the urethra, using a flow chart diagram.

Ans: Model answer (flow chart in words): Urea is first made in the liver, which changes the ammonia (produced in the metabolism of proteins) to urea, and the urea enters the blood. Flow: Blood carrying urea -> Renal artery -> arteriole -> Glomerulus of a nephron -> (by pressure filtration, urea is filtered out of the glomerulus with water, salts and sugars) -> Bowman's capsule, as part of the glomerular filtrate -> Renal tubule (proximal convoluted tubule -> Loop of Henle -> distal convoluted tubule; some urea is also added from the blood capillaries to the renal tubule by tubular secretion) -> Collecting duct -> Renal pelvis -> Ureter -> Urinary bladder (where urine is temporarily stored) -> Urethra -> passed out of the body. Blood cells and plasma proteins are not filtered out at the glomerulus because they are larger in size, and the useful materials in the filtrate are reabsorbed into the blood capillaries around the renal tubule, so mainly the wastes, including the urea molecule, travel on to the urethra.

Correct answer: Axons of sensory and motor neurons

Q: 11. The part of the brain which you use in recalling your memories is:

Options: (a) Cerebellum (b) Limbic system (c) Thalamus (d) Hypothalamus

Correct answer: Limbic system

Q: 12. Which of these acts an exocrine as well as endocrine gland?

Options: (a) Pituitary (b) Thyroid (c) Adrenal (d) Pancreas

Correct answer: Pancreas

Q: 13. In the inner ear, vibrations make pressure waves in the fluid of;

Options: (a) Cochlea (b) Stapes (c) Auditory nerve (d) Semi-circular canals

Correct answer: Cochlea

mcqs.q: 1. Insulin is a hormone and is secreted by;
mcqs.why: Insulin is secreted by the islets of Langerhans, the endocrine cells of the pancreas. The liver and stomach do not secrete insulin.

mcqs.q: 2. One of the following is a muscular layer of the eyeball:
mcqs.why: Book misprint corrected: the book keys Sclera, but the sclera is the tough outer fibrous coat, not a muscular layer. The middle coat, the choroid with the ciliary body whose muscles focus the lens, is the muscular layer; retina is the light-sensitive layer, cornea is transparent outer coat, and a cone is a photoreceptor cell.

mcqs.q: 3. The part of neuron that carries the signals away from the cell body:
mcqs.why: The axon carries nerve impulses away from the cell body towards the next neuron or effector. Dendrites carry signals towards the cell body, while Schwann cells and the myelin sheath only insulate the axon.

mcqs.q: 4. One of the following is responsible for the detection of changes in the environment:
mcqs.why: Receptors are the parts of the body which receive the changes (stimuli) taking place in the environment. Neurons only carry the impulse, effectors produce the response, and coordinators process the information.

mcqs.q: 5. Which of the following is true about the cerebral cortex?
options: It is located deep in the brain.
It is located at the back of the brain.
It is part of the peripheral nervous system.
It is the folded outer covering of the brain.
mcqs.why: The cerebral cortex is the outer region of the cerebrum with many folds and convolutions that increase its surface area, and it is made of grey matter. It is not deep inside, not only at the back, and it belongs to the central nervous system.

mcqs.q: 6. Light rays focus behind the retina, instead of focussing on the surface of the retina. This condition is known as:
mcqs.why: In hypermetropia (long sightedness) the eyeball is too short, so light rays focus behind the retina and close objects look blurred. In myopia the rays focus in front of the retina instead.

mcqs.q: 7. Microscopic gaps between the neuron endings are:
mcqs.why: A synapse is the microscopic gap between the ending of one neuron and the start of the next, across which the signal is passed. Transmitters are the chemicals released at the synapse, not the gap itself.

mcqs.q: 8. The largest part of the brain is:
mcqs.why: The cerebrum is the largest part of the brain, divided into two cerebral hemispheres joined by the corpus callosum. The cerebellum, medulla oblongata and thalamus are all much smaller parts.

mcqs.q: 9. Intelligence is under the control of:
mcqs.why: The cerebrum is responsible for intelligence, thinking, reasoning and decision making. The cerebellum coordinates movement and balance, while the thalamus relays sensory information and the hypothalamus controls body conditions such as hunger and thirst.

mcqs.q: 10. Mixed nerves are made of;
options: Cell bodies of sensory and motor neurons
Axons of sensory and motor neurons
mcqs.why: A mixed nerve contains both sensory and motor fibres together, and a nerve fibre is the axon of a neuron. It is the axons, not the cell bodies, that run inside a nerve.

mcqs.q: 11. The part of the brain which you use in recalling your memories is:
mcqs.why: The limbic system, lying in an arc between the thalamus and cerebrum, is important in the formation of memories and processes responses like hunger, thirst, fear and anger. The cerebellum deals with balance and coordinated movement.

mcqs.q: 12. Which of these acts an exocrine as well as endocrine gland?
mcqs.why: The pancreas has both activities: as an exocrine gland it releases digestive juice through a duct, and as an endocrine gland its islets of Langerhans release insulin and glucagon into the blood. Pituitary, thyroid and adrenal are purely endocrine glands.

mcqs.q: 13. In the inner ear, vibrations make pressure waves in the fluid of;
mcqs.why: In the internal ear the vibrations create pressure waves in the fluid of the cochlea, where the hair cells of the organ of Corti act as sound receptors. The semi-circular canals are concerned with balance, not hearing.

mcqs.q: Which hormone increases the blood glucose level by promoting the breakdown of glycogen to glucose in the liver and muscles?
mcqs.why: Glucagon does the opposite work of insulin: it increases blood glucose by promoting breakdown of glycogen to glucose in the liver and muscles and increasing release of glucose from the liver into the blood. Insulin lowers blood glucose.

mcqs.q: Which lens is used to correct short sightedness (myopia), in which light rays focus in front of the retina?
mcqs.why: Myopia is caused by an unusually long eyeball, so rays focus in front of the retina. A concave lens in glasses or contact lenses spreads the rays so they focus onto the retina and distant objects become clear. A convex lens is used for long sightedness.

lessons.title: Short Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • A reflex arc runs receptor, sensory neuron, spinal cord, associative neuron, motor neuron, effector, and the brain is generally not involved.
  • Epilepsy can come from genetic brain changes, head injury, stroke, brain infection or drug abuse.
  • Paralysis is a vascular brain disease: a clot blocks fine vessels or vessels rupture due to high blood pressure.
  • The pituitary is the master gland because TSH, ACTH and LH control the thyroid, adrenal cortex and gonads.
  • Nervous coordination is electrical and fast; chemical coordination is hormonal, carried by blood, and slower.
  • Oestrogen develops female secondary sexual characters; progesterone prepares the body for pregnancy.
  • ADH makes renal tubules reabsorb large quantities of water from the glomerular filtrate.

Solved Exercises

Exercise B: Write short answers to the following questions.

Q: 1. How do reflex action work in human beings?

Ans: A reflex action is an automatic, immediate, quick involuntary, fixed response to an environmental change (stimulus), and generally the brain is not involved in it. It is performed through a short and simple pathway of neurons called the reflex arc. The action starts with a sensory neuron present in a receptor, which takes the impulse to the spinal cord; here an associative neuron shifts the impulse to the motor neuron, which takes the impulse to the effector. In the book's figure the steps are: Step-1 arrival of stimulus and activation of receptor, Step-2 activation of a sensory neuron, Step-3 information processing in CNS, Step-4 activation of a motor neuron, and Step-5 response by effector. For example, when a finger touches the tip of a needle, the hand is retracted at once, and the pain is felt afterwards because we feel pain when the message is sent to the brain.

Q: 2. What are the causes of epilepsy and paralysis?

Ans: Epilepsy may be caused by changes in the brain due to genetic reasons. Severe head injuries, stroke, brain infections and drug abuse may also cause epilepsy. Paralysis is a vascular disease of the brain: it occurs when either a blood clot is stuck in the fine blood vessels of the brain, or due to the rupturing of blood vessels in the brain due to high blood pressure. This causes damage to that part of the brain, and the part of the body controlled by the affected part of the brain stops functioning.

Q: 3. What happens if Islets of Langerhans secrete insulin but not glucagon?

Ans: Insulin decreases blood glucose levels, either by metabolizing it or by converting it into fats, so if only insulin is secreted the blood glucose level will keep falling. Glucagon does the opposite work: it increases blood glucose levels by promoting the breakdown of glycogen to glucose in the liver and muscles, and it also increases the release of glucose from the liver to the blood. Without glucagon, the body will have no way to raise the blood glucose level again when it falls too low. In this way the balance between the two hormones, which normally keeps the blood glucose level normal through the negative feedback mechanism, will be disturbed.

Q: 4. Why is the pituitary gland known as the master gland?

Ans: The pituitary gland is generally termed as the 'master gland' of the body because the hormones secreted by it control other endocrine glands. Its thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH) controls the development and secretion of the thyroid hormone (thyroxin), and its adreno-cortico-trophic hormone (ACTH) acts on the cortex part of the adrenal gland to release the adrenal hormone. Its luteinising hormone (LH) is needed for the release of egg cells from the ovary in females and, in males, it stimulates the testes to produce sex hormones. In this way the pituitary gland, through its hormones, regulates the working of the thyroid, adrenal glands and gonads, besides controlling the growth of the body through its growth hormone.

Q: 5. Differentiate between the two types of coordination system.

Ans: There are two types of coordination, nervous coordination and chemical coordination. In nervous coordination the mode of coordination is electrical: the receptors are the sense organs (eyes, ears, nose, tongue, skin), the coordinator is the brain and spinal cord, and the effectors are muscles and glands. The message is electrical (nerve impulse), it is carried by neurons, and the response is the contraction of muscles and secretions from glands; this response is fast because nervous coordination works at the speed of electricity. In chemical coordination the mode of coordination is hormonal: the receptors and effectors are many body parts (e.g. kidneys, liver, stomach etc.), and the coordinator is the endocrine glands. The message is in the form of chemicals (e.g. hormones), it is carried by the blood, and the response is of various types, e.g. growth and reabsorption of water by the kidneys; this response is slower than the response of nervous coordination.

Q: 6. What is the role of insulin and glucagon?

Ans: Insulin decreases blood glucose levels either by metabolizing it or by converting it into fats, and it reduces the blood glucose level by promoting its entry into the body cells. If the body fails to produce insulin, it leads to diabetes mellitus. Glucagon does the opposite: it increases blood glucose levels by promoting the breakdown of glycogen to glucose in the liver and muscles. It also increases the release of glucose from the liver to the blood. In this way insulin and glucagon together keep the blood glucose level normal, under the negative feedback mechanism.

Q: 7. What characters are controlled by the ovarian hormones?

Ans: The ovaries produce two hormones. Oestrogens bring about the development of the secondary sexual characters in the female, e.g. the development of the breast; the book's summary table adds that oestrogen causes the release of an egg from the ovary and regulates the female secondary sex characteristics. Progesterone prepares the female body for maintaining the state of pregnancy. So the characters controlled by the ovarian hormones are the female secondary sexual characters, the release of the egg from the ovary, and the preparation of the body for pregnancy.

Q: 8. State the hormones of the pituitary and thyroid glands and write their functions.

Ans: Pituitary gland, anterior lobe: (i) Growth hormone increases the cell division of somatic cells and promotes the growth of the body; if it is secreted in excess during early life it results in gigantism, and its under-secretion in early life causes dwarfism. (ii) Thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH) controls the development and secretion of the thyroid hormone (thyroxin). (iii) Adreno-cortico-trophic hormone (ACTH) acts on the cortex part of the adrenal gland to release the adrenal hormone. (iv) Luteinising hormone (LH) is needed for the release of egg cells from the ovary (ovulation) in females, and in males it stimulates the testes to produce sex hormones. Pituitary gland, posterior lobe: (i) Antidiuretic hormone (ADH) or vasopressin affects the renal tubules to reabsorb large quantities of water from the glomerular filtrate. (ii) Oxytocin contracts the uterus muscles during childbirth and stimulates the flow of milk from the breasts during lactation. Thyroid gland: (i) Thyroxine increases the metabolism of the body and produces heat in the body, and it promotes growth. (ii) Calcitonin stimulates the transfer of calcium ions from the blood to the bone, where the calcium ions can be used to generate bone tissue, and in this way it maintains blood calcium levels.

Q: 9. Label the different parts of the brain in the following diagram.

Ans: Diagram (in words): The diagram is the book's Fig. 12.5 view of the human brain inside the cranium (skull), cut lengthwise, with the spinal cord leaving it from below, and the leader lines point to its different parts. The large folded upper part is the Cerebrum (forebrain); the small oval part wrapped by the cerebrum is the Thalamus, and just below it lies the Hypothalamus. The small part under the cerebral hemisphere, between the forebrain and the hindbrain, is the Midbrain, and the small round part hanging below the hypothalamus is the Pituitary gland. At the back, the folded round part is the Cerebellum (hindbrain); in front of its lower part is the Pons, and below the pons the posterior part is the Medulla Oblongata, which narrows down into the Spinal cord. In the book's grouping, the forebrain consists of cerebrum, thalamus and hypothalamus, the hindbrain consists of cerebellum, pons and medulla oblongata, and the medulla oblongata, pons and midbrain are collectively called the brain stem.

mcqs.q: In a reflex arc, which neuron carries the impulse from the receptor to the spinal cord?
mcqs.why: A reflex action starts with a sensory neuron present in a receptor, which takes the impulse to the spinal cord. There an associative neuron shifts it to a motor neuron, which carries it to the effector.

mcqs.q: Which condition may be caused by changes in the brain due to genetic reasons, severe head injuries, stroke, brain infections or drug abuse?
mcqs.why: The solved answer lists genetic changes in the brain, severe head injuries, stroke, brain infections and drug abuse as causes of epilepsy. Paralysis is instead a vascular disease of the brain caused by a clot or ruptured vessel.

mcqs.q: Paralysis occurs when a blood clot is stuck in the fine blood vessels of the brain, or when brain blood vessels rupture due to:
mcqs.why: Paralysis is a vascular disease of the brain: a clot blocks fine brain vessels, or vessels rupture due to high blood pressure. The damaged brain part stops working, so the body part it controls stops functioning.

mcqs.q: If the islets of Langerhans secreted insulin but not glucagon, the blood glucose level would:
options: Keep falling, with no way to raise it again
mcqs.why: Insulin decreases blood glucose by metabolising it or converting it into fats, while glucagon raises it again. Without glucagon the balance of the negative feedback mechanism is disturbed and glucose keeps falling.

mcqs.q: The pituitary gland is called the master gland because:
options: It is the largest gland of the body
Its hormones control other endocrine glands
It is present inside the brain stem
mcqs.why: Pituitary hormones such as TSH, ACTH and LH control the thyroid gland, the adrenal cortex and the gonads respectively, so the pituitary regulates the working of other endocrine glands and is called the master gland.

mcqs.q: In nervous coordination, the message is carried by neurons in the form of:
mcqs.why: Nervous coordination is electrical: the message is an electrical nerve impulse carried by neurons from receptors through the brain and spinal cord to muscles and glands, which is why its response is fast.

mcqs.q: Compared with nervous coordination, the response in chemical coordination is:
options: Slower, because hormones are carried by the blood
mcqs.why: In chemical coordination the message is a chemical (hormone) carried by the blood from endocrine glands to body parts, so the response, such as growth or water reabsorption by kidneys, is slower than the electrical nervous response.

mcqs.q: Which ovarian hormone brings about the development of secondary sexual characters in the female, such as development of the breast?
mcqs.why: Oestrogens develop the female secondary sexual characters, for example development of the breast, and also cause release of an egg from the ovary. Progesterone instead prepares the female body for maintaining pregnancy.

mcqs.q: Progesterone, secreted by the ovaries, mainly:
options: Prepares the female body for maintaining the state of pregnancy
Controls the growth of the body
Increases the metabolism of the body
mcqs.why: The solved answer states that progesterone prepares the female body for maintaining the state of pregnancy. Growth is controlled by growth hormone, water reabsorption by ADH, and metabolism mainly by thyroxine.

mcqs.q: Antidiuretic hormone (ADH) from the posterior lobe of the pituitary acts on the renal tubules to:
options: Reabsorb large quantities of water from the glomerular filtrate
Transfer calcium from blood to bone
mcqs.why: ADH (vasopressin) affects the renal tubules to reabsorb large quantities of water from the glomerular filtrate. Transfer of calcium to bone is the work of calcitonin, and contraction of the uterus during childbirth is the work of oxytocin.

lessons.title: Detailed Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Receptor types: photoreceptors (light, eyes), sono-receptors (sound, ears), chemoreceptors (chemicals, tongue and nose), mechanical receptors (pressure, skin).
  • Meninges protect the brain; cerebrospinal fluid in the ventricles cushions the brain and spinal cord.
  • The cerebral hemispheres communicate through the corpus callosum; cortex is grey matter, the layer beneath is white matter.
  • Cerebellum controls balance and coordinates voluntary movements; medulla controls breathing, heart rate and blood pressure.
  • Endocrine glands are ductless and pour hormones directly into the blood to reach target tissues.
  • Hormones regulate reactions rather than initiating new ones, and their secretion is controlled by negative feedback.
  • Rods contain rhodopsin for dim light; cones contain iodopsin and visualise colours.

Solved Exercises

Exercise C: Write detailed answers to the following questions:

Q: 1. Explain the different types of receptors in human beings.

Ans: Receptors are the parts of the body which receive the changes (stimuli) taking place in our environment. The book describes the following types. (1) Photoreceptors, which perceive light, e.g. the eyes; they are also known as visual receptors. (2) Sono-receptors, which perceive sound waves, e.g. the ears. (3) Chemoreceptors, which perceive different chemicals, like the tongue and the nose. (4) Mechanical receptors, which perceive pressure and are mostly found in the skin. There are many other receptors which feel pain, hunger, thirst, pleasure, emotions etc. Of these, the book describes two in detail: the eye, a pair of ball-shaped photoreceptors present in the orbits on the face, whose innermost layer, the retina, contains the photoreceptor cells, rods and cones; and the ear, the sono-receptor which receives sound waves through its external, middle and internal parts, the special hair cells of the organ of Corti in the cochlea being the receptor cells for sound, while the semi-circular canals of the internal ear help in maintaining the balance of the body.

Q: 2. Describe the structure of the human brain.

Ans: Inside the cranium, the brain is covered by three layers of membranes, collectively called meninges, whose function is to protect the brain from harmful substances. The brain contains fluid-filled ventricles, continuous with the central canal of the spinal cord; the fluid within them is called the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), which bathes the neurons of the brain and the spinal cord and cushions against physical and mechanical stresses. The human brain is divided into three parts. (a) Forebrain: this is the largest area of the brain and is most highly developed in humans. Its cerebrum is the largest part of the brain, divided into two halves called cerebral hemispheres, which communicate with each other by means of a large band called the corpus callosum; its outer region, the cerebral cortex, has many folds and convolutions, which increase its surface area, and is made of grey matter (containing cell bodies and non-myelinated axons), while the material beneath the cortex is white matter (containing myelinated axons). The cerebrum receives sensory information, processes it, stores some in memory for future use, directs voluntary movements, and is responsible for intelligence, thinking, reasoning and decision making; the speech centre is also present in the cerebrum, which is unique to human beings. The thalamus is wrapped by the cerebrum and carries sensory information, especially from the eyes and ears and generally from the skin and other internal organs of the body, to the limbic system and cerebrum. The limbic system is located in an arc between the thalamus and cerebrum; it processes responses like hunger, thirst, fear, anger, tranquillity, pleasure and sexual responses, and a portion of it is also important in the formation of memories; the hypothalamus is a part of the limbic system and lies below the thalamus. (b) Midbrain: it is reduced in human beings and is present under the cerebral hemisphere; it controls reflex movements of the eyes and hearing reflexes, and it is a relay centre that connects the forebrain with the hindbrain. (c) Hindbrain: it consists of the cerebellum, which controls the balance of the body and coordinates the voluntary movements of the body, and is also involved in the learning and memory storage for showing different behaviours; the pons, located above the medulla, which controls transitions between sleep and wakefulness and the rate and pattern of breathing; and the medulla oblongata, the posterior part of the brain, which controls automatic functions like breathing, heart rate, circulation of blood, blood pressure, swallowing and vomiting. Medulla oblongata, pons and midbrain connect the rest of the brain to the spinal cord and are collectively called the brain stem.

Q: 3. Write a comprehensive note on chemical coordination in human beings.

Ans: Chemical coordination is done through special chemicals called hormones. In animals, hormones are synthesised in endocrine glands, which are also called ductless glands, because these glands do not have any duct or tube to release their secretion at the site of action or target site; they release their secretion in the blood, which takes it to the tissues or organs where it is required. Hormones are organic compounds produced in the endocrine glands, poured directly into the blood and transported to respective target tissues where they affect; they do not initiate new biochemical reactions but produce their effects by regulating the reactions, and they may either stimulate or inhibit a function. Hormones also control some long-term changes in the body, such as the rate of metabolic activity, rate of growth, and sexual maturity; most hormones are chemically proteins, but some are derivatives of fatty acids, i.e. steroids. The human endocrine system consists of about 20 endocrine glands found in different parts of the body. The pituitary gland, an oval structure attached to the hypothalamus of the brain and generally termed the 'master gland' of the body, secretes growth hormone, thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH), adreno-cortico-trophic hormone (ACTH) and luteinising hormone (LH) from its anterior lobe, and antidiuretic hormone (ADH) and oxytocin from its posterior lobe. The thyroid gland, situated above the larynx, secretes thyroxine, which increases the metabolism of the body and promotes growth, and calcitonin, which maintains blood calcium levels. The pancreas has both exocrine and endocrine activity; as an endocrine gland, its special cells, the islets of Langerhans, secrete insulin, which decreases blood glucose levels, and glucagon, which increases blood glucose levels. A pair of adrenal glands is present, one on top of each kidney; the outer adrenal cortex secretes steroid hormones collectively known as corticosteroids, which control the metabolism of minerals and glucose, while the inner adrenal medulla produces adrenaline and noradrenaline, which are secreted in stressful and emergency situations. The gonads, testes in males and ovaries in females, produce testosterone, and oestrogens and progesterone, which bring about the secondary sexual characters. The secretion of hormones is controlled by the negative feedback mechanism: feedback means the regulation of a process by the output of the process, and when the output of a process slows down or stops the process, it is called negative feedback; for example, when blood glucose rises after a meal, the islets of Langerhans sense the increase and secrete insulin, which reduces the blood glucose level, and when blood with normal glucose level passes through the islets, they stop the secretion of insulin.

Q: 4. Discuss any two disorders of the human eye.

Ans: Sometimes a defect occurs in the working of the eyes; in these disorders the lens of the eye is not able to adjust itself to focus the image on the retina, hence the vision is disturbed.
