(1) Short sightedness or near sightedness, technically known as myopia, is an eye disorder in which a person can see closer objects clearly, but the distant objects are not clearly visible. It is caused by an unusually long eyeball; in short sightedness, light rays do not focus on the surface of the retina, rather the rays focus in front of the retina, and since the light is focussed too early, a blurred image is left on the retina. This problem can be rectified by using concave lenses in glasses or in contact lenses, which ensure that light is focussed onto the retina of the eye so that distant objects do not appear blurry; short-sightedness can also be cured with laser eye surgery, in which a laser is used to reshape the cornea to correct its curve. (2) Long sightedness or farsightedness, technically known as hypermetropia, is a disorder in which a person can see distant objects clearly, but the close objects are not clearly visible. The disorder is caused when the eyeball is too short or the shape of the lens is not round; in long-sightedness, light rays do not focus on the surface of the retina, rather the rays focus behind the retina, and since the light is focussed behind the retina, a blurred image is left on the retina. Long-sightedness is rectified by using a convex lens in glasses or in contact lenses, which ensures that light is focussed onto the retina of the eye so that close objects do not appear blurry; it can also be cured with laser eye surgery, in which a laser is used to reshape the cornea and improve the curve, therefore light is better focussed on the retina.

Q: 5. Describe the causes, symptoms and treatments of paralysis.

Ans: Causes: Paralysis is a vascular disease of the brain. It occurs when either a blood clot is stuck in the fine blood vessels of the brain, or due to the rupturing of blood vessels in the brain due to high blood pressure. This causes damage to that part of the brain; this damage may be permanent or temporary, and as a result the part of the body controlled by the affected part of the brain stops functioning. Symptoms: The patient of paralysis is unable to move the muscles of one side of their body or both sides. Paralysis may also affect the arms or the legs, and sometimes the whole body. Treatments: There is currently no cure for paralysis. The existing treatments only help a person to adapt to this way of life by making them independent; patients are given physiotherapy to improve their muscle weakness, and mobility aids such as wheelchairs and orthoses (braces designed to improve the function of a limb) are also used for patients of paralysis.

Q: 6. Describe the causes, symptoms and treatments of epilepsy.

Ans: Epilepsy (fits or 'mirgi') is a type of functional disorder of the nervous system in which suddenly excessive discharge of nerve impulses takes place from the brain; the abnormal bursts of impulses from neurons which cause the body to behave strangely are called seizures, and people generally call it fits. Causes: Epilepsy may be caused by changes in the brain due to genetic reasons; severe head injuries, stroke, brain infections and drug abuse may also cause epilepsy. Symptoms: Some epilepsy patients simply experience an odd feeling, while others may have convulsions (shaking of the body) or may lose consciousness. The body becomes rigid and stiff, the patient's hands are clenched, and they frequently bite their tongue. Treatments: In the treatment of epilepsy, seizures are controlled; anti-epileptic drugs (AEDs) are used for the treatment of epilepsy. AEDs do not cure epilepsy, but they can prevent seizures from occurring. As emergency aid to a patient who suffered from a seizure, the book's Fig. 12.17 advises: do not put anything in the mouth, note the duration of the seizure, offer help after the seizure ends, put a cushion under the head, loosen tight clothing, and turn the patient on side.

Q: 7. Explain the mechanism of vision by the eyes.

Ans: The light rays coming through the cornea and lens make an image on the retina. The lens, held by suspensory ligaments which are attached with the ciliary body, focuses images from different distances on the retina, and the muscles of the ciliary body control the focussing of the lens; the pupil, the small hole in the centre of the iris, controls the amount of light entering the eye, and the contraction and dilation of the pupil is also a reflex function, as it automatically adjusts to the intensity of light. The photoreceptor cells, i.e. rods and cones of the retina, produce nerve impulses in the neurons present in the retina: rods are used to perceive dim light, they give us the image of the object but not its colours and detail, and they contain a purplish-red pigment called rhodopsin, which the body synthesises from vitamin A; cones are responsible for visualising colours and contain the pigment iodopsin, and at the fovea, the thin portion of the retina where only cones are densely packed, the visual acuity (resolution) is the greatest. The axons of these neurons are part of the optic nerve. The optic nerve carries information in the form of nerve impulses from the retina to the cerebrum of the brain. Here, the impulses are processed to produce a meaningful sensation of shape and colour.

mcqs.q: Photoreceptors are the receptors which perceive:
mcqs.why: Photoreceptors, also called visual receptors, perceive light; the eyes are the example, and their retina contains the photoreceptor cells rods and cones. Sound is perceived by sono-receptors and chemicals by chemoreceptors.

mcqs.q: The tongue and the nose act as chemoreceptors because they perceive:
mcqs.why: Chemoreceptors perceive different chemicals, and the tongue and nose are the given examples. Mechanical receptors in the skin perceive pressure, while eyes perceive light and ears perceive sound.

mcqs.q: The brain is protected inside the cranium by three layers of membranes, collectively called:
mcqs.why: The brain is covered by three membrane layers collectively called meninges, which protect it from harmful substances. The fluid-filled cavities are the ventricles, and their fluid is the cerebrospinal fluid.

mcqs.q: The two cerebral hemispheres communicate with each other by means of a large band called the:
mcqs.why: The cerebrum is divided into two halves called cerebral hemispheres, which communicate with each other through a large band called the corpus callosum. The brain stem is made of medulla, pons and midbrain.

mcqs.q: Which part of the hindbrain controls the balance of the body and coordinates voluntary movements?
mcqs.why: The cerebellum controls the balance of the body and coordinates its voluntary movements, and is also involved in learning and memory storage for behaviours. The medulla controls automatic functions such as breathing and heart rate.

mcqs.q: Breathing, heart rate, blood pressure, swallowing and vomiting are controlled by the:
mcqs.why: The medulla oblongata, the posterior part of the brain, controls automatic functions like breathing, heart rate, circulation of blood, blood pressure, swallowing and vomiting. The cerebrum deals with thought and voluntary action.

mcqs.q: Endocrine glands are called ductless glands because they:
options: Release their secretion directly into the blood
Release their secretion through a duct
mcqs.why: Endocrine glands have no duct or tube to carry their secretion to the target; they release hormones into the blood, which transports them to the tissues or organs where they are required.

mcqs.q: Hormones produce their effects by:
options: Regulating the biochemical reactions, stimulating or inhibiting a function
mcqs.why: Hormones do not initiate new biochemical reactions; they produce their effects by regulating the reactions, and they may either stimulate or inhibit a function. They also control long-term changes such as growth and sexual maturity.

mcqs.q: Short sightedness (myopia) is caused by an unusually long eyeball, so light rays focus:
mcqs.why: In myopia the light is focussed too early, in front of the retina, leaving a blurred image on the retina, so distant objects are not clear while closer objects are seen clearly. Focus behind the retina occurs in hypermetropia.

mcqs.q: Rods of the retina are used to perceive dim light and contain a purplish-red pigment called:
mcqs.why: Rods perceive dim light, give the image of the object but not its colours and detail, and contain the purplish-red pigment rhodopsin, which the body synthesises from vitamin A. Cones contain iodopsin and visualise colours.

lessons.title: Initiating and Planning
lessons.notes_html:
Solved Exercises

Initiating and Planning

Q: 1. Analyse why plants (like sunflower) have a very slow response to stimuli.

Ans: Plants and other organisms (unicellular organisms, fungi etc.) have only chemical coordination; they have no nervous system, no neurons and no sense organs like animals. The book's Tidbit states that the response of chemical coordination is slower than the response of nervous coordination, which works at the speed of electricity. In a plant such as the sunflower, the message is therefore carried only in the form of chemicals, which move slowly from one part of the plant to another through its tissues. Because of this, the plant's response to a stimulus is very slow compared with the quick electrical response of an animal, whose receptors, neurons and effectors act almost at once.

Q: 2. Visualise nervous and hormonal coordination by comparing electrical transmission in wires with the transmission of nerve impulse in neurons and by comparing convection currents in liquids to the hormonal transmission in blood.

Ans: Nervous coordination can be visualised like electrical transmission in wires: just as an electrical signal travels very fast along a wire to a fixed point, a nerve impulse, which is a wave of electrochemical change that travels through neurons, moves at the speed of electricity along a fixed pathway, from the receptor through the coordinator (brain and spinal cord) to a specific effector, so the response is quick and directed to one place. Hormonal coordination can be visualised like convection currents in a liquid: just as convection currents slowly carry heat through the whole liquid, hormones are poured directly into the blood and are transported slowly by the blood to their respective target tissues in different parts of the body. This is why the book states that the response of chemical coordination is slower than the response of nervous coordination, and why hormonal effects are spread out and long-lasting, e.g. growth and the reabsorption of water by the kidneys.

Q: 3. Compare the BGC (blood glucose concentration) of a healthy person with a patient suffering from Diabetes mellitus.

Ans: The book's BGC test table gives the comparison. In a healthy person, the blood glucose after an 8 to 10 hours fast is from 70 to 99 mg/100ml (diagnosis: Normal), and 2 hours after a 75-gram glucose intake it is less than 140 mg/100ml (Normal). The in-between range, fasting from 100 to 125 mg/100ml or from 140 to 200 mg/100ml after glucose intake, is diagnosed as pre-diabetes. A patient suffering from Diabetes mellitus has a fasting BGC of 126 mg/100ml and above, and over 200 mg/100ml 2 hours after a glucose intake. The reason is that if the body fails to produce insulin it leads to diabetes mellitus, so the blood glucose cannot be decreased normally; in diabetes, excess glucose inhibits water reabsorption by the kidneys, producing large amounts of urine, which results in dehydration and can cause kidney damage, and diabetic patients also experience loss of body weight, weakening of muscles and tiredness.

lessons.title: Activities
lessons.notes_html:
Solved Exercises

Activities

Q: 1. Record the difference in quickness of response of the two types of coordination (by asking a student to say a few words in front of the class and observe the change in heartbeat).

Ans: Model answer: When the student says a few words in front of the class, the speaking itself is a voluntary action of nervous coordination and its response is immediate, because in nervous coordination the messages travel as nerve impulses through neurons at the speed of electricity. The change in heartbeat is a chemical (hormonal) effect: in the emotion of speaking in front of the class, hormones such as adrenaline are secreted into the blood and are carried by the blood to the heart, so the heartbeat speeds up only after a short delay, and it also takes time to return to normal. The record therefore shows what the book states: the response of chemical coordination is slower than the response of nervous coordination, which works at the speed of electricity.

Q: 2. Perform an experiment in which a scale held at its lower end between the thumb and index finger is allowed to fall and then recording the time taken to catch it again.

Ans: Model answer: Hold a scale at its lower end between the thumb and index finger of the student, allow it to fall, and record the time taken, or the distance fallen, before the student catches it again. The falling scale is the stimulus: the receptors (the eyes and the skin of the fingers) receive it and send the information through sensory neurons to the coordinator (the brain and spinal cord), and the motor neurons carry the message to the muscles of the thumb and fingers, the effectors, which contract and catch the scale. The very short time taken to catch it shows the quickness of nervous coordination, whose messages travel through neurons at the speed of electricity. Repeating the experiment and recording each time gives the student's reaction time.

Q: 3. Identify different parts and draw a labelled diagram of the longitudinal section of the eye of a sheep or bull.

Ans: Diagram (in words): In the longitudinal section of the eye of a sheep or bull, the same parts are identified as in the book's Fig. 12.9, Structure of the Human Eye. The wall of the eyeball consists of three layers: the outer most white, tough layer is the Sclera, whose anterior part is transparent and bulging and forms the Cornea; the middle layer is the Choroid, which is thick in the anterior part and makes the ciliary body, and its coloured portion in the anterior centre is the Iris, with the small hole, the Pupil, in its centre, and behind the pupil lies the Lens. The third, innermost layer is the Retina, which contains the photoreceptor cells, rods and cones; at the posterior pole of the eye is the yellowish Fovea, and the Optic disk (blind spot) is the spot from where the Optic nerve leaves the eye. The space between the cornea and the lens is the Aqueous chamber, and the space between the lens and the retina is the Vitreous chamber. Figure labels: Sclera, Choroid, Retina, Iris, Lens, Pupil, Cornea, Aqueous chamber, Vitreous chamber, Fovea, Optic disk (blind spot), Optic nerve.

Q: 4. Perform an experiment in which the shin muscle of a frog is made to contract in a Petri dish filled with methylene blue and using 12 V DC current.

Ans: Model answer: Place the shin muscle of a frog in a Petri dish filled with methylene blue and pass a 12 V DC current through it; the muscle is observed to contract. In the body, muscles are effectors, and in nervous coordination they receive the coordinator's message in the form of nerve impulses, which are waves of electrochemical change travelling through neurons. The electric current in this experiment acts in the same way as the electrical nerve impulse, so the muscle responds by contracting, just as it contracts when a motor neuron brings the impulse to it in the living body. The experiment thus shows that in nervous coordination the effectors work on electrical signals, which is why this coordination is fast.

Q: 5. Check the vision of a friend to diagnose whether he/she is suffering from long or short-sightedness.

Ans: Model answer: Ask the friend to look at a distant object and then at a close object, e.g. the writing of a book. If the friend can see closer objects clearly but the distant objects are not clearly visible, he/she is suffering from short sightedness (myopia), which is caused by an unusually long eyeball, in which the light rays focus in front of the retina instead of on its surface. If the friend can see distant objects clearly but the close objects are not clearly visible, he/she is suffering from long sightedness (hypermetropia), which is caused when the eyeball is too short or the shape of the lens is not round, so the light rays focus behind the retina. As the book states, short sightedness is rectified by using concave lenses and long sightedness by using convex lenses.

Q: 6. Perform an experiment in which one student flashes a spotlight into the eye of another and record the time taken for the eye to contract its pupil.

Ans: Model answer: Flash a spotlight into the eye of the student and, at the same moment, start recording the time; observe the pupil and note the time taken for the eye to contract its pupil. The book explains that the pupil is the small hole in the centre of the iris which controls the amount of light entering the eye, and that the contraction and dilation of the pupil is also a reflex function, as it automatically adjusts to the intensity of light. In the strong light of the spotlight, the pupil therefore contracts quickly and involuntarily, to reduce the amount of light entering the eye. The recorded time is the time of this pupil reflex, a reflex action in which the response is produced without conscious willing.

lessons.title: Multiple Choice Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • The axial skeleton (skull, vertebrae, ribs, sternum) lies centrally; the appendicular skeleton is the limbs plus pectoral and pelvic girdles.
  • Skull joints are immoveable (fused); joints between vertebrae are slightly moveable.
  • Calcium phosphate makes bone stronger than cartilage; the main cartilage matrix protein is collagen.
  • Ligaments attach bone to bone at a joint; tendons attach muscle to bone.
  • In osteoporosis bones become weak and brittle; arthritis is inflammation of the joints.
  • Origin is the muscle attachment on the fixed bone; insertion is the attachment on the moving bone.

Solved Exercises

Exercise A: Select the correct answer.

Q: 1. Which of these is a part of the appendicular skeleton?

Options: (a) Ribs (b) Sternum (c) Pectoral girdle (d) Vertebral column

Correct answer: Pectoral girdle

Q: 2. The joints between the skull bones are an example of:

Options: (a) Ball and socket joints (b) Hinge joints (c) Immoveable joints (d) Slightly moveable joints

Correct answer: Immoveable joints

Q: 3. Which type of joint is present between the vertebrae?

Options: (a) Fixed joint (b) Slightly moveable joint (c) Ball-and-socket joint (d) Hinge joint

Correct answer: Slightly moveable joint

Q: 4. Which of the following is not part of the axial skeleton

Options: (a) Sternum (b) Vertebrae (c) Leg bones (d) Skull

Correct answer: Leg bones

Q: 5. Bones are stronger than cartilage due to the presence of:

Options: (a) Collagen fibres (b) Osteocytes (c) Calcium phosphate (d) Lacunae

Correct answer: Calcium phosphate

Q: 6. The main protein in the matrix of cartilage is:

Options: (a) Collagen (b) Osteo-nectin (c) Keratin (d) Actin

Correct answer: Collagen

Q: 7. Which connective tissue attaches two bones at a joint?

Options: (a) Ligament (b) Tendon (c) Cartilage (d) Marrow

Correct answer: Ligament

Q: 8. In which disease do the bones become weak and brittle?

Options: (a) Osteoporosis (b) Osteoarthritis (c) Rheumatoid arthritis (d) Vertebral column

Correct answer: Osteoporosis

Q: 9. The point where the muscle attaches to the fixed bone is called:

Options: (a) Tendon (b) Ligament (c) Insertion (d) Origin

Correct answer: Origin

Q: 10. Arthritis is defined as inflammation in:

Options: (a) Bones (b) Joints (c) Cartilage (d) Muscles

Correct answer: Joints

mcqs.q: 1. Which of these is a part of the appendicular skeleton?
mcqs.why: The appendicular skeleton consists of the bones of the limbs and the pectoral and pelvic girdles. Ribs, sternum and vertebral column belong to the axial skeleton in the centre of the body.

mcqs.q: 2. The joints between the skull bones are an example of:
mcqs.why: In immoveable joints the bones are fused together and allow no movement, as in the joints among the bones of the skull. Hinge and ball-and-socket joints are freely movable joints.

mcqs.q: 3. Which type of joint is present between the vertebrae?
mcqs.why: The joints between the vertebrae allow only little movement, so they are slightly moveable joints. They are not fixed, because the vertebral column can bend a little, and they are not hinge or ball-and-socket joints.

mcqs.q: 4. Which of the following is not part of the axial skeleton
mcqs.why: The axial skeleton is built from the skull, vertebrae, ribs and sternum of the head, neck and chest. Leg bones belong to the appendicular skeleton of the limbs and girdles.

mcqs.q: 5. Bones are stronger than cartilage due to the presence of:
mcqs.why: During mineralisation, calcium phosphate is deposited in the collagen fibres and makes the bones hard and strong. Cartilage lacks this heavy mineral deposit, so it stays softer and more flexible.

mcqs.q: 6. The main protein in the matrix of cartilage is:
mcqs.why: Collagen is the main protein in the matrix of cartilage, and bone mineralisation also deposits calcium phosphate in collagen fibres. Keratin is a skin and hair protein, and actin is a muscle protein.

mcqs.q: 7. Which connective tissue attaches two bones at a joint?
mcqs.why: Ligaments are tough bands of connective tissue which hold the bones at the joints in place, attaching bone to bone. Tendons attach muscles to bones instead.

mcqs.q: 8. In which disease do the bones become weak and brittle?
mcqs.why: In osteoporosis, demineralisation makes the bones soft, weak and fragile, so they bend and break easily, especially in old people and women. The arthritides are diseases of the joints, not of bone strength.

mcqs.q: 9. The point where the muscle attaches to the fixed bone is called:
mcqs.why: The point where a muscle attaches to the fixed bone is the origin, while the point where it attaches to the moving bone is the insertion. When the muscle contracts, it pulls the moving bone at the insertion.

mcqs.q: 10. Arthritis is defined as inflammation in:
mcqs.why: Arthritis is the disorder of the joints where they get inflamed, causing pain, stiffness and swelling. It damages the joints permanently and in later stages can cause complete immobility of the joint.

lessons.title: Short Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Bones are dynamic living tissue: osteocytes, nerves and blood vessels, growth, repair and calcium exchange with blood.
  • Vesalius wrote de Humani Corpris Fabrica in 1543 with 277 illustrations made with Titian.
  • Immovable joints (skull) allow no movement; slightly movable joints (vertebrae, ribs) allow little movement; freely movable joints include hinge (elbow, knee) and ball-and-socket (hip, shoulder).
  • Osteoarthritis: cartilage wears away; rheumatoid arthritis: immune system attacks joints; gouty arthritis: uric acid crystals in joints.
  • Flexors bend a limb (biceps); extensors straighten it (triceps); they work as antagonistic pairs.
  • Bones give shape and support, help movement, protect organs, make blood cells in marrow, and store mineral salts.

Solved Exercises

Exercise B: Write short answers to the following questions.

Q: 1. Why are bones considered as dynamic structures?

Ans: Bones are considered dynamic because the skeleton is a living tissue, not a dead framework. It contains living cells (osteocytes in the bone matrix) and also has nerves and blood vessels, which keep the osteocytes alive. It can grow, adapt to stress and repair itself after injury. Calcium also keeps moving between the bones and the blood (mineralisation and demineralisation), so the bone is constantly changing.

Q: 2. What is the contribution of Vesalius in understanding the human skeleton?

Ans: Andreas Vesalius (1514-1564), born in Brussels and professor of Anatomy at Padua University in Italy, wrote the first major book on human anatomy in 1543, called 'de Humani Corpris Fabrica' (The Fabric of the Human Body). Working with the artist Titian, who produced 277 anatomical illustrations for the book, he explained the different parts of the human skeleton, including the number of bones. He also described the source and position of each muscle and provided information on their respective functions.

Q: 3. Describe the function of three major types of joints and give an example of each.

Ans: Immovable joints: the bones are fused together and do not allow any movement; they hold the bones firmly together, e.g. the joints among the bones of the skull. Slightly movable joints: these allow little movement, e.g. the joints of the vertebral column and ribs. Freely movable joints: these allow free movements; they include hinge joints (elbow and knee) and ball-and-socket joints (hip and shoulder).

Q: 4. How are different types of arthritis caused?

Ans: In osteoarthritis, the most common type, the cartilage at the joint starts to wear away over time, until in extreme cases the bones come into direct bone-on-bone contact; it occurs most often in older people. Rheumatoid arthritis is an autoimmune disease in which the body's immune system attacks healthy joints, which become inflamed and swollen. Gouty arthritis is caused by higher than normal levels of uric acid in the blood and the deposit of large amounts of uric acid in the lining of the joints in the form of crystals.

Q: 5. Differentiate between a skeletal muscle's origin and insertion.

Ans: One end of a skeletal muscle is always attached with some fixed bone while the other end is attached to a moving bone. The point where the muscle attaches to the fixed bone is called the origin. The point where the muscle attaches to the moving bone is called the insertion. When the muscle contracts, it pulls the moving bone at the insertion.

Q: 6. State the functions of flexors and extensors.

Ans: Flexors and extensors are the opposing (antagonistic) muscles of a pair. A flexor bends a limb: when the biceps contracts, its insertion with the radius bone pulls the bone upward and the lower arm moves upwards, causing flexion, so the biceps is the flexor. An extensor straightens the limb: when the triceps contracts, its insertion with the ulna bone pulls the bone back, the biceps relaxes, and the lower arm extends, so the triceps is the extensor.

Q: 7. What are ligaments and tendons? What function do they perform?

Ans: Ligaments are tough bands of connective tissue which hold the bones at the joints in place. Tendons are tough connective tissues which attach muscles to bones. When a muscle contracts, the tendon exerts a pulling force on the attached bone, and as a result the bone is pulled towards the muscle, producing movement.

Q: 8. State five functions of bones.

Ans: The five functions given in the book are: (1) bones form the hard structure of the body and give it a definite shape and support; (2) skeletal muscles are attached to the bones, so the bones help in movement; (3) bones protect delicate organs, e.g. the skull protects the brain, the vertebral column protects the spinal cord and the rib cage protects the lungs and heart; (4) bone marrow produces the red blood cells, platelets and white blood cells; (5) bones store mineral salts (calcium, potassium, phosphorus), which is why the bones remain hard and strong.

mcqs.q: Bones are considered dynamic structures because the skeleton contains living cells called:
mcqs.why: The skeleton is living tissue containing living osteocytes in the bone matrix, kept alive by nerves and blood vessels. Bones can grow, adapt to stress, repair after injury, and exchange calcium with the blood.

mcqs.q: Andreas Vesalius published the first major book on human anatomy, de Humani Corpris Fabrica, in the year:
mcqs.why: Vesalius (1514-1564), professor of Anatomy at Padua University, wrote de Humani Corpris Fabrica in 1543, with 277 anatomical illustrations produced with the artist Titian, explaining the parts and number of bones of the skeleton.

mcqs.q: The joints among the bones of the skull, in which the bones are fused and allow no movement, are:
mcqs.why: Immovable joints have bones fused together, allowing no movement, and they hold the bones firmly together; the joints among the skull bones are the standard example. Hinge and ball-and-socket joints are freely movable.

mcqs.q: Which joints allow only little movement, as in the vertebral column and ribs?
mcqs.why: Slightly movable joints allow little movement, for example the joints of the vertebral column and ribs. Immovable joints allow no movement at all, while hinge and ball-and-socket joints allow free movement.

mcqs.q: The elbow and the knee are examples of which freely movable joint?
mcqs.why: Freely movable joints include hinge joints at the elbow and knee, and ball-and-socket joints at the hip and shoulder. Hinge joints bend and straighten the limb like a door hinge.

mcqs.q: In osteoarthritis, the most common type of arthritis, the joint problem develops because:
options: Uric acid crystals deposit in the joints
The immune system attacks healthy joints
The cartilage at the joint wears away over time
Calcium leaves the bones for the blood
mcqs.why: In osteoarthritis the cartilage at the joint starts to wear away over time, until in extreme cases the bones come into direct bone-on-bone contact; it occurs most often in older people. Uric acid crystals cause gouty arthritis instead.

mcqs.q: Rheumatoid arthritis is an autoimmune disease in which:
options: The body immune system attacks healthy joints, which become inflamed and swollen
Bones lose calcium and become brittle
Uric acid forms crystals in the joints
mcqs.why: In rheumatoid arthritis the immune system attacks healthy joints, which become inflamed and swollen. Wearing away of cartilage describes osteoarthritis, and uric acid crystals describe gouty arthritis.

mcqs.q: Gouty arthritis is caused by higher than normal levels of which substance in the blood, deposited as crystals in the joints?
mcqs.why: Gouty arthritis is caused by higher than normal levels of uric acid in the blood, with large amounts of uric acid deposited in the lining of the joints in the form of crystals, causing inflammation.

mcqs.q: The insertion of a skeletal muscle is the point where the muscle attaches to:
mcqs.why: One end of a skeletal muscle attaches to a fixed bone at the origin, and the other end attaches to a moving bone at the insertion. When the muscle contracts, it pulls the moving bone at the insertion.

mcqs.q: When the biceps contracts and pulls the radius upward so the lower arm bends, the biceps acts as a:
mcqs.why: A flexor bends a limb: when the biceps contracts, its insertion with the radius pulls the bone upward and the lower arm moves up in flexion. The triceps is the opposing extensor that straightens the arm.

lessons.title: Detailed Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Locomotion is due to contraction of skeletal muscles attached to bones by tendons; muscles pull only, so they work in antagonistic pairs.
  • Axial skeleton has 80 bones; appendicular skeleton has 126 bones of limbs and girdles.
  • Skull has 22 bones (cranium 8 plus face 14); vertebral column has 33 vertebrae: 7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 9 pelvic.
  • There are 12 pairs of ribs; 10 pairs join the sternum and the lower 2 pairs are floating ribs.
  • Hinge joints work at elbow and knee; ball-and-socket joints at hip and shoulder allow movement in every direction.
  • Osteoporosis follows calcium loss from bones; arthritis treatment uses analgesics, NSAIDs and joint replacement (arthroplasty).

Solved Exercises

Exercise C: Write detailed answers to the following questions:

Q: 1. Describe the role of the skeleton and muscles in locomotion.

Ans: Locomotion (free movement) is a life characteristic of all living animals, and for all types of movements the skeleton plays a basic role. The skeleton is the framework of hard structures that provides physical support and protection; the human skeleton is an endoskeleton made of living tissues. Skeletal muscles are attached to the bones of the skeleton by tough connective tissue called tendons, and their contractions help us in movement and locomotion; locomotion and all other types of movements are due to the contraction of muscles of the body. Muscles can only pull bones, they cannot push bones, so most skeletal muscles are arranged in antagonistic pairs: when one muscle of the pair contracts to exert a pull, the other relaxes or elongates to allow the effect of the contraction. Joints, formed at the meeting point of two or more bones, allow the bones to move to different extents and give mobility to the body. The human body has over 500 muscles responsible for all types of movement. For example, at the elbow the biceps (flexor) and triceps (extensor) work as an opposing pair to flex and extend the lower arm.

Q: 2. Differentiate between the axial and appendicular skeleton and describe the major components of both.

Ans: The axial skeleton lies in the centre of the body around which the whole body is built; it consists of 80 bones of the head, neck and chest. The appendicular skeleton consists of 126 bones of the limbs and the pectoral and pelvic girdles. Axial components: (1) Skull, made of the cranium (8 bones, which protect the brain) and 14 facial bones. (2) Vertebral column, extending from the skull to the pelvis, with 33 vertebrae: 7 cervical (neck), 12 thoracic (chest), 5 lumbar (back) and 9 pelvic vertebrae forming the sacrum (fusion of anterior five) and coccyx (fusion of four posterior). (3) Chest bone and ribs: 12 pairs of ribs attached dorsally to the vertebrae, 10 pairs connecting anteriorly with the sternum, the lower 2 pairs being floating ribs; the rib cage protects the heart and lungs. (4) Middle ear bones: three ossicles in each ear, the malleus, incus and stapes. (5) Neck bone: the single hyoid bone. Appendicular components: (1) Pectoral girdle, 4 bones (2 on each side), attaching the forelimbs to the vertebral column. (2) Forelimbs: arms contain 6 bones (3 in each arm) and hands 54 bones (27 in each hand). (3) Pelvic girdle, 2 bones, attaching the hind limbs to the vertebral column. (4) Hind limbs: legs contain 8 bones (4 in each leg) and both feet 52 bones (26 in each foot). Diagram (in words): Fig. 13.1 Human Skeleton labels, on the axial side, Cranium (08 bones) and Face (14 bones) together as Skull (22 bones), Middle ear Ossicles (03 bones in each), Neck bone (01 bone), Chest bone (01 bone), Rib cage (24 bones) and Vertebral column (26 bones); on the appendicular side, Pectoral girdle (04 bones) 02 on each side, Arms (06 bones) 03 on each side, Pelvic girdle (02 bones) 01 on each side, Hands (54 bones) 27 on each side, Legs (08 bones) 04 on each side and Feet (52 bones) 26 on each side.

Q: 3. Discuss different types of joints and their role.

Ans: Joints are formed at the meeting point of two or more bones. They keep our bones together by holding them with each other, and they also allow the bones to move to different extents and give mobility to our body. On the basis of the extent of movement they allow, joints are classified into three categories. (a) Immovable joints: the bones are fused together and do not allow any movement, e.g. the joints present among the bones of the skull. (b) Slightly movable joints: these allow little movement, e.g. joints of the vertebral column, ribs etc. (c) Freely movable joints: these allow free movements, and have two major types: (i) hinge joints, which allow movements only in two directions and are present at the elbow and the knee; (ii) ball-and-socket joints, which allow movement in all directions (up, down, forward and backward), e.g. the hip joint and shoulder joint. At a joint, ligaments hold the bones in place, cartilage covers the ends of the bones and reduces friction, and synovial fluid is present between the bones (Fig. 13.8 Structure of a joint, labelled: Muscle, Bone, Cartilage, Synovial fluid, Ligament, Tendon). Diagram (in words): Fig. 13.6 shows a Fixed or immovable joint between the Cranium bones of the skull, a Slightly movable joint between the Vertebrae, and a Freely movable joint where the Femur fits into the Pelvis.

Q: 4. Write the causes and treatments of arthritis and osteoporosis.

Ans: Osteoporosis: Bones are formed by mineralisation, in which calcium phosphate is deposited in collagen fibres to make the bones hard, and this calcium is absorbed from the food we eat. When a person is not taking sufficient calcium in their daily diet, their bones start becoming weak; demineralisation (calcium moving from the bones to the blood to maintain its level) makes the bones soft and fragile, so they start bending and can be broken easily. This disorder is osteoporosis, and it occurs especially in old people and in women. The book's remedy follows from its cause: taking sufficient calcium in the daily diet, so that the bones do not lose calcium and become weak. Arthritis: Arthritis is the disorder of the joints where they get inflamed; it is a degenerative disease that damages the joints permanently, causing pain, stiffness and swelling, thickening of the membranes lining the joints, decreased fluid production and increased friction, and in later stages complete immobility and permanently swollen, de-shaped joints. Its types are caused differently: osteoarthritis by cartilage wearing away (usually in weight-bearing joints of older people), rheumatoid arthritis by the immune system attacking healthy joints, and gouty arthritis by excess uric acid deposited as crystals in the joints. Treatment of arthritis focuses on relieving symptoms and improving joint function: analgesics (pain killers) and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) are used, and surgery can also be performed in which the affected joint is replaced with an artificial joint (arthroplasty).

mcqs.q: Skeletal muscles can move bones only by pulling them, because muscles:
options: Can push but cannot pull bones
Can only pull bones and cannot push them
Work without any attachment to bones
mcqs.why: Muscles can only pull bones, they cannot push them, so skeletal muscles are arranged in antagonistic pairs: when one contracts to exert a pull, the other relaxes or elongates to allow the movement.

mcqs.q: The axial skeleton, lying in the centre of the body, consists of how many bones of the head, neck and chest?
mcqs.why: The axial skeleton consists of 80 bones of the head, neck and chest, around which the whole body is built. The appendicular skeleton consists of 126 bones of the limbs and girdles.

mcqs.q: The appendicular skeleton consists of how many bones of the limbs and the pectoral and pelvic girdles?
mcqs.why: The appendicular skeleton consists of 126 bones of the limbs and the pectoral and pelvic girdles. The axial skeleton has 80 bones; 54 is the number of bones in both hands and 22 in the skull.

mcqs.q: The skull is made of the cranium and the facial bones, with bone numbers:
mcqs.why: The skull is made of the cranium of 8 bones, which protect the brain, and 14 facial bones, making 22 bones in total (8 + 14 = 22). The first option reverses the two numbers.

mcqs.q: The vertebral column contains 7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar and 9 pelvic vertebrae, giving a total of:
mcqs.why: Adding the groups from the solved answer: 7 cervical + 12 thoracic + 5 lumbar + 9 pelvic = 33 vertebrae in total, extending from the skull to the pelvis. The 9 pelvic vertebrae form the sacrum (5 fused) and coccyx (4 fused).

mcqs.q: Of the 12 pairs of ribs, the lower pairs that do not connect anteriorly with the sternum, called floating ribs, number:
mcqs.why: There are 12 pairs of ribs attached dorsally to the vertebrae; 10 pairs connect anteriorly with the sternum, while the lower 2 pairs are the floating ribs. Together the ribs and sternum form the rib cage protecting the heart and lungs.

mcqs.q: Ball-and-socket joints, such as the hip and shoulder joints, allow movement:
options: In all directions: up, down, forward and backward
mcqs.why: Ball-and-socket joints allow movement in every direction (up, down, forward and backward), as at the hip and shoulder. Hinge joints at the elbow and knee allow movement in a more limited way.

mcqs.q: At a freely movable joint, friction between the ends of the bones is reduced by:
options: Cartilage covering the ends of the bones
mcqs.why: At a joint, ligaments hold the bones in place, cartilage covers the ends of the bones and reduces friction, and synovial fluid is present between the bones. Tendons attach muscles to bones and do not cover the joint surfaces.

mcqs.q: Osteoporosis develops when demineralisation takes place, which means:
options: Calcium is deposited into collagen fibres
Calcium moves from the bones to the blood, making bones soft and fragile
mcqs.why: When the diet lacks sufficient calcium, demineralisation moves calcium from the bones to the blood to maintain its level, so the bones become soft and fragile, start bending and can break easily. Deposit of calcium phosphate into fibres is mineralisation, the opposite process.

mcqs.q: In arthroplasty, the surgical treatment used for a badly damaged arthritic joint, the affected joint is:
mcqs.why: Treatment of arthritis focuses on relieving symptoms and improving joint function with analgesics and NSAIDs, and surgery can be performed in which the affected joint is replaced with an artificial joint; this operation is called arthroplasty.

lessons.title: Activities
lessons.notes_html:
Solved Exercises

Activities

Q: 1. Identify and draw labelled diagrams of different bones of the axial and appendicular skeleton from real specimen models or charts.

Ans: Diagram (in words): Using Fig. 13.1 Human Skeleton, the axial skeleton is labelled: Cranium (08 bones), Face (14 bones), together Skull (22 bones); Middle ear Ossicles (03 bones in each); Neck bone (01 bone); Chest bone (01 bone); Rib cage (24 bones); Vertebral column (26 bones). The appendicular skeleton is labelled: Pectoral girdle (04 bones), 02 on each side; Arms (06 bones), 03 on each side; Pelvic girdle (02 bones), 01 on each side; Hands (54 bones), 27 on each side; Legs (08 bones), 04 on each side; Feet (52 bones), 26 on each side. On a model or chart, identify each bone in this order: skull at the top, vertebral column down the centre, rib cage and sternum in the chest, then the girdles and the limb bones.

Q: 2. Describe the movement of various human joints through observation of models.

Ans: On models, the three kinds of movement can be observed. At an immovable joint (skull bones) the bones are fused and no movement is possible. At a slightly movable joint (between the vertebrae, and the ribs) only a little movement is possible. At freely movable joints the movement is free: a hinge joint (elbow, knee) moves only in two directions, like a hinge, while a ball-and-socket joint (hip, shoulder) moves in all directions: up, down, forward and backward. Diagram (in words): Fig. 13.7 shows a Hinge Joint at the knee, drawn like a hinge, and a Ball-and-Socket Joint where the round head of one bone fits into the cup-like socket of the pelvis.

Q: 3. Describe the movement of biceps and triceps through presentation of the movement of the elbow.

Ans: Bend the lower arm upwards: this is the flexed state. When the biceps muscle contracts, its insertion with the radius bone pulls the bone upward; at the same time the triceps muscle relaxes and the lower arm moves upwards, causing flexion, so the biceps is the flexor and the triceps the extensor. Now straighten the arm to the hanging (extended) state: when the triceps muscle contracts, its insertion with the ulna bone pulls the bone back, the biceps relaxes, and the lower arm moves down easily, resulting in extension. Diagram (in words): Fig. 13.10 Action of biceps and triceps at the elbow has two arms: the bent arm is labelled Biceps contracts, Triceps relaxes, Flexion; the straight arm is labelled Triceps contracts, Biceps relaxes, Extension.

lessons.title: Science, Technology and Society
lessons.notes_html:
Solved Exercises

Science, Technology and Society

Q: 1. Relate your skeleton and its functioning with daily life.

Ans: In daily life the skeleton works for us in every activity. It forms the hard structure of the body and gives it a definite shape, so we can stand erect and sit. Because skeletal muscles are attached to the bones, we can walk, run, write and lift things. The skull protects the brain, the vertebral column protects the spinal cord, and the lungs and heart are protected in the rib cage during everyday knocks and falls. Bone marrow produces our red blood cells, platelets and white blood cells, and the bones store mineral salts (calcium, potassium, phosphorus) which keep them hard and strong.

Q: 2. Relate the principle of leverage to the action of the elbow joint.

Ans: The elbow is a hinge joint, and the lower arm works as a lever moving at this joint. Muscles can only pull bones, they cannot push them, so the lever is moved by pulls: when the biceps contracts, its tendon pulls at its insertion on the radius bone and the lower arm (the lever) is raised, causing flexion. When the triceps contracts, it pulls at its insertion on the ulna bone and pulls the lever back down, causing extension. The antagonistic pair thus moves the same lever in opposite directions.

Q: 3. State the principles of arthroplasty for the replacement of joints.

Ans: Arthroplasty is a surgery that involves replacing a damaged, worn out or diseased joint with an artificial joint. It is the surgical treatment used when arthritis has damaged a joint permanently: the affected joint is removed and replaced with an artificial joint so that joint function improves and pain is relieved. Adults of any age can be considered for a knee replacement, although most are carried out on people between the ages of 60 and 80. The most common reason for knee replacement surgery is osteoarthritis.

lessons.title: Multiple Choice Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Asexual reproduction uses mitosis and produces identical offspring rapidly and in large numbers, without genetic variation.
  • Hydra reproduces asexually by budding; grafting is an artificial vegetative propagation method.
  • Parthenogenesis is development of a new animal from an unfertilized egg.
  • The embryo sac forms inside the ovule of the flower.
  • Fertilization is the union of male and female gametes; it restores the diploid chromosome number and forms the zygote.
  • External fertilization occurs in fish and amphibians; internal fertilization occurs in mammals.

Solved Exercises

Exercise A: Select the correct answer.

Q: 1. One of the following is not true for asexual reproduction:

Options: (a) Rapid propagation (b) Genetic variations (c) Mitosis (d) Large number of organisms

Correct answer: Genetic variations

Q: 2. A Hydra reproduces asexually by:

Options: (a) Spore formation (b) Multiple fission (c) Budding (d) Binary fission

Correct answer: Budding

Q: 3. One of the following methods is artificial vegetative propagation of plants:

Options: (a) Grafting (b) Spore formation (c) Budding (d) Binary fission

Correct answer: Grafting

Q: 4. In parthenogenesis, a new animal develops from:

Options: (a) Sperm (b) Fertilized egg (c) Unfertilized egg (d) Common body cell

Correct answer: Unfertilized egg

Q: 5. In a flower, the embryo sac is formed inside the:

Options: (a) Anther (b) Filament (c) Ovule (d) Style

Correct answer: Ovule

Q: 6. The union of male and female gametes is known as:

Options: (a) Fertilization (b) Oogenesis (c) Spermatogenesis (d) Gametogenesis

Correct answer: Fertilization

Q: 7. All multicellular animals develop from a single cell, called:

Options: (a) Egg (b) Sperm (c) Zygote (d) Blood cell

Correct answer: Zygote

Q: 8. Which of the following restores diploid number of chromosomes?

Options: (a) Ovulation (b) Oogenesis (c) Fertilization (d) Spermatogenesis

Correct answer: Fertilization

Q: 9. In which of the following animals does external fertilization occur?

Options: (a) Fish and amphibians (b) Reptiles (c) Birds (d) Mammals

Correct answer: Fish and amphibians

Q: 10. Internal fertilization occurs in:

Options: (a) Fish (b) Amphibians (c) Aquatic animals (d) Mammals

Correct answer: Mammals

mcqs.q: 1. One of the following is not true for asexual reproduction:
mcqs.why: Asexual reproduction involves mitosis only, gives rapid propagation and large numbers of genetically identical offspring, so genetic variation is the feature that does NOT belong to it.

mcqs.q: 2. A Hydra reproduces asexually by:
mcqs.why: In Hydra a small outgrowth or bud develops on the parent body, grows, and then separates to live as a new individual, which is asexual reproduction by budding.

mcqs.q: 3. One of the following methods is artificial vegetative propagation of plants:
mcqs.why: In grafting, done by man, the branch of a desired variety is attached onto the stem of another plant so it grows and bears better quality fruit; it is an artificial vegetative method.

mcqs.q: 4. In parthenogenesis, a new animal develops from:
mcqs.why: Parthenogenesis is development of a new animal directly from an egg that has not been fertilized by any sperm, so no zygote is formed in this process.

mcqs.q: 5. In a flower, the embryo sac is formed inside the:
mcqs.why: The ovule (megasporangium) inside the ovary contains the megaspore mother cell, and the surviving megaspore develops into the embryo sac, the female gametophyte.

mcqs.q: 6. The union of male and female gametes is known as:
mcqs.why: Fertilization is the fusion of a male gamete (sperm) with a female gamete (egg), and this union produces the diploid zygote from which the new individual develops.

mcqs.q: 7. All multicellular animals develop from a single cell, called:
mcqs.why: Every multicellular animal begins life as one single cell, the zygote, formed by the fusion of sperm and egg, and this zygote divides repeatedly to form the whole body.

mcqs.q: 8. Which of the following restores diploid number of chromosomes?
mcqs.why: Gametes formed by meiosis are haploid (n); at fertilization the haploid sperm and haploid egg fuse, so the zygote again has the diploid (2n) number of chromosomes.

mcqs.q: 9. In which of the following animals does external fertilization occur?
mcqs.why: Fish and amphibians release their gametes into the surrounding water, where the sperm and egg fuse outside the body, which is external fertilization.

mcqs.q: 10. Internal fertilization occurs in:
mcqs.why: In mammals the egg stays inside the female reproductive duct and the sperm fertilizes it inside the body, which is internal fertilization, unlike fish and amphibians.

lessons.title: Short Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Vegetative methods preserve the good quality of a useful parent plant, so grafting and cloning give better yield.
  • Internal fertilization gives better chances of gamete fusion than external fertilization in water.
  • Population planning controls rapid population growth; Pakistan had nearly 208 million people in the 2017 census.
  • Cross-pollination, not self-pollination, brings more variations because gametes of two parents fuse.
  • HIV spreads through body fluids, infected needles and infected blood; antiretroviral drugs hinder its growth but there is no cure.
  • A flower has four whorls: calyx (sepals), corolla (petals), androecium (stamens) and gynoecium (carpels).
  • Seeds need water to soften the seed coat and activate enzymes, and oxygen for cellular respiration.

Solved Exercises

Exercise B: Write short answers to the following questions.

Q: 1. How can vegetative methods of reproduction, be used to achieve better yield?

Ans: Vegetative methods give better yield because the new plants are exact copies of a useful parent plant, so its good quality is preserved. In grafting, the branch of a desired variety is attached on to the stem of an ordinary plant, and the grafted branch grows and bears fruits of better quality; grafting is used to get better quality and quantity of fruits in almost all fruit trees. Cloning makes identical copies of useful plants, which is very helpful in horticulture where we want to preserve the quality of the yield, and it also helps to increase agricultural output. Cutting is a convenient and inexpensive method of propagation, so large numbers of good plants can be raised cheaply.

Q: 2. Differentiate between internal and external fertilization. Which type of fertilization will ensure better chances of fusion of gametes?

Ans: In external fertilization, both the male and female animals release their gametes into their surroundings, usually water, and fusion of gametes takes place outside the body in water; the young ones also develop outside the mother's body, as in fish and amphibians. Because there are more chances of the loss of gametes, both animals release gametes in great numbers. In internal fertilization, the egg (ovum) of the female is not released out of the body; it stays in the reproductive duct of the female and the sperm of the male fertilizes the egg inside the body, as in many land animals. Internal fertilization ensures better chances of fusion of gametes, because the gametes meet inside the protected reproductive duct instead of being scattered and lost in water.

Q: 3. What is population planning? Why is it important?

Ans: Population planning means controlling the rapid growth of population through an effective family planning program, changing social attitudes and improving the status of women. It is important because Pakistan has one of the world's highest population growth rates (about 2.4% annually; the 2017 census counted nearly 208 million people). Rapid population growth puts great pressure on agricultural land and hinders prospects of economic and social development. A growing population needs job opportunities and a stable source of income, and producing too many children places poor households under stress due to shortage of resources, so children grow up malnourished and often without access to effective education and healthcare. Population planning is therefore essential to raise the living standards and avoid the serious problem of rapid population growth.

Q: 4. How does self-pollination bring more variations in plants?

Ans: As printed, this question names self-pollination, but according to the book's own text self-pollination does not bring more variations. The book defines self-pollination as pollination that involves just one flower, or flowers on the same plant, so both gametes come from the same plant and the offspring get a blend of the characteristics of essentially one parent only. It is cross-pollination — pollination that involves two flowers of different plants of the same species — that brings pollen from a different plant, so at fertilization the gametes of two different parents fuse and the offspring show a blend of characteristics from both parents. More variations in plants therefore come from cross-pollination, not from self-pollination.

Q: 5. How can the spread of HIV be controlled? What is the role of the community and NGOs in the control of AIDS?

Ans: HIV passes from an infected person to a healthy person through body fluids as a result of engaging in sexual activity, and it can also be transmitted through the use of infected needles or transfusion of infected blood, so its spread is controlled by avoiding these routes; the book's Tidbit adds that practicing Islamic Teaching is the only best remedy in controlling AIDS. There is no cure for HIV or AIDS, and the medications usually include antiretroviral drugs that are taken to hinder the growth of HIV. The National AIDS Control Programme and its provincial units educate common people as well as parliamentarians, media personnel, educationists and religious leaders, and organise events like World AIDS Day to raise awareness. Many NGOs coordinate HIV/AIDS prevention and control activities in all the provinces of Pakistan and are active in educating people and supporting HIV/AIDS patients, although they are reaching less than 5 percent of the vulnerable population.

Q: 6. Name the four whorls present in a flower and also describe the components of each whorl.

Ans: The parts of a flower are present on the swollen tip called the receptacle, in the form of four concentric whorls, or rings. (1) Calyx: the outermost whorl, made of sepals, which are usually green and protect the inner parts of a developing flower before it opens. (2) Corolla: the next whorl, made of petals; most flowers have coloured petals. (3) Androecium: the third whorl, which contains the male reproductive structures called stamens; each stamen consists of an anther and a filament — the anther contains pollen sacs (microsporangia), which produce microspores, and the stalk-like filament supports the anther. (4) Gynoecium: the innermost whorl, which contains the female reproductive structures called carpels; the enlarged base of a carpel is the ovary, the style is stalk-like, its tip is called the stigma, and inside the ovary there are one or many ovules (megasporangia), which produce megaspores.

Q: 7. How are wind-pollinated flowers different from insect-pollinated flowers?

Ans: Insect-pollinated flowers attract and use insects, bats, birds or other animals to transfer pollen from one flower to the other. They have brightly coloured and large petals to attract insects, fragrance which attracts insects, and nectar, a solution of sugars which is a food source for many insects; their pollens are sticky, which stick to the legs of insects visiting the flowers, and their stigmas are sticky or shaped in a way that facilitates the transfer of pollen grains — examples are Bougainvillea, Rose, Sunflower and Orchids. Wind-pollinated flowers, in contrast, lack scent or fragrance and do not produce nectar. Their pollens are small, smooth and easily removable from the anther, there are wings on the pollen which increase buoyancy, the stigmas are feathery to catch pollen from the wind, the anthers are large and borne on long stalks, and pollens are produced in large numbers to compensate for excessive losses — examples are conifers, grasses, cereals, poplar, oak and walnut.

Q: 8. Why do seeds need water and oxygen for germination?

Ans: Seeds need water because germination starts with the absorption of water through the micropyle. Water softens the seed coat and makes it burst, and it also helps to activate enzymes that digest the food of seeds and make it available to the growing embryo. Seeds need oxygen because the cells of the seed embryo use oxygen for cellular respiration so that they can get energy from stored food. Without this energy the embryo cannot become active and grow into a seedling.

Q: 9. Label the following diagram of a flower.

Ans: Diagram (in words): The diagram is Fig. 14.12, Parts of a flower. At the centre stands the carpel, made of the stigma at the tip, the stalk-like style below it, and the enlarged ovary at the base, with the ovules inside the ovary. On either side of the carpel stand the stamens, each made of an anther at the top, containing the pollen sacs, supported on a stalk-like filament. Around these are the large coloured petals, and below them the green sepals. All the parts of the flower sit on the swollen tip at the base, the receptacle. The leader lines in the exercise diagram therefore read: Stigma, Anther, Petal, Style, Filament, Ovary (with Ovules inside it), Sepal and Receptacle.

Q: 10. Label the following diagram of the female reproductive system of a rabbit.

Ans: Diagram (in words): The diagram is Fig. 14.26, The Female Reproductive System of a Rabbit. It is Y-shaped. At the top of each arm is a small blue ovary, the gonad in which the egg is formed inside a follicle. Next to each ovary opens an oviduct (fallopian tube). Each oviduct opens into a part of the uterus, so the two long arms of the Y are the horns of uterus. Each horn of uterus opens in a narrow portion called the cervix (plural: cervixes in the text; the figure labels them Cervices). Both cervixes open into a single canal at the base of the Y, called the birth canal or vagina. The leader lines in the exercise diagram therefore read: Ovary, Oviduct, Horns of uterus, Cervixes and Birth canal.

lessons.title: Detailed Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Alternation of generations: the diploid sporophyte plant body alternates with the haploid gametophyte (pollen grain and embryo sac).
  • Double fertilisation: one sperm forms the zygote with the egg, the second forms the triploid endosperm with the fusion nucleus.
  • Vegetative propagation uses leaves (Bryophyllum), stems (stolon, rhizome, bulb, corm, tuber) and roots (suckers).
  • Gametogenesis involves meiosis: spermatogenesis makes four spermatids per primary spermatocyte; oogenesis gives one egg with polar bodies.
  • After fertilisation the ovule becomes the seed and the ovary becomes the fruit.
  • Germination needs water, oxygen and a suitable temperature (5-30 degrees C); epigeal lifts cotyledons up, hypogeal leaves them below ground.

Solved Exercises

Exercise C: Write detailed answers to the following questions:

Q: 1. Describe the alternation of generation in a flowering plant.

Ans: In the life cycle of the major groups of plants, two different stages or generations are involved: the sporophyte (spore producing) generation and the gametophyte (gamete producing) generation. These two generations alternate with each other, i.e. the sporophyte develops into gametophyte and vice versa; this type of life cycle is called alternation of generation. The complete body of a flowering plant represents the sporophyte generation, which is diploid (2n). It produces haploid (n) spores by meiosis, and the spores develop into the haploid gametophyte generation. Gametophytes develop within the flowers of the plant. The female gametophyte or embryo sac develops from the megaspore: the ovule (megasporangium) contains a diploid megaspore mother cell, which undergoes meiosis and produces four haploid megaspores; one haploid megaspore survives and divides by mitosis to make eight haploid nuclei, two nuclei migrate to the centre and fuse to form a fusion nucleus, and one nucleus out of the remaining six forms the egg cell, so the embryo sac contains seven cells — the egg, the five non-functional cells, and the fusion nucleus. The male gametophyte or pollen grain develops from the microspore: each microspore mother cell in the pollen sacs (microsporangia) of the anther undergoes meiosis and produces four haploid microspores, and a microspore undergoes mitosis to give the two-celled pollen grain, with a tube cell and a generative cell. The gametophyte generation produces haploid gametes by mitosis. After pollination, the generative cell forms two sperms, and in double fertilisation one sperm fuses with the egg to form a diploid zygote while the second sperm fuses with the fusion nucleus to produce a triploid (3n) nucleus, which develops into the endosperm. The haploid gametes thus fuse to form a diploid zygote, which develops into an embryo inside the seed, and when the seed germinates the embryo develops into a new plant — the next sporophyte stage — so the two generations keep alternating.

Q: 2. Explain the different plant structures modified for vegetative propagation.

Ans: Vegetative propagation is a type of asexual reproduction in which a plant produces a new generation by using its vegetative parts i.e. stems, leaves and roots. Through leaves: in plants such as Bryophyllum, the leaves have buds at their margins; when a leaf falls on the ground, the buds form tiny shoots, and when the shoots break off from the original leaf, they fall on the ground and develop roots. Through stem: many plants use their specialised stems to develop a new plant. The strawberry plant reproduces by its above ground horizontal stem called stolon, which produces leaves and roots at its nodes, and a new plantlet can grow from each node. Ferns and ginger reproduce from the rhizome, a horizontal underground stem capable of producing the shoot and root systems of a new plant. Tulips, onions and lilies reproduce through bulbs — underground buds that have fleshy leaves extending from them; bulbs are food storage units, they contain several buds near the node, and bulbs divide naturally to produce new plants. Colocasia and garlic reproduce through corms, which resemble a bulb but do not have fleshy leaves; branches of the corm stem produce new, miniature corms known as cormels. The potato plant reproduces by an underground, swollen, fleshy stem called the tuber; above each small leaf on the tuber is a well-developed axillary bud, commonly called an eye, and eyes can grow into new potato plants. Through root: red raspberries and many other shrubs reproduce through their specialised roots; the root can give rise to a shoot, and these new shoots are called root sprouts or 'suckers', which, if detached from the original plant, can grow into independent plants.

Q: 3. Explain gametogenesis.

Ans: In animals, sex cells or gametes are produced in special organs called gonads (testes in males and ovaries in females), and the process of producing new generations in which the male and female animals make gametes in their gonads is called gametogenesis. The formation of gametes involves meiosis, which results in a reduction of the number of chromosomes in gametes to haploid (n) as compared to the diploid (2n) number in other body cells. The formation of male gametes or sperms is called spermatogenesis, while the formation of female gamete or ovum is called oogenesis. Spermatogenesis: in the testes, there are many diploid gametes mother cells called primary spermatocytes; each primary spermatocyte divides by meiosis and makes four haploid (n) cells called spermatids, and each spermatid develops into a motile sperm (in Fig. 14.23 the sequence is shown as Spermatogonium — Growth — Primary spermatocyte — Meiosis I — Secondary spermatocyte — Meiosis II — Spermatids — Differentiation — Sperms). Oogenesis: in the follicle of the ovary, there are diploid gametes mother cells called primary oocytes, which divide by meiosis; as a result of the first meiotic division, two haploid cells are produced — the larger cell is called the secondary oocyte while the smaller cell is called the first polar body. In meiosis II, the secondary oocyte produces two haploid cells i.e. a second polar body and an egg (shown in Fig. 14.23 as Oogonium — Primary oocyte — Secondary oocyte and First polar body — Ootid and Second polar body — Ovum). The male gametes then join with the female gamete to form a zygote, which develops into a new individual.

Q: 4. How are seeds produced? What is the structure of a seed?

Ans: Seeds are produced as a result of sexual reproduction in flowering plants. For fertilisation of the egg, the pollen grains are transferred from the anther to the stigma of the flower; this is called pollination. When a pollen grain reaches the stigma, its tube cell forms a pollen tube that grows through the stigma and the style, reaches the ovary and enters the ovule through a small opening called the micropyle. The generative cell of the pollen grain forms two sperms, which enter the embryo sac to reach the egg. One sperm fuses with the egg and forms a diploid zygote, which develops into an embryo; the second sperm fuses with the fusion nucleus and produces a triploid (3n) nucleus, which develops into a tissue called the endosperm, which provides nourishment to the embryo — this double fertilisation is a unique characteristic of flowering plants. After fertilisation, the ovule is said to be matured and is now called the seed, and the ovary changes into fruit. Structure of a seed: a seed (mature ovule) is a miniature plant with a protective cover. The seed coat, or testa, is the outer covering of the seed; it is black or brown in colour and protects the embryo (in some seeds, e.g. peanut, the seed coat is very thin, while in coconut it is thick and hard). On one end of the seed coat is a small scar, the hilum, which indicates the place of attachment of the seed in the fruit, and near the hilum is the micropyle, a minute pore through which the seed absorbs water at the time of germination. Beneath the seed coat is the embryo, which consists of the cotyledons (one leaf-like cotyledon in a monocot seed and two large, fleshy cotyledons in a dicot seed), the plumule — a minute bud at the upper end of the hypocotyl which gives rise to the future stem — and the radicle, the lower part of the hypocotyl, which gives rise to the future root; the portion between the plumule and the cotyledons is called the epicotyl and the portion between the cotyledons and the radicle is called the hypocotyl. The endosperm is a tissue formed from the endosperm nucleus which stores nutrients; dicot seeds have no endosperm while monocot seeds have endosperm, and in monocot seeds the cotyledon absorbs nutrients from the endosperm and transfers them to the embryo. Diagram (in words): Fig. 14.18 shows a dicot (bean) seed split into two halves, labelled Epicotyl, Plumule, Hypocotyl, Radicle, Cotyledons and Seed coat, and a monocot (maize) seed, labelled Cotyledon, Plumule and Seed coat.

Q: 5. Write a comprehensive note on seed germination and its types.

Ans: The development of the embryo of a seed into a seedling is called seed germination. In the dry seed the embryo is alive but inactive; when it is placed in the soil under suitable conditions, the embryo becomes active and grows into a seedling. Germination of the seed starts with the absorption of water through the micropyle. This is followed by the emergence of the radicle, which forms the first root; after the radicle breaks the seed coat, the plumule begins to grow to form a shoot. Conditions necessary for germination: viable or living seeds should have sufficient food for germination, and the environmental conditions must also be in place — (1) Water: seeds absorb water through the micropyle; water softens the seed coat and makes it burst, and helps to activate enzymes that digest the food of seeds and make it available to the growing embryo. (2) Oxygen: the cells of the seed embryo use oxygen for cellular respiration so that they can get energy from stored food. (3) Suitable temperature: germination of seeds occurs over a wide range of temperature between 5°C to 30°C, and a suitable temperature is necessary for the enzymes to function properly. Types of germination (on the basis of the growth of the plumule there are two types): In epigeal germination, the hypocotyl elongates and it forces cotyledons to come above the ground — the Key Points add that the hypocotyl curves and then straightens, due to which the cotyledons are pulled up into the air — and the seed coat also emerges from the soil; seeds of melons, cucumber and beans show epigeal germination. In hypogeal germination, the epicotyl elongates and the cotyledons remain below the surface of the ground, e.g. maize grain, pea etc.

mcqs.q: In alternation of generations, the complete body of a flowering plant represents which generation?
mcqs.why: The complete body of a flowering plant is the sporophyte generation, which is diploid (2n); it produces haploid spores by meiosis, and those spores develop into the gametophyte generation.

mcqs.q: How many cells does the mature embryo sac contain, as described in this unit?
options: Seven cells: the egg, five non-functional cells and the fusion nucleus
Two cells: the egg and the fusion nucleus
mcqs.why: One surviving megaspore divides by mitosis to make eight haploid nuclei; two fuse in the centre as the fusion nucleus and one forms the egg, so the embryo sac contains seven cells in total.

mcqs.q: In double fertilisation, the second sperm fuses with the fusion nucleus to produce:
options: A triploid (3n) nucleus that develops into the endosperm
mcqs.why: One sperm fuses with the egg to form the diploid zygote, while the second sperm fuses with the fusion nucleus (2n) to produce a triploid (3n) nucleus, which develops into the endosperm.

mcqs.q: Bryophyllum reproduces vegetatively through its:
options: Leaves, which bear buds at their margins that form tiny shoots
mcqs.why: In Bryophyllum the leaves have buds at their margins; when a leaf falls on the ground the buds form tiny shoots which break off, fall on the ground and develop roots.

mcqs.q: The strawberry plant reproduces by means of its:
options: Bulb, an underground bud with fleshy leaves
Stolon, an above-ground horizontal stem producing leaves and roots at its nodes
mcqs.why: The strawberry reproduces by its above-ground horizontal stem called the stolon, which produces leaves and roots at its nodes, and a new plantlet can grow from each node.

mcqs.q: The "eye" of a potato tuber is actually:
options: A scar left by a fallen leaf only
A well-developed axillary bud that can grow into a new potato plant
A stored food granule inside the tuber
The point where roots come out
mcqs.why: The potato tuber is an underground swollen fleshy stem; above each small leaf on it is a well-developed axillary bud commonly called an eye, and eyes can grow into new potato plants.

mcqs.q: In spermatogenesis, each primary spermatocyte finally produces:
options: One sperm and three polar bodies
Four haploid spermatids, each developing into a motile sperm
mcqs.why: Each diploid primary spermatocyte in the testes divides by meiosis and makes four haploid (n) cells called spermatids, and each spermatid develops into a motile sperm.

mcqs.q: In oogenesis, the first meiotic division of the primary oocyte produces:
options: A larger secondary oocyte and a smaller first polar body
Two spermatids and two polar bodies
A zygote and a polar body
mcqs.why: In the follicle of the ovary the primary oocyte divides by meiosis I into two haploid cells: the larger secondary oocyte and the smaller first polar body; meiosis II then gives the egg and a second polar body.

mcqs.q: After fertilisation in a flowering plant, the ovule and the ovary become respectively:
mcqs.why: After fertilisation the matured ovule is called the seed, containing the embryo formed from the zygote, while the ovary changes into the fruit.

mcqs.q: In hypogeal germination:
options: The hypocotyl elongates and pushes the cotyledons above the ground
The epicotyl elongates and the cotyledons remain below the surface of the ground
The cotyledons come into the air as the hypocotyl straightens
The seed coat emerges from the soil with the plumule
mcqs.why: In hypogeal germination, as in maize grain and pea, the epicotyl elongates and the cotyledons stay below the ground; in epigeal germination the hypocotyl elongates and lifts the cotyledons above the ground.

lessons.title: Analyse and Interpret
lessons.notes_html:
Solved Exercises

Exercise D: Analyse and interpret the following.

Q: 1. Write the mode of reproduction of an onion, corn, ginger and potato.

Ans: Onion reproduces asexually by vegetative propagation through its bulb — bulbs are underground buds that have fleshy leaves extending from them, they are food storage units containing several buds, and bulbs divide naturally to produce new plants. Corn (maize) reproduces sexually by seeds: it is a monocot seed, produced after pollination and fertilisation in the flower, in which the matured ovule becomes the seed. Ginger reproduces asexually by vegetative propagation through its rhizome, a horizontal underground stem capable of producing the shoot and root systems of a new plant under suitable conditions. Potato reproduces asexually by vegetative propagation through its tuber, an underground, swollen, fleshy stem; above each small leaf on the tuber is a well-developed axillary bud, commonly called an eye, and the eyes can grow into new potato plants.

Q: 2. Make a list of ripened seeds and fruits that are eaten in our society.

Ans: After fertilisation the ovule is matured and is called the seed, and the ovary changes into the fruit, so the ripened ovules (seeds) and ripened ovaries (fruits) named in this unit that are eaten in our society include the following. Ripened seeds eaten: pea, gram, bean, maize (corn), peanut and coconut — the unit describes the seeds of pea, gram and bean, the maize grain, and peanut and coconut as seed examples. Ripened fruits eaten: banana and grapes — the unit names bananas and seedless varieties of grapes as fruits, formed by parthenocarpy, in which the ovary develops into a fruit without the fertilisation of the egg present in its ovule, so there is no seed in the fruit.

Q: 3. Germinate a few gram seeds and examine the different requirements of water, temperature and oxygen by putting them in various conditions.

Ans: Model result, from the conditions for germination given in the unit: gram seeds placed on moist cotton in air at a suitable temperature germinate — they absorb water through the micropyle, the water softens the seed coat and makes it burst and activates enzymes that digest the stored food, the radicle emerges first and forms the first root, and then the plumule grows to form a shoot; gram is a dicot seed, and its germination is of the type in which the cotyledons' stored food feeds the embryo. Seeds kept dry, without water, do not germinate, because no water is absorbed to soften the seed coat or activate the enzymes. Seeds kept in boiled, cooled water covered so that air (oxygen) cannot reach them do not germinate properly, because the cells of the seed embryo need oxygen for cellular respiration to get energy from stored food. Seeds kept in a very cold place also fail to germinate well, because germination occurs over a temperature range of about 5°C to 30°C and a suitable temperature is necessary for the enzymes to function properly. The experiment therefore shows that water, oxygen and a suitable temperature are all necessary for seed germination, and that the seeds must be viable and have sufficient stored food.

lessons.title: Activities
lessons.notes_html:
Solved Exercises

Activities

Q: 1. Identify different stages of budding in prepared slides of yeast and draw diagrams.

Ans: In yeast, a unicellular fungus, budding begins when a small outgrowth, called a bud, grows on the side of the parent cell. Then the nucleus of the parent cell divides into two, and one of the daughter nuclei enters into the bud. The bud grows in size, and it may separate from the parent cell or may remain attached to it, as shown in Fig. 14.4, Budding in Yeast, where several oval yeast cells carry buds of different sizes. Diagram (in words): draw a large oval parent yeast cell; then the same cell with a small bud on its side; then the nucleus divided into two with one daughter nucleus inside the bud; then the enlarged bud, either still attached to the parent cell or separated as a new cell.

Q: 2. Examine the specimens of onion, corn, ginger and potato and write the mode of their reproduction. Describe how these are cultivated to get new plants.

Ans: Onion is a bulb: an underground bud with fleshy leaves that stores food and contains several buds near the node; bulbs divide naturally to produce new plants, so onion bulbs are planted in soil and each bud grows into a new plant.
