Corn is grown from its seed, the monocot maize grain produced by sexual reproduction after pollination and fertilisation; the grains are sown in soil and, under suitable conditions of water, oxygen and temperature, the embryo germinates and develops into a new plant (sporophyte). Ginger is a rhizome, a horizontal underground stem capable of producing the shoot and root systems of a new plant; pieces of rhizome are placed in the soil under suitable conditions and grow into new ginger plants. Potato is a tuber, an underground, swollen, fleshy stem whose well-developed axillary buds are called eyes; tubers, or pieces bearing eyes, are planted in the soil and the eyes grow into new potato plants.

Q: 3. Identify different parts of a flower.

Ans: Diagram (in words): A flower is made up of specialised leaves present on the swollen tip called the receptacle, and its parts form four concentric whorls. The outermost whorl (calyx) is made of usually green sepals, which protect the inner parts of a developing flower before it opens. The next whorl (corolla) is made of petals, which are coloured in most flowers. The third whorl (androecium) contains the stamens; each stamen has an anther, which contains pollen sacs (microsporangia) producing microspores, supported on a stalk-like filament. The innermost whorl (gynoecium) contains the carpels; each carpel has an enlarged base, the ovary, containing one or many ovules (megasporangia), a stalk-like style, and the stigma at its tip — these are the labels of Fig. 14.12, Parts of a flower: Stamen (Anther, Filament), Carpel (Ovary, Stigma, Style), Ovules, Petal, Sepal and Receptacle.

Q: 4. Identify and draw the component of the seeds of pea or gram.

Ans: Pea and gram are dicot seeds. Diagram (in words): On the outside is the seed coat or testa, the outer covering, black or brown in colour, which protects the embryo; on one end of the seed coat is the small scar, the hilum, which indicates the place of attachment of the seed in the fruit, and near the hilum is the micropyle, a minute pore through which the seed absorbs water at the time of germination. Beneath the seed coat lies the embryo: two large, fleshy cotyledons (a dicot seed has two cotyledons, and dicot seeds have no endosperm, the food being stored for the embryo), the plumule, a minute bud at the upper end of the hypocotyl which gives rise to the future stem, and the radicle, the lower part of the hypocotyl, which gives rise to the future root; the portion between the plumule and the cotyledons is the epicotyl and the portion between the cotyledons and the radicle is the hypocotyl — the labels shown for the dicot (bean) seed in Fig. 14.18 are Epicotyl, Plumule, Hypocotyl, Radicle, Cotyledons and Seed coat.

Q: 5. Perform an experiment to investigate the necessary conditions for seed germination.

Ans: Model experiment and result, using the conditions stated in the unit: take gram or bean seeds in four sets. Set 1 is kept on moist cotton in open air at room temperature; Set 2 is kept dry, without water; Set 3 is kept in boiled, cooled water with a layer that shuts out air, so the seeds get water but no oxygen; Set 4 is kept moist in a very cold place. Only the seeds of Set 1 germinate: germination starts with the absorption of water through the micropyle, followed by the emergence of the radicle, which forms the first root, and then the plumule grows to form a shoot. Set 2 shows that water is necessary, because water softens the seed coat and makes it burst and activates enzymes that digest the food of the seed. Set 3 shows that oxygen is necessary, because the cells of the seed embryo use oxygen for cellular respiration to get energy from stored food. Set 4 shows that a suitable temperature is necessary, because germination occurs between 5°C to 30°C and the enzymes must function properly. The seeds must also be viable, living seeds with sufficient food for germination.

Q: 6. Draw different stages of binary fission in amoeba after observing through slides or charts.

Ans: Diagram (in words): Fig. 14.2, Binary fission in Amoeba, shows four stages in a vertical series. Stage 1: a single amoeba, an irregular-shaped cell with a nucleus, labelled 'Amoeba divides after it has grown to a certain size'. Stage 2: the amoeba with its pseudopodia pulled in and its nucleus elongated and dividing into two, labelled 'The pseudopodia are pulled in and the nucleus divides'. Stage 3: the cell body pinched in the middle into a dumb-bell shape with one new nucleus in each half, labelled 'The cell body begins to divide when the nucleus has split'. Stage 4: two separate daughter amoebae, labelled 'Two daughter amoebae are formed'. This agrees with the text: in protists such as Amoeba, the nucleus of the parent organism divides into two, followed by the division of cytoplasm, so two daughter cells of almost equal size are formed.

lessons.title: Science, Technology and Society
lessons.notes_html:
Solved Exercises

Science, Technology and Society

Q: 1. Grow plants at home using asexual reproduction methods.

Ans: Model answer, using the methods given in the unit: at home, new plants can be grown asexually by stem cuttings — cut pieces of stem from a plant such as rose, grape vine or chrysanthemum and plant them in sand over soil or compost, as in Fig. 14.9, and the cutting grows into a whole new plant; root cuttings are used for plants like sweet potato and blackberries. Onion bulbs can be planted, since bulbs divide naturally to produce new plants, and potato tubers can be planted so that their eyes (axillary buds) grow into new potato plants. Bryophyllum leaves can be laid on the ground, where the buds at their margins form tiny shoots that break off, develop roots and grow into new plants. All these methods are vegetative propagation, so the new plants are produced from a single parent without the fusion of gametes.

Q: 2. Describe commercially important applications of asexual reproduction in plants.

Ans: Asexual reproduction is commercially important in horticulture and agriculture. Grafting is used to get better quality and quantity of fruits: the branch of a desired variety is grafted on to the stem of an ordinary plant, and this method is used to propagate almost all fruit trees (e.g. almond, plum, cherries etc.) and many ornamental trees. Cutting is a convenient and inexpensive method of propagation: stem cuttings are used for grape vine, rose and chrysanthemum, and root cuttings for sweet potato and blackberries. Cloning is used for making identical copies of useful plants; it is very helpful in horticulture where we want to preserve the quality of the yield, and cloning also helps us to increase agricultural output. Natural vegetative structures are also used commercially — bulbs of onion, rhizomes of ginger and tubers of potato are planted to raise new crops that are copies of the parent plant.

Q: 3. Justify cloning as a form of asexual reproduction.

Ans: Cloning is a technique of asexual reproduction in which a population of genetically identical individuals is produced from a single parent, using tissues or cells of the parent, as shown in Fig. 14.11, Cloning of a plant, where tissue pieces from a parent plant are placed in a suitable medium, the tissues develop into small plants, and the new plants are sown to grow. It is asexual reproduction because only one parent is involved and there is no fusion of gametes (sex cells) from two parents. The book's definition of asexual reproduction also states that the resulting offsprings are similar to the parent, that this type of reproduction does not create genetic variations and that the offsprings are clones — which is exactly what cloning produces.

Q: 4. State the advantages and disadvantages of having large families.

Ans: The unit's discussion of population planning stresses the disadvantages of large families. Producing too many children often places poor households under stress due to shortage of resources, and children grow up malnourished and often without access to effective education and healthcare. Rapid population growth puts great pressure on agricultural land and hinders prospects of economic and social development, and a growing population requires that job opportunities and some stable source of income be made available. The growth of population beyond available resources is one of the manifestations of poverty. Against this, the only advantage that can be claimed for a large family is that it has more members to share the family's work and, when grown up, to earn — but the book's text presents large families mainly as a burden on the family's and the country's resources, which is why population planning has become a compelling need.

Q: 5. Debate the social implications of AIDS and other sexually transmitted diseases.

Ans: Model points for the debate, from the unit: Sexually Transmitted Diseases (STDs), also called Sexually Transmitted Infections (STIs), are infections acquired through sexual activity with infected people, and include many bacterial and viral infections. AIDS is one of the most severe and fatal sexually transmitted diseases; it is a viral infection caused by Human Immuno-deficiency Virus (HIV), which attacks and destroys white blood cells, so the main defence system of the body is weakened. HIV can also pass through infected needles or transfusion of infected blood, there is no cure for HIV or AIDS, and antiretroviral drugs only hinder the growth of HIV — so society must rely on prevention and education. According to the latest National HIV estimates there are approximately 97,400 cases of HIV/AIDS in Pakistan, and AIDS is more common in people who inject drugs. The National AIDS Control Programme and its provincial units educate common people as well as parliamentarians, media personnel, educationists and religious leaders, and organise events like World AIDS Day to raise awareness, while NGOs coordinate prevention and control activities and support patients but reach less than 5 percent of the vulnerable population — so the social implication is that the whole community, not only doctors, must be educated and involved in controlling these diseases.

lessons.title: Multiple Choice Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Genes are short segments of DNA; the different forms of a gene are called alleles.
  • Natural selection produces changes in populations, and speciation forms a new gene pool.
  • A plant of genotype AaBb produces four types of gametes: AB, Ab, aB and ab.
  • Phenotype is the physical expression of the genes; genotype is the genetic makeup.
  • DNA wrapped around histone proteins forms a round nucleosome.
  • A dominant allele completely masks the recessive allele in a heterozygote.
  • The central dogma is DNA → RNA → Protein; I^A and I^B alleles show co-dominance.

Solved Exercises

Exercise A: Select the correct answer.

Q: 1. Genes are short segments of:

Options: (a) Proteins (b) Carbohydrates (c) DNA (d) Lipids

Correct answer: DNA

Q: 2. The various forms of a gene responsible for the same trait are called:

Options: (a) Centromere (b) Character (c) Trait (d) Allele

Correct answer: Allele

Q: 3. Natural selection operates to produce changes in:

Options: (a) Individuals (b) Populations (c) Races (d) Phyla

Correct answer: Populations

Q: 4. How many different types of gametes will be produced by a plant having a genotype AaBb?

Options: (a) Three (b) Four (c) Six (d) Eight

Correct answer: Four

Q: 5. Speciation is the evolutionary process by which ______.

Options: (a) A new gene pool is formed (b) Evolutionary path of a species converge (c) Hybrid species is formed (d) Shows differences in physical traits

Correct answer: A new gene pool is formed

Q: 6. Phenotype is the expression of:

Options: (a) Genetic makeup (b) Physical makeup (c) Chemical composition (d) Metabolism

Correct answer: Genetic makeup

Q: 7. The round structure formed when DNA coils around the histone protein is:

Options: (a) Centromere (b) Chiasma (c) Nucleosome (d) Chromatin

Correct answer: Nucleosome

Q: 8. An allele which completely masks the effect of other allele in a heterozygote:

Options: (a) Dominant (b) Recessive (c) Co-dominant (d) Incomplete dominant

Correct answer: Dominant

Q: 9. The central dogma is best represented by

Options: (a) DNA + RNA = Protein (b) DNA → RNA + Protein (c) DNA → RNA → Protein (d) Protein → RNA → DNA

Correct answer: DNA → RNA → Protein

Q: 10. Type of dominance pattern followed by I^A and I^B alleles of the human blood group system:

Options: (a) Complete dominance (b) Co-dominance (c) Incomplete dominance (d) None of the above

Correct answer: Co-dominance

Q: 11. What are the possible genotypes of the parents of homozygous recessive individual?

Options: (a) Homozygous dominant (b) Homozygous recessive (c) Heterozygous (d) Both 'b' and 'c'

Correct answer: Both 'b' and 'c'

mcqs.q: 1. Genes are short segments of:
mcqs.why: A gene is the fundamental unit of heredity and is a segment of DNA consisting of a specific sequence of nucleotides that carries the code for protein synthesis.

mcqs.q: 2. The various forms of a gene responsible for the same trait are called:
mcqs.why: The different forms of the same gene, occupying the same locus on homologous chromosomes and controlling the same trait, are called alleles, such as T and t for height.

mcqs.q: 3. Natural selection operates to produce changes in:
mcqs.why: Natural selection favours individuals best adapted to the environment, and over generations this changes the genetic make-up of whole populations, not single individuals.

mcqs.q: 4. How many different types of gametes will be produced by a plant having a genotype AaBb?
mcqs.why: Working: genotype AaBb has two heterozygous gene pairs. Gametes get one allele of each gene: A or a with B or b, giving AB, Ab, aB and ab — that is 2 x 2 = 4 different types of gametes.

mcqs.q: 5. Speciation is the evolutionary process by which ______.
options: A new gene pool is formed
Evolutionary path of a species converge
mcqs.why: Speciation is the formation of a new species; accumulated variations separate a population so that a new, distinct gene pool is formed which can no longer merge with the old one.

mcqs.q: 6. Phenotype is the expression of:
mcqs.why: BOOK MISPRINT: the book key marks "Genetic makeup", but genetic makeup is the genotype. Phenotype is the observable physical expression of the genes, e.g. a Tt plant has genotype Tt but the tall physical appearance is its phenotype, so "Physical makeup" is correct.

mcqs.q: 7. The round structure formed when DNA coils around the histone protein is:
mcqs.why: The long DNA molecule wraps around a bundle of histone proteins, and the round structure made of histones with DNA wrapped around them is called a nucleosome.

mcqs.q: 8. An allele which completely masks the effect of other allele in a heterozygote:
mcqs.why: A dominant allele completely masks the effect of the other allele in a heterozygote; for example T masks t in Tt, so the heterozygous plant appears tall.

mcqs.q: 9. The central dogma is best represented by
mcqs.why: The central dogma is the one-way flow of information: DNA is transcribed into RNA (mRNA), and the mRNA is translated at the ribosome into protein, i.e. DNA → RNA → Protein.

mcqs.q: 10. Type of dominance pattern followed by I^A and I^B alleles of the human blood group system:
mcqs.why: Alleles I^A and I^B are both fully expressed together in a heterozygote I^A I^B, producing both antigens A and B and blood group AB; this joint full expression is co-dominance.

mcqs.q: 11. What are the possible genotypes of the parents of homozygous recessive individual?
mcqs.why: Working: a homozygous recessive child (e.g. tt) must receive one recessive allele t from each parent. A homozygous recessive parent (tt) gives t, and a heterozygous parent (Tt) can also give t, but a homozygous dominant (TT) gives only T. So the parents can be homozygous recessive or heterozygous — both (b) and (c).

mcqs.q: A man with blood group AB marries a woman with blood group O. Which blood groups are expected in their children?
options: A and B in about equal numbers
mcqs.why: Working: man genotype I^A I^B gives gametes I^A and I^B; woman genotype ii gives only gamete i. Punnett outcomes: I^A i (group A, since I^A dominates i) and I^B i (group B, since I^B dominates i), each 1/2 of children. No child gets I^A I^B or ii, so no AB or O children.

mcqs.q: In Mendel's dihybrid cross, the F2 phenotypic ratio of round yellow : round green : wrinkled yellow : wrinkled green seeds is:
mcqs.why: Working: P cross RRYY x rryy gives F1 all RrYy. F1 gametes are RY, Ry, rY, ry. The 4 x 4 Punnett square gives 16 boxes; counting phenotypes: 9/16 round yellow, 3/16 round green, 3/16 wrinkled yellow, 1/16 wrinkled green — ratio 9 : 3 : 3 : 1.

mcqs.q: In the Japanese 4 O'clock plant, red (RR) crossed with white (rr) gives pink (Rr) flowers. The F2 ratio of red : pink : white is:
mcqs.why: Working: F1 is all Rr (pink, incomplete dominance). F1 self-cross Rr x Rr: gametes R and r from each parent. Punnett outcomes: 1 RR (red) : 2 Rr (pink) : 1 rr (white), so the F2 phenotypic ratio is 1 : 2 : 1.

mcqs.q: A person with genotype I^A I^B has blood group AB because:
options: Allele I^A completely hides allele I^B
No antigen is produced on the red blood cells
Both alleles are fully expressed and both antigens A and B are produced
The two alleles blend into a new antigen
mcqs.why: Alleles I^A and I^B are co-dominant: in genotype I^A I^B neither masks the other, both are completely expressed, antigen A and antigen B are both produced, and the blood group is AB.

lessons.title: Short Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • AB x O parents: children are I^A i (group A) or I^B i (group B), about half each; no AB or O children.
  • Crossing over in prophase of meiosis exchanges genes between homologous chromatids and creates new gene combinations.
  • DNA wraps around histones to form nucleosomes, arranged like beads on a string in the chromatin fiber.
  • In artificial selection people select desirable organisms; major cereals were developed from wild grasses.
  • Complete dominance: Tt appears tall; incomplete dominance blends (pink Rr); co-dominance expresses both alleles (AB blood group).
  • Genotype ii gives blood group O (no antigen); I^B i gives group B because I^B dominates i.

Solved Exercises

Exercise B: Write short answers to the following questions.

Q: 1. If a man with type AB blood group marries a woman with type O blood group. What type of blood group do you expect in the offsprings?

Ans: The man has genotype I^A I^B and the woman has genotype ii. Step 1 — Gametes: the man produces two types of gametes, I^A and I^B, while the woman produces only one type, i. Step 2 — Offspring: I^A with i gives I^A i, and I^B with i gives I^B i. Step 3 — Phenotypes: allele I^A is dominant over i, so I^A i children have blood group A, and allele I^B is dominant over i, so I^B i children have blood group B. Therefore about half the children are expected to have blood group A and half blood group B; no child will have blood group AB or O.

Q: 2. How can crossing bring variations?

Ans: Crossing over takes place during prophase of meiosis. In this process, the chromatids of homologous chromosomes exchange genes with each other. As a result, chromosomes with different combinations of genes are formed in different gametes. When such gametes take part in fertilization, the offspring get new gene combinations, so variations are produced.

Q: 3. How are DNA and proteins packed to form a chromosome?

Ans: Chromosomes are composed of chromatin material. In eukaryotes the chromatin material is composed of DNA and histone proteins. The long molecule of DNA is wrapped around a bundle of histones, and the structure made of histones and the DNA wrapped around them is called a nucleosome. The nucleosomes are arranged in the form of beads on a string, and this string of beads coils to form the chromatin fiber, which further coils to form the structure of the chromosome.

Q: 4. How is artificial selection used for the improvement of crops?

Ans: In artificial selection, people instead of nature select the organisms they want to reproduce, and only plants with desirable characteristics are allowed to reproduce. By the repeated application of artificial selection, essentially all present-day crops have been reshaped from their wild ancestors; for example, the major cereals rice, wheat, maize, sorghum and millet were all developed from wild grasses. In this way many plant varieties (cultivars) of wheat, rice, potato and apple etc. have been produced for better quantity and quality of food.

Q: 5. Differentiate between different types of dominant relations.

Ans: Dominance relations are of three types. (1) Complete dominance: one allele is completely dominant over the other, e.g. the allele for tallness T is completely dominant over the allele for dwarfness t, so in the heterozygous condition Tt, T hides the effect of t and the plant appears tall. (2) Incomplete dominance: an allele does not completely mask the action of the second allele, and the heterozygous individual shows a blending of both phenotypes, e.g. in the Japanese 4 O'clock plant the cross of red (RR) and white (rr) gives pink (Rr) flowers in F1, and the F2 ratio is 1 red : 2 pink : 1 white. (3) Co-dominance: it is not an intermediate expression; different alleles of a gene are completely expressed in the heterozygous condition, e.g. in the ABO blood group system a person with genotype I^A I^B expresses both antigens A and B and has AB blood group.

Q: 6. Write down the phenotypes of the individuals in the following table. Genotype — Phenotype: I^A I^A or / I^B I^B / I^B i / I^A i / ii / I^A I^B

Ans: According to the ABO blood group table given in this unit (allele I^A makes antigen A on RBCs, allele I^B makes antigen B, and allele i produces no antigen): I^A I^A — Blood Group A (antigen A produced; the printed row ends with 'or' and the same phenotype A applies to I^A i, which is listed separately below). I^B I^B — Blood Group B (antigen B). I^B i — Blood Group B, because allele I^B is dominant over i. I^A i — Blood Group A, because allele I^A is dominant over i. ii — Blood Group O, because allele i is recessive and no antigen is produced. I^A I^B — Blood Group AB, because alleles I^A and I^B are co-dominant and both antigens A and B are produced.

mcqs.q: A child of an AB father (I^A I^B) and an O mother (ii) has blood group A. What is the genotype of this child?
mcqs.why: Working: father gives gametes I^A or I^B, mother gives only i. A group A child received I^A from the father and i from the mother, so the genotype is I^A i; I^A is dominant over i, giving blood group A.

mcqs.q: Why can no child of an AB parent and an O parent have blood group O?
options: Because the O parent gives a dominant allele
Because the AB parent has no i allele to pass on, so no child can be ii
Because blood group O never appears in children
Because both parents give I^A only
mcqs.why: Working: blood group O needs genotype ii, one i from each parent. The AB parent (I^A I^B) produces only I^A and I^B gametes and never i, so every child is I^A i or I^B i and none can be ii.

mcqs.q: Crossing over takes place during which stage?
mcqs.why: Crossing over takes place during prophase of meiosis, when the chromatids of homologous chromosomes exchange genes with each other, forming new gene combinations in the gametes.

mcqs.q: How does crossing over produce variations in offspring?
options: It doubles the number of chromosomes in gametes
Chromatids of homologous chromosomes exchange genes, so gametes carry new combinations of genes
It changes the sequence of a single nucleotide
It allows only dominant alleles to pass on
mcqs.why: During crossing over the chromatids of homologous chromosomes exchange genes, so chromosomes with different combinations of genes form in different gametes, and fertilization with such gametes gives offspring new gene combinations.

mcqs.q: The structure made of a bundle of histones with DNA wrapped around it is called:
mcqs.why: The long molecule of DNA is wrapped around a bundle of histones, and the structure made of histones and the DNA wrapped around them is called a nucleosome; nucleosomes lie like beads on a string.

mcqs.q: In artificial selection, who selects the organisms that will reproduce?
options: People, who allow only organisms with desirable characteristics to reproduce
mcqs.why: In artificial selection people instead of nature select the organisms they want to reproduce, and only plants with desirable characteristics are allowed to reproduce, improving crops in quantity and quality.

mcqs.q: The major cereals rice, wheat, maize, sorghum and millet were developed by artificial selection from:
mcqs.why: By repeated application of artificial selection, present-day crops were reshaped from their wild ancestors; the major cereals rice, wheat, maize, sorghum and millet were all developed from wild grasses.

mcqs.q: In complete dominance, a heterozygous plant Tt (T = tall, t = dwarf) appears:
options: Of medium height, blending both alleles
Both tall and dwarf at the same time
Tall, because T completely hides the effect of t
mcqs.why: Working: genotype Tt carries dominant allele T and recessive allele t. In complete dominance T completely masks t in the heterozygote, so the phenotype of every Tt plant is tall, not dwarf or medium.

mcqs.q: A person with genotype ii has blood group O because:
options: Allele i is recessive and produces no antigen on the red blood cells
Allele i is co-dominant with itself
Both antigens A and B are produced
mcqs.why: Allele I^A makes antigen A and I^B makes antigen B, but allele i produces no antigen; a person with genotype ii therefore has no antigen A or B and the blood group is O.

mcqs.q: A person with genotype I^B i has blood group B because:
options: Alleles I^B and i blend to give group B
Allele I^B is dominant over i, so antigen B is produced
No antigen is produced at all
mcqs.why: Working: genotype I^B i has one I^B allele and one recessive i allele. I^B is dominant over i, so antigen B is made on the red blood cells and the phenotype is blood group B.

lessons.title: Detailed Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • A chromosome has two chromatids joined at a centromere and is made of DNA plus histone proteins; a gene sits at a fixed locus.
  • Central dogma steps: transcription makes mRNA from a DNA template; translation links amino acids at the ribosome using tRNA.
  • Mendel used peas: easy to grow, three-month life cycle, pure-breeding strains and seven clear characteristics.
  • Law of independent assortment: alleles separate independently in gamete formation; dihybrid F2 ratio is 9 : 3 : 3 : 1.
  • Sources of variation: recombination, crossing over, random fertilization, mutation and environmental conditions.
  • Variations feed natural selection, and their accumulation over generations produces new species (evolution).

Solved Exercises

Exercise C: Write detailed answers to the following questions:

Q: 1. Relate the structure of chromosome with DNA and gene. Draw a concept chart to explain your answer.

Ans: Chromosomes are thread-like structures present in cells; in eukaryotic cells they are found within the nucleus. When a cell is not dividing, its chromatin is in the form of fine threads scattered in the nucleus, and during cell division the chromatin coils and makes the compact structures of chromosomes. A chromosome consists of two identical halves called chromatids, attached at a point called the centromere. Chromosomes are composed of chromatin material, which in eukaryotes is made of DNA and histone proteins: the long DNA molecule is wrapped around histones to form nucleosomes, and the coiling of this material forms the chromosome. Genes are located on chromosomes and, like chromosomes, genes are also in pairs. A gene is the fundamental physical and functional unit of heredity; it is a segment of DNA consisting of a specific sequence and number of nucleotides that has a code for protein synthesis, and it determines a trait or character such as eye colour, earlobe shape and hair texture. The location of a gene on the chromosome is called its locus, and the transfer of genes to the next generation takes place through gametes. Diagram (in words): The concept chart, based on Fig. 15.1 'Location and Packing of Hereditary Material (DNA) in the cell', is read from the smallest level upwards — at the bottom is the 'Double helix' of DNA; the DNA is wound on nucleosomes, shown as 'Beads on a string — DNA wound on nucleosomes' with the label 'Nucleosomes'; these make up the 'Chromatin fiber'; and the coiled chromatin fiber finally forms the X-shaped 'Chromosome' at the top. A gene is one specific segment of this DNA at a fixed locus on the chromosome.

Q: 2. Explain with the help of a diagram the relationship amongst DNA, RNA and proteins.

Ans: Every cell contains instructions for making characters in its DNA in the form of chemical codes called genes, and the cells use these instructions to produce particular proteins; the proteins made by a cell make its characters. This flow of information is called the central dogma, and protein synthesis takes place in two major steps. Transcription: in the first step, the two strands of DNA unzip and separate from each other, and one strand of DNA acts as a template for making a single strand of Ribonucleic acid (RNA) called messenger RNA (mRNA); in this way the instructions present in the strand of DNA are copied on the mRNA. Translation: the mRNA leaves the cell nucleus and travels to the ribosome, which attaches with the mRNA; another type of RNA called transfer RNA (tRNA) carries specific amino acids to the ribosome, and the amino acids are linked together in a specific sequence, eventually forming a protein. DNA can also make more DNA by DNA synthesis (replication). Diagram (in words): Fig. 15.3 'The Central Dogma' shows three levels — at the top, 'DNA' drawn as a double helix with coloured base bars, with a circular arrow above it labelled 'DNA synthesis (replication)'; a downward arrow labelled 'DNA synthesis (transcription)' leads to the middle level 'RNA', drawn as a single row of coloured bars; a second downward arrow labelled 'Protein synthesis (translation)' leads to the bottom level 'PROTEIN', drawn as a chain of round amino-acid units. The key beside the figure lists Adenine (A), Thymine (T), Cytosine (C), Guanine (G), Uracil (U) and Amino acid.

Q: 3. Explain why Mendel selected peas as a subject for studying genetics?

Ans: Gregor Mendel, an Austrian monk, performed his famous experiments on the garden pea plant during the years 1856–1864 and discovered the fundamental mechanism of inheritance, so he is regarded as the 'Father of Genetics'. The garden pea was a good choice for several reasons given in this unit. Pea plants are easy to grow and are fairly resistant to pests. They have a reasonably short generation time, completing their life cycle (from seed to next-generation seed) in three months, so results from breeding experiments could be obtained rapidly. Most importantly, the pea plants Mendel used were pure breeding (true-breeding) strains; for example, his pure breeding strain of violet-flowered pea produced violet-flowered offspring exclusively when allowed to self-pollinate. Every pea plant contains both male and female reproductive parts and normally reproduces through self-pollination, while cross-pollination can also be done by hand, as shown in Fig. 15.5. Pea plants also have seven easily distinguishable characteristics, such as round versus wrinkled seeds and purple (violet) versus white flowers, which helped Mendel to easily observe and calculate the results of his crosses among plants.

Q: 4. Explain the law of independent assortment with the help of an example and chart.

Ans: In a dihybrid cross, the inheritance of two characteristics is studied at a time. Mendel crossed true-breeding plants having round yellow seeds (genotype RRYY) with plants having wrinkled, green seeds (rryy). Step 1 — P generation: RRYY × rryy. Step 2 — Gametes: the first parent produces RY gametes and the second produces ry gametes. Step 3 — F1 generation: all offspring are RrYy and show only the dominant characteristics, i.e. round and yellow seeds. Step 4 — Gametes of F1: the F1 plants (RrYy) produce four types of gametes, i.e. RY, Ry, rY and ry, which shows that alleles R and r segregated independently of the alleles Y and y. Step 5 — F2 generation: when the F1 hybrids were self-fertilized, there were 16 combinations of alleles in the F2 generation, giving four different types of seeds in the ratio 9:3:3:1 — 9/16 round and yellow, 3/16 round and green, 3/16 wrinkled and yellow, and 1/16 wrinkled and green. This discovery is called the law of independent assortment, which states that 'alleles separate independently of one another during the formation of gametes.' Diagram (in words): The chart in Fig. 15.9 'Independent assortment of alleles' is a 4 × 4 Punnett square. The four gametes of one F1 parent (RY, Ry, rY, ry) are written across the top and the same four gametes of the other F1 parent are written down the side; each of the 16 boxes contains the resulting genotype (such as RRYY, RRYy, RrYY, RrYy in the first row) with its phenotype written below it (Round Yellow, etc.). Counting the boxes gives 9 round yellow : 3 round green : 3 wrinkled yellow : 1 wrinkled green, as listed in the F2 generation box beside the chart.

Q: 5. Describe the sources of variations. Explain the importance of variations in organisms.

Ans: Variations are differences in traits between individuals of the same species, and they are produced due to genetic differences among individuals, while environmental conditions also play a role. The main sources of variations described in this unit are: (a) Genetic recombination of chromosomes — gametes are produced by meiosis, during which the homologous chromosomes separate and move independently to different nuclei, so new combinations of chromosomes are produced in the daughter cells (gametes). (b) Crossing over — during prophase of meiosis, the chromatids of homologous chromosomes exchange genes, which results in chromosomes with different combinations of genes in different gametes. (c) Random fertilization — each gamete has a unique genetic composition because of the recombination of chromosomes and genes in meiosis, so when gametes combine randomly during fertilization, the organisms produced are different from all others of the species. (d) Mutation — mutation is any change in the nucleotide sequence of DNA; alleles arise by mutation, the original allele being the wild type and the new allele the mutant allele, and if there were no mutations there would be no variation. (e) Environmental conditions — the environment has no role in the initial production of variations, but once variations are produced, the individuals with variations best suited to that environment have more chances of survival. Importance: variations are necessary for natural selection, because natural selection favours individuals with traits that are best adapted to their environment and enables them to change when the environment changes; the accumulation of such variations, generation after generation, ultimately results in the production of new species, i.e. evolution.

Q: 6. Draw a cross between two pea plants. One of them has round green seeds (RRyy) while the other has wrinkled yellow seeds (rrYY).

Ans: This is a dihybrid cross, in which the inheritance of two characteristics (seed shape and seed colour) is studied at a time; R (round) is dominant over r (wrinkled) and Y (yellow) is dominant over y (green), as in Mendel's dihybrid cross in this unit. Step 1 — P generation: round green parent RRyy × wrinkled yellow parent rrYY. Step 2 — Gametes: the RRyy parent can produce only one type of gamete, Ry, and the rrYY parent can produce only one type of gamete, rY. Step 3 — F1 generation: Ry + rY gives RrYy in every offspring, so all F1 plants have round yellow seeds, showing only the dominant characteristics. Step 4 — F1 gametes: each F1 plant (RrYy) produces four types of gametes, RY, Ry, rY and ry, because the alleles separate independently of one another during gamete formation. Step 5 — F2 generation (F1 self-pollinated): the 16 combinations give the phenotypic ratio 9:3:3:1, i.e. 9/16 round yellow, 3/16 round green, 3/16 wrinkled yellow and 1/16 wrinkled green seeds. Diagram (in words): Draw a 4 × 4 Punnett square with the F1 gametes RY, Ry, rY and ry written across the top and the same four gametes down the side. The 16 boxes contain, row by row: RRYY, RRYy, RrYY, RrYy (all round yellow); RRYy, RRyy, RrYy, Rryy (round yellow, round green, round yellow, round green); RrYY, RrYy, rrYY, rrYy (round yellow, round yellow, wrinkled yellow, wrinkled yellow); RrYy, Rryy, rrYy, rryy (round yellow, round green, wrinkled yellow, wrinkled green). Counting the phenotypes gives 9 round yellow : 3 round green : 3 wrinkled yellow : 1 wrinkled green.

mcqs.q: The two identical halves of a chromosome, joined at the centromere, are called:
mcqs.why: A chromosome consists of two identical halves called chromatids, attached at a point called the centromere; the chromosome itself is made of chromatin material of DNA and histone proteins.

mcqs.q: The fixed location of a gene on a chromosome is called its:
mcqs.why: Genes are located on chromosomes in pairs, and the location of a gene on the chromosome is called its locus; the transfer of genes to the next generation takes place through gametes.

mcqs.q: In transcription, the role of one strand of DNA is to act as:
options: A template for making a single strand of messenger RNA
A carrier of amino acids to the ribosome
The site where amino acids are linked
A copy of the whole chromosome
mcqs.why: In transcription the two strands of DNA unzip and separate, and one strand acts as a template for making a single strand of messenger RNA (mRNA), copying the instructions of the DNA onto the mRNA.

mcqs.q: During translation, transfer RNA (tRNA) works by:
options: Copying DNA into mRNA inside the nucleus
Carrying specific amino acids to the ribosome, where they are linked in sequence to form a protein
Unzipping the two strands of DNA
mcqs.why: In translation the mRNA travels to the ribosome and tRNA carries specific amino acids to the ribosome; the amino acids are linked together in a specific sequence, eventually forming a protein.

mcqs.q: Why was the garden pea a good choice for Mendel's experiments?
options: It completes its life cycle in three months, is easy to grow and has pure-breeding strains
It has only one distinguishable characteristic
It reproduces only by cross-pollination done by insects
Its flowers have no male parts
mcqs.why: Pea plants are easy to grow, fairly resistant to pests, complete their life cycle in three months so results come rapidly, and Mendel's strains were pure breeding; they also have seven easily distinguishable characteristics.

mcqs.q: The law of independent assortment states that:
options: Dominant alleles always hide recessive alleles
Alleles separate independently of one another during the formation of gametes
Genes on the same chromosome never separate
F1 offspring always show both parental traits equally
mcqs.why: Working: F1 plants RrYy produced four gamete types RY, Ry, rY and ry in equal kinds, showing alleles R/r segregated independently of Y/y. This is the law of independent assortment: alleles separate independently during gamete formation.

mcqs.q: In the cross RRyy (round green) x rrYY (wrinkled yellow), the F1 generation is:
options: Half round green and half wrinkled yellow
All RrYy with round yellow seeds
All RRYY with round yellow seeds
mcqs.why: Working: RRyy parent gives only gamete Ry; rrYY parent gives only gamete rY. Every offspring is Ry + rY = RrYy. R (round) dominates r and Y (yellow) dominates y, so all F1 seeds are round and yellow.

mcqs.q: Mutation is defined in this unit as:
options: The exchange of genes between chromatids
Any change in the nucleotide sequence of DNA
mcqs.why: Mutation is any change in the nucleotide sequence of DNA; alleles arise by mutation, the original allele being the wild type and the new allele the mutant allele, and without mutations there would be no variation.

mcqs.q: Why are variations necessary for natural selection?
options: They stop evolution from taking place
They make every individual identical to its parents
Natural selection favours individuals with traits best adapted to the environment, and accumulated variations can produce new species
They remove the role of the environment completely
mcqs.why: Variations are necessary for natural selection because it favours individuals with traits best adapted to their environment; accumulation of such variations generation after generation ultimately results in new species, i.e. evolution.

mcqs.q: Random fertilization is a source of variation because:
options: Each gamete has a unique genetic composition, so gametes combining randomly produce offspring different from all others of the species
It changes the nucleotide sequence of DNA
It exchanges genes between homologous chromatids
It takes place during prophase of meiosis
mcqs.why: Each gamete has a unique genetic composition because of recombination of chromosomes and genes in meiosis, so when gametes combine randomly during fertilization, the organisms produced are different from all others of the species.

lessons.title: Activities
lessons.notes_html:
Solved Exercises

Activity

Q: 1. Draw the chromosomes of a plant cell after observing it in a prepared slides / unlabelled charts.

Ans: Observe the prepared slide (or the unlabelled chart) under the microscope and identify the thread-like structures, the chromosomes, inside the nucleus of the plant cell; then draw what is observed. Diagram (in words): Draw the nucleus containing several thread-like chromosomes. Each chromosome is drawn as a compact structure made of two identical halves; each half is labelled 'chromatid', and the point where the two chromatids are joined is labelled 'centromere' — the centromere holds the two chromatids together until they separate during cell division. When the cell is not dividing, the same material appears as fine threads of chromatin scattered in the nucleus, so a dividing cell, in which the chromatin has coiled into compact chromosomes, should be selected for the drawing.

Activities

Q: 1. Record the heights of class fellows to predict which kind of variation it is?

Ans: Measure and record the height of every class fellow. The heights will not fall into a few clear-cut groups; instead they will show a wide range of phenotypes ranging from one extreme (shortest) to the other (tallest), with a lot of intermediate heights in between. This is continuous variation, because, as given in this unit, height is one of the characters that show continuous variation and such characters are controlled by many genes — the same is true of weight and IQ. So the recorded heights of the class fellows are predicted to be an example of continuous variation.

Q: 2. Present the data of class fellows' heights in graphical form.

Ans: Arrange the recorded heights in increasing order and group them into classes (for example, classes of 5 cm each), then count how many class fellows fall in each class and plot the counts as bars. Diagram (in words): Draw a bar graph with 'Height classes' on the horizontal axis, running from the shortest class on the left to the tallest class on the right, and 'Number of class fellows' on the vertical axis. The bars are short at both extremes, rise gradually towards the middle, and are tallest for the middle height classes, giving a bell-shaped pattern. This smooth gradation from one extreme to the other, with most individuals in the middle, is the graphical evidence that height shows continuous variation.

lessons.title: Science, Technology and Society
lessons.notes_html:
Solved Exercises

Science, Technology and Society

Q: 1. Describe various possibilities if humans could control the functioning of genes.

Ans: A gene is a unit of inheritance that can be copied and passed on to the next generation, and genes control characters because the instructions present in DNA are used by cells to produce particular proteins, and the proteins made by a cell make its characters. If humans could control the functioning of genes, they could in principle switch a gene on or off and so control which proteins a cell makes and which characters appear. This would open possibilities such as improving economically important plants like wheat and rice by selecting and controlling the genes for desired characters, and correcting characters produced by faulty (mutant) alleles, since alleles arise by mutation. The unit also shows the limit of such control: characters like height, weight and IQ are controlled by many genes, so they could not be changed by controlling a single gene.

Q: 2. Prepare a report using newspaper clippings on the recent advances and future possibilities in genetics.

Ans: Model report outline based on this unit: collect newspaper clippings about genetics and arrange them under the ideas studied in this unit — (i) genes as segments of DNA that code for proteins and control inheritance of characters; (ii) the central dogma, DNA → RNA → protein, which explains how a gene works; (iii) artificial selection and crop improvement, by which new varieties of wheat, rice and other crops and new breeds of animals are produced; and (iv) variation and evolution, where new gene combinations arise by recombination and crossing over during meiosis. For each clipping, write a short note linking the news item to one of these ideas, and end the report with the future possibilities that follow from the unit, such as further improvement of crop yield by selection and a better understanding of how genes produce the various proteins of the body.

Q: 3. Rationalise life as a product of the diversity brought about by chromosomes, genes and DNA.

Ans: The beauty of nature is because of the diversity among living organisms, and the basis of this biodiversity lies in the genetic variations that occur among organisms. The hereditary material DNA is packed into chromosomes, and chromosomes carry genes in pairs, with alternative forms called alleles. During meiosis, homologous chromosomes separate and move independently and crossing over of genes takes place, so recombination of chromosomes and crossing over during meiosis produce new combinations in the gametes, and random fertilization makes every new organism different from all others of its species. Because life is built from this DNA–gene–chromosome system, the endless diversity of form, size, colour, habit and physiology among individuals is a direct product of chromosomes, genes and DNA.

Q: 4. Outline the scientific findings and some of the technological advances that led to the modern concept of gene.

Ans: The modern concept of the gene was built step by step from findings given in this unit. Chromosomes were discovered by Waldeyer in 1876, and the name chromosome was given to these structures as they readily absorb dyes and become coloured (chromo = colour, soma = body). Gregor Mendel's experiments on the garden pea plant in 1856–1864 discovered the fundamental mechanism of inheritance and gave the laws of segregation and independent assortment, showing that hereditary information is in the form of paired genes (alleles). Later work on the composition of chromatin showed that in eukaryotes it is made of DNA and histone proteins packed as nucleosomes, and the gene was finally defined as the fundamental physical and functional unit of heredity — a segment of DNA, with a specific sequence and number of nucleotides, that codes for protein synthesis through transcription and translation (the central dogma).

Q: 5. Analyse the concept of the gene to produce various proteins of the body.

Ans: Genes are segments of DNA, each consisting of a specific sequence and number of nucleotides that has a code for protein synthesis, and different genes determine different traits, such as the genes for eye colour, earlobe shape and hair texture. A gene produces its protein in two steps: in transcription, one strand of DNA acts as a template and its instructions are copied onto messenger RNA; in translation, the mRNA travels to the ribosome and transfer RNA carries specific amino acids there, which are linked together in a specific sequence to form the protein. Because each gene has its own nucleotide sequence, each gene codes for a different protein, and the proteins made by a cell make its characters; in this way the many genes of the body produce its various proteins.

Q: 6. Describe the importance of scientific investigation and mathematical knowledge in genetics.

Ans: Scientific investigation is a pursuit to find the answer to a question using the scientific method, which is a systematic process that involves using measurable observations to formulate, test or modify a hypothesis. This is exactly how genetics developed: Mendel observed his pea crosses, counted the offspring and formulated the laws of inheritance from the results. Mathematical knowledge is essential because in genetics the information is in the form of large mathematical data — for example the 3:1 phenotypic ratio in the F2 of a monohybrid cross, the 1 RR : 2 Rr : 1 rr genotype ratio in incomplete dominance, and the 9:3:3:1 ratio of a dihybrid cross. Therefore, knowledge of mathematics is required for data analysis to interpret the data obtained from genetic experiments and to predict the results of crosses.

Q: 7. Explain how genetics can predict the progeny of two individuals which are crossed.

Ans: Genetics predicts the progeny of a cross from the genotypes of the parents. First, the alleles of each parent are written, e.g. a tall pea plant TT and a short plant tt. Next, the gametes are found by applying the law of segregation: the paired alleles separate during gamete formation, so each gamete receives one or the other allele but not both — TT gives only T gametes and tt gives only t gametes, so all F1 progeny are Tt and tall. If the F1 (Tt) are self-pollinated, each parent gives T and t gametes, and combining them gives TT, Tt, Tt and tt, i.e. a 3:1 ratio of tall to short in F2. For two characters, the law of independent assortment is used and a Punnett chart of the gametes predicts the progeny in the 9:3:3:1 ratio, so the genotypes and phenotypes of the offspring, and their expected proportions, are known before the cross is made.

Q: 8. Describe the effects of the environment that lead to the selection of a variant which is more adapted to it.

Ans: The environment has no role in the initial production of variations, but once variations are produced, the individuals with variations best suited to that particular environment have more chances of survival. Natural selection works in this way: organisms overproduce, resources are limited, so they compete with one another; during this competition the individuals with better variations are able to survive, while the individuals with poor adaptability are excluded from the environment. The survivors reproduce and pass on their favourable variations, so each new generation has a higher proportion of individuals with better variations, and through continuous natural selection the population changes entirely. The unit's example is pesticide resistance in flour beetles: the few beetles whose variation enabled them to resist the pesticide survived, their offspring inherited the resistance, and the percentage of resistant individuals increased until even high concentrations of the pesticide could not kill them.

lessons.title: Multiple Choice Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Energy flow in an ecosystem is unidirectional and ends as heat loss.
  • The atmosphere is the largest reservoir of nitrogen.
  • A food web is made of interlocking food chains.
  • Reduce, Reuse and Recycle are the three Rs for a better environment.
  • Denitrification reduces nitrates and nitrites to nitrogen gas.
  • Rhizobium with leguminous plants is an example of mutualism.

Solved Exercises

Exercise A: Select the correct answer.

Q: 1. Energy flow through an ecosystem is always:

Options: (a) Unidirectional (b) Cyclic (c) Reversible (d) Multidirectional

Correct answer: Unidirectional

Q: 2. The largest reservoir of nitrogen on our planet is:

Options: (a) Ocean (b) Atmosphere (c) Phage DNA (d) Fossil fuels

Correct answer: Atmosphere

Q: 3. Overgrazing results in:

Options: (a) Soil erosion (b) Retention of useful species (c) Productive soils (d) All of the above

Correct answer: Soil erosion

Q: 4. The three R's responsible for a better environment are:

Options: (a) Reduce, Reuse, Recycle (b) Read, Register, Recall (c) Random, Reduce, Recall (d) Reduce, Rebuild, Restrict

Correct answer: Reduce, Reuse, Recycle

Q: 5. A food web consists of:

Options: (a) Interlocking food chains (b) Producers, consumers and decomposers (c) A portion of a food chain (d) A set of similar consumers

Correct answer: Interlocking food chains

Q: 6. Predation helps to maintain balance in:

Options: (a) Community (b) Population (c) Ecology (d) Ecosystem

Correct answer: Ecosystem

Q: 7. An ecological pyramid refers to the:

Options: (a) Pyramid of energy (b) Pyramid of number (c) Pyramid of biomass (d) All of the above

Correct answer: All of the above

Q: 8. When the oxides of nitrogen (NO, NO2) and sulphur (SO, SO2, SO3) interacts with water vapours then the acids produced are:

Options: (a) Acetic and Citric acid (b) Sulphuric and Nitric acid (c) Hydrochloric and Nitric acid (d) Sulphuric and Citric acid

Correct answer: Sulphuric and Nitric acid

Q: 9. The process in which nitrates and nitrites are reduced to nitrogen gas by bacteria is:

Options: (a) Assimilation (b) Denitrification (c) Ammonification (d) Nitrification

Correct answer: Denitrification

Q: 10. The relationship between Rhizobium bacteria and leguminous plants is an example of:

Options: (a) Parasitism (b) Mutualism (c) Commensalism (d) None of these

Correct answer: Mutualism

mcqs.q: 1. Energy flow through an ecosystem is always:
mcqs.why: Energy enters as sunlight, passes through trophic levels as food and is finally lost as heat, so it flows in one direction only and never cycles back.

mcqs.q: 2. The largest reservoir of nitrogen on our planet is:
mcqs.why: Most of the air is nitrogen gas N2, so the atmosphere holds far more nitrogen than oceans, fossil fuels or any other reservoir on the planet.

mcqs.q: 3. Overgrazing results in:
mcqs.why: Overgrazing removes the plant cover that binds the soil, so the exposed soil is washed and blown away. It does not retain useful species or make soils productive.

mcqs.q: 4. The three R's responsible for a better environment are:
mcqs.why: The three Rs are Reduce, Reuse and Recycle: use less, use things again, and process waste into new products to protect the environment.

mcqs.q: 5. A food web consists of:
options: A portion of a food chain
mcqs.why: A single consumer eats more than one producer and is eaten by more than one consumer, so many food chains link together into an interlocking food web.

mcqs.q: 6. Predation helps to maintain balance in:
mcqs.why: Predators capture and feed on prey, controlling prey numbers and their distribution and abundance, which keeps the whole ecosystem in balance.

mcqs.q: 7. An ecological pyramid refers to the:
options: Pyramid of energy, pyramid of number and pyramid of biomass
mcqs.why: The book's keyed option 'All of the above' was replaced by this explicit combined option: an ecological pyramid can show energy, numbers or biomass at successive trophic levels, so the combined option covers all three named types.

mcqs.q: 8. When the oxides of nitrogen (NO, NO2) and sulphur (SO, SO2, SO3) interacts with water vapours then the acids produced are:
mcqs.why: Sulphur oxides with water vapour give sulphuric acid and nitrogen oxides with water vapour give nitric acid; these are the acids of acid rain.

mcqs.q: 9. The process in which nitrates and nitrites are reduced to nitrogen gas by bacteria is:
mcqs.why: In denitrification, bacteria such as Pseudomonas convert nitrates and nitrites back into molecular nitrogen gas, which is lost to the atmosphere.

mcqs.q: 10. The relationship between Rhizobium bacteria and leguminous plants is an example of:
mcqs.why: Rhizobium in root nodules gets food from the legume and in return converts atmospheric nitrogen into nitrates for the plant, so both partners benefit, which is mutualism.

lessons.title: Short Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • A species breeds naturally to produce fertile offspring.
  • The biosphere is about 20 km thick across air, earth and water.
  • A population is one species; a community is many populations together.
  • Nitrosomonas makes nitrites and Nitrobacter makes nitrates.
  • Deforestation destroys habitats and dries out forest soils.
  • Parasitism benefits the parasite and harms the host.

Solved Exercises

Exercise B: Write short answers to the following questions.

Q: 1. Define the terms: species, biosphere and ecosystem.

Ans: Species: A species is a group of similar organisms that can breed with one another naturally to produce fertile offsprings. Members of the same species have the same needs and compete with one another for them. Biosphere: The parts of the earth where life exists is called the biosphere. It is the broadest level of ecological organisation, about 20 km thick, and extends into the atmosphere (air), lithosphere (earth) and hydrosphere (water). Ecosystem: An ecosystem is the basic structural and functional unit of ecology. It is a natural area where the living organisms (plants and animals) and their environment interact and exchange materials between them, and this interaction leads to functional stability of the ecosystem.

Q: 2. Differentiate between population and community.

Ans: A population is a group of individuals belonging to the same species, living in the same place at the same time and sharing the same resources, e.g. population of students in a school, population of frogs in a pond, or population of pine trees in the forest. A community consists of all the interacting organisms of different populations living in an area. For example, all the fish, turtles, plants, algae and bacteria in the pond make up a community. Thus a population is of one species only, while a community is made of many different populations.

Q: 3. Differentiate between food chain and food web.

Ans: A food chain is a sequence of consumptions through which energy and nutrients are taken in and used up; simply, it is a process of eating and being eaten, e.g. Grass -> Grasshopper -> Rat -> Snake -> Eagle. All food chains begin from producers and go to consumers. The feeding relationships in a community cannot be represented by simple food chains, because a single consumer eats more than one producer and is eaten by more than one consumer. Thus, many simple food chains are linked together and make a food web, which is a graphical description of feeding relationships among the organisms in an ecological community.

Q: 4. How does deforestation affect the environment?

Ans: Deforestation is the unwise and unplanned destruction or removal of trees. Its most dramatic impact is a loss of habitat for millions of species, because animals and plants live in forests and many cannot afford the destruction of their homes. Deforestation also results in climate change: forest soils are moist, but without protection from sun-blocking tree cover they quickly dry out, and without trees to return water vapours back into the atmosphere and to absorb the greenhouse gases responsible for global warming, many former forest lands can quickly become barren deserts.

Q: 5. Distinguish between herbivore, carnivore, and omnivore.

Ans: Consumers are classified according to what they eat. A consumer that eats only producers is a herbivore, e.g. horse; primary consumers such as insects, rabbits, goats, sheep and cows are also called herbivores because they feed directly on producers. A consumer that eats only other consumers is a carnivore, e.g. lion; those which feed on herbivores are called carnivores, like lizards and frogs. A consumer that eats both producers and consumers is an omnivore, e.g. humans and bear.

Q: 6. Outline the role of bacteria in the nitrogen cycle.

Ans: Bacteria play a role at every stage of the nitrogen cycle. Nitrogen fixing bacteria, for example genus Rhizobium, convert nitrogen gas (N2) to ammonium, often living in symbiotic relationships with legumes such as beans and peas. Decomposers consume dead organic matter and convert its nitrogen to ammonium, and in nitrification Nitrosomonas converts ammonia into nitrites while Nitrobacter converts nitrites into nitrates. In denitrification, bacteria (Pseudomonas) convert nitrates to molecular nitrogen, which is rapidly lost to the atmosphere.

Q: 7. How can overpopulation affect the environment?

Ans: Overpopulation is arguably the most critical threat to the environment. The ever-increasing human population requires more food, which has resulted in extensive agriculture: more land brought under cultivation destroys habitats, forests are destroyed, clearing causes soil erosion, and excessive irrigation and overuse of fertilizers, pesticides and herbicides pollute and make water toxic. Due to the tremendous increase in population, urbanisation and industrialisation, more sewerage enters the rivers and more gases are released into the atmosphere, so environmental conditions become gradually worse and the degradation and depletion of resources follow.

Q: 8. Name any five sources of water pollution.

Ans: Any five sources named in the book are: (1) Incomplete treatment of sewage - domestic sewage water from households is discharged into rivers and lakes. (2) Oil spills during the filling of oil tankers or due to accidents of tankers. (3) Industrial effluent - industries generate waste materials, some containing very toxic compounds of mercury, cadmium, lead, chromium and arsenic. (4) Insecticides such as DDT, which rainwater may carry into streams, rivers and lakes. (5) Chemical fertilizers, most of which are not absorbed by the crops and are washed away by rainwater into lakes or rivers. Other sources in the book are herbicides, leakage from landfills, animal wastes and leakage from underground petroleum storage.

Q: 9. Differentiate between parasitism and mutualism.

Ans: Both are types of symbiosis, a close interaction between organisms of different species for an extended time. In parasitism, an organism called a parasite lives on or in the body of a larger living organism called the host, gets its nourishment from its host's tissues and causes harm to it, so the parasite always benefits and the host is harmed. In mutualism, both the partners are mutually benefited and none of them is harmed, e.g. the nitrogen fixing bacteria in the root nodules of leguminous plants get food from the plants and in return convert atmospheric nitrogen into nitrates and pass them on to the host plant.

Q: 10. Define nitrogen fixation and nitrification.

Ans: Nitrogen fixation is the process where N2 is converted to ammonium with the help of certain bacteria, for example genus Rhizobium, which often form symbiotic relationships with legumes (e.g. beans, peas); high-energy natural events such as lightning, forest fires and hot lava flows can also cause fixation of smaller amounts of nitrogen. Nitrification is the process by which some of the ammonium produced by decomposition is converted to nitrate. It is accomplished by two groups of bacteria: one group (Nitrosomonas) converts ammonia into nitrites and a second group (Nitrobacter) converts nitrites into nitrates.

mcqs.q: What is a species?
options: A group of similar organisms that can breed naturally to produce fertile offspring
The parts of the earth where life exists
A group of different populations living in an area
A natural area where organisms interact with their environment
mcqs.why: The solved answer defines a species as similar organisms that breed with one another naturally to produce fertile offspring; members share the same needs and compete for them.

mcqs.q: How thick is the biosphere, the broadest level of ecological organisation?
mcqs.why: The biosphere is about 20 km thick and extends into the atmosphere, lithosphere and hydrosphere, covering all parts of the earth where life exists.

mcqs.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes a population from a community?
options: A population has many species, a community has one species
A population is non-living, a community is living
A population is one species in one place, a community is many interacting populations in an area
A population lives in water, a community lives on land
mcqs.why: A population is individuals of the same species in the same place at the same time, while a community is all the interacting organisms of different populations in an area.

mcqs.q: In the food chain Grass -> Grasshopper -> Rat -> Snake -> Eagle, which organism is eaten by the snake?
mcqs.why: Reading the chain in order, the snake eats the rat and is itself eaten by the eagle; the grasshopper is eaten by the rat, not by the snake.

mcqs.q: Why can feeding relationships in a community not be shown by a single simple food chain?
options: Because producers do not provide food
Because a consumer eats more than one producer and is eaten by more than one consumer
Because energy flows in a cycle
mcqs.why: The solved answer explains that one consumer feeds on several producers and has several predators, so many chains link together to form a food web.

mcqs.q: What is the most dramatic impact of deforestation?
options: Loss of habitat for millions of species
mcqs.why: Animals and plants live in forests and many cannot survive the destruction of their homes, so habitat loss for millions of species is the most dramatic impact.

mcqs.q: What happens to forest soil when sun-blocking tree cover is removed?
options: It turns into fertile desert soil
mcqs.why: Forest soils are moist, but without protection from sun-blocking tree cover they quickly dry out, and former forest land can become barren desert.

mcqs.q: A consumer that eats only other consumers is called a:
mcqs.why: A carnivore such as a lion eats only other consumers; a herbivore eats only producers and an omnivore such as humans and bear eats both.

mcqs.q: Which bacterium converts ammonia into nitrites during nitrification?
mcqs.why: In nitrification Nitrosomonas converts ammonia into nitrites, and then Nitrobacter converts the nitrites into nitrates; Pseudomonas works in denitrification instead.

mcqs.q: Which bacterium converts nitrates to molecular nitrogen in denitrification?
mcqs.why: The solved answer names Pseudomonas as the denitrifying bacterium that converts nitrates to molecular nitrogen, which is rapidly lost to the atmosphere.

mcqs.q: How does extensive agriculture caused by overpopulation harm the environment?
options: It destroys habitats and clearing causes soil erosion
It reduces the use of fertilizers
mcqs.why: More food demand brings more land under cultivation, which destroys habitats and forests, while clearing causes soil erosion and fertilizers and pesticides pollute water.

mcqs.q: Which of these is a source of water pollution named in the solved answers?
options: Incomplete treatment of sewage discharged into rivers and lakes
mcqs.why: Domestic sewage from households discharged into rivers and lakes is listed first among the sources, along with oil spills, industrial effluent, insecticides and chemical fertilizers.

mcqs.q: Industrial effluent is dangerous because some of it contains toxic compounds of:
options: Mercury, cadmium, lead, chromium and arsenic
mcqs.why: The solved answer states that industries generate waste materials, some containing very toxic compounds of mercury, cadmium, lead, chromium and arsenic.

mcqs.q: In parasitism, what is the effect on the two partners?
options: The parasite benefits and the host is harmed
The host benefits and the parasite is harmed
mcqs.why: A parasite lives on or in the host, takes nourishment from its tissues and causes harm, so the parasite always benefits and the host is harmed; in mutualism both benefit.

mcqs.q: Besides bacteria, which natural events can also fix nitrogen in smaller amounts?
options: Lightning, forest fires and hot lava flows
mcqs.why: The solved answer says high-energy natural events such as lightning, forest fires and hot lava flows can also cause fixation of smaller amounts of nitrogen.

lessons.title: Detailed Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • The nitrogen cycle has fixation, uptake and decay, nitrification and denitrification.
  • Energy flow is non-cyclic while material flow is cyclic.
  • Only about 10% of energy passes to the next trophic level.
  • Competition and predation control population sizes in ecosystems.
  • Decomposers recycle nutrients through biogeochemical cycles.
  • Biomass decreases upwards: 809, 37, 11 and 1.5 g/m2.

Solved Exercises

Exercise C: Write detailed answers to the following questions:

Q: 1. Describe the nitrogen cycle in detail. What would happen if the nitrogen cycle stopped working?

Ans: Nitrogen (N) is an essential component of DNA, RNA and proteins, the building blocks of life, and all organisms require nitrogen to live and grow. Although most of the air is N2, most atmospheric nitrogen is unavailable to organisms because the strong triple bond in N2 makes it relatively inert, so it must first be converted to ammonium (NH4+), nitrate (NO3-) or organic nitrogen. The cycle has four main stages. 1. Nitrogen fixation: N2 is converted to ammonium with the help of certain bacteria, e.g. genus Rhizobium, which often form symbiotic relationships with legumes (beans, peas); lightning, forest fires and hot lava flows also fix smaller amounts. 2. Nitrogen uptake and decay: the ammonia produced is incorporated into proteins and other organic compounds by bacteria or another soil organism; when these organisms die, decomposers break the organic compounds and nitrogen is converted to ammonium, which is available for use by plants or for further transformation to nitrate through nitrification. 3. Nitrification: Nitrosomonas converts ammonia into nitrites and Nitrobacter converts nitrites into nitrates. 4. Denitrification: oxidized forms such as nitrate and nitrite (NO2) are converted to molecular nitrogen (N2) and, to a lesser extent, nitrous oxide gas by bacteria (Pseudomonas); molecular nitrogen is rapidly lost to the atmosphere. Denitrification is the only nitrogen transformation that removes nitrogen from ecosystems, and it roughly balances the amount fixed by the nitrogen fixers. Diagram (in words): Fig. 16.12 Nitrogen Cycle - at the top, ATMOSPHERIC NITROGEN N2, with ATMOSPHERIC FIXATION on one side and INDUSTRIAL FIXATION (commercial fertilizer) on the other, and NITROUS OXIDE N2O; BIOLOGICAL FIXATION (by legume plants) and plant uptake take nitrogen down to HARVESTABLE PRODUCT, Plant Residues and ORGANIC MATTER in the soil; in the soil, Immobilization links ORGANIC MATTER and AMMONIUM NH4, AMMONIA NH3 is shown with Volatilization, Animal Manures enter the soil, Nitrification converts AMMONIUM NH4 to NITRATE NO3-, Denitrification returns nitrate to the atmosphere, and LEACHING LOSS removes nitrate from the soil. If the nitrogen cycle stopped working, nitrogen would no longer be fixed into ammonium and nitrates, plants could not take it up to make proteins and other compounds, and the nitrogen in dead organisms would not be returned in usable forms. Since nitrogen is essential for DNA, RNA and proteins, organisms could not live and grow, the recycling of this essential nutrient would cease, and the ecological balance maintained by biogeochemical cycles would break down.

Q: 2. Compare the flow of materials and the flow of energy in the ecosystem.

Ans: The existence of the living world depends upon the flow of energy and circulation of materials through the ecosystem, but the two flows differ. Flow of energy is non-cyclic: the sun is the ultimate source of energy in all ecosystems, providing it in the form of sunlight, of which only a tiny fraction reaches the Earth and producers can use only a small part. Producers transform sunlight into chemical energy (food) through photosynthesis, and this chemical energy flows through the ecosystem in the form of food. When respiration occurs, energy is released; the organism uses a portion for its metabolism and other activities, while the rest is lost in the surroundings as heat. The ultimate fate of all energy in ecosystems is to be lost as heat, so energy does not recycle in the ecosystem. Flow of materials is cyclic: producers obtain inorganic materials (carbon dioxide, water etc.) from the environment and use them to prepare organic material (food); the materials are passed from organism to organism as one organism is consumed by another. Ultimately all organisms die and become detritus; decomposers feed on detritus and break the organic materials into inorganic ones, which are returned to the environment to be taken up again. In this way, the materials are recycled in the ecosystem. Diagram (in words): Fig. 16.6 Flow of materials and energy in ecosystem - Sun at the top sends energy (red arrows, Flow of Energy) down to Producers; energy passes from Producers to Herbivores (Primary consumers), to Carnivores (Secondary consumers) and to Decomposers, with Heat lost at each step; materials (blue arrows, Flow of Materials) move in a circular loop from Producers to Herbivores, Carnivores and Decomposers and back to Producers.

Q: 3. Write a note on the energy flow through different components of an ecosystem.

Ans: The sun is the ultimate source of energy in all ecosystems and provides energy in the form of sunlight, but only a tiny fraction of sunlight reaches the Earth and producers can use only a small part of it. Producers (green plants and algae, and some bacteria) transform sunlight into chemical energy (food) through photosynthesis; they themselves utilise a part of this food, while consumers and decomposers utilise the remaining food. The chemical energy then flows through the ecosystem in the form of food: primary consumers (herbivores) feed directly on producers, secondary consumers feed on primary consumers, and tertiary consumers are the top consumers. At each trophic level the amount of energy reduces during transfer to the next level: when producers capture sunlight they convert only a small percentage into their biomass, the rest is used in metabolic processes and is also lost, and in general only 10% of the energy consumed by one level is available to the next. For example, if rabbits consume 1000 K Cal of plant energy, they might only be able to form 100 K Cal of new rabbit tissues. When respiration occurs, energy is released, a portion is used for metabolism and other activities, and the rest is lost in the surroundings as heat, so the ultimate fate of all energy is to be lost as heat and it does not recycle. Diagram (in words): Fig. 16.5 Flow of energy in an ecosystem - Sunlight 1000 J reaches the producer (plant); 990 J is Lost to environment, 10 J passes As Food to the herbivore (rabbit); 9 J is Lost to environment and 1 J passes As Food to the carnivore (eagle), the arrows representing the movement of energy through the ecosystem.

Q: 4. What are the different ways through which organisms of the ecosystem interact with each other?

Ans: In all ecosystems, the organisms living in the same area interact with each other; these interactions may be intraspecific, i.e. between organisms of the same species, or inter-specific, i.e. between organisms of different species. a. Competition is an interaction between organisms for limited supply of at least one resource (such as food, water and space); it may be intraspecific (among members of the same species) or inter-specific (among individuals of different species), e.g. lions and leopards compete for prey (zebras) and many plant species compete for soil or sunlight. Competition maintains a balance between the resources and the size of populations: the species able to use a resource more efficiently leaves less for the weaker species, resulting in a reduction in the size of the weaker population or its complete elimination. b. Predation is an inter-specific interaction in which the predator captures, readily kills and feeds on an individual of another species, called the prey, e.g. a lion attacking a zebra (Fig. 16.13). Predation has important effects on the distribution and abundance of organisms; a prey in an area without its natural predator becomes a menace, as rabbits introduced in Australia multiplied enormously without a predator. Some plants, e.g. pitcher plant, sundew and Venus flytrap, also live as predators, capturing insects with modified leaves, secreting enzymes on them and absorbing the digested food. c. Symbiosis literally means 'living together' and is a close interaction between organisms of different species for an extended time, in which one species always benefits while the second may be harmed, not affected or benefited. Its three types are parasitism, mutualism and commensalism, described in detail in the answer on symbiosis.

Q: 5. Discuss the biotic components of the ecosystem.

Ans: An ecosystem consists of two major components, abiotic and biotic, both equally important for its proper functioning. The biotic components are the living components of an ecosystem, and they are of three types. 1. Producers: Autotrophs are able to produce food by utilising energy and inorganic nutrients, so they are called producers. The producers themselves utilise a part of this food while consumers and decomposers utilise the remaining food. Green plants and algae are the major producers; they carry out photosynthesis, using sunlight for the preparation of food. Some types of bacteria are also producers and carry out chemosynthesis, using energy stored in inorganic molecules to produce food. 2. Consumers: Consumers cannot prepare food and depend upon other organisms for their food; all animals, most protists, all fungi and many bacteria are included, and they are also called heterotrophs. They are of three types: (i) Primary consumers, also called herbivores, feed directly on producers - insects, rabbits, goats, sheep and cows on land, and crustaceans (arthropods), molluscs and some fishes in water. (ii) Secondary consumers feed on primary consumers (herbivores) or producers; those which feed on herbivores are called carnivores, like lizards and frogs. (iii) Tertiary consumers are the top consumers and get their food from primary consumers and secondary consumers, e.g. lion, tiger and hawk. Consumers may also be classified by what they eat: a herbivore eats only producers, a carnivore eats only other consumers, and an omnivore eats both producers and consumers. 3. Decomposers: Decomposers are also called saprophytes; they get their energy by decomposing the remains of dead animals and plants, and many bacteria and fungi are included in this group.
