They are also called cleaners of the ecosystem, because they help to run various biogeochemical cycles like the nitrogen cycle and carbon cycle, and in this way valuable nutrients are recycled for reuse.

Q: 6. Write notes on the three types of symbiosis.

Ans: Symbiosis literally means 'living together'. It is defined as a close interaction between organisms of different species for an extended time; although one species always benefits in a symbiotic relationship, the second species may be harmed, not affected or benefited. There are three types of symbiosis. (i) Parasitism: An organism called a parasite lives on or in the body of a larger living organism called the host; the parasite gets its nourishment from its host's tissues and causes harm to it, and the diseases in host organisms caused by parasites are called infestations. Parasites such as aphids, lice, leeches, fleas, ticks and mosquitoes remain on the outside of their hosts' bodies and are called ectoparasites, while many parasites live inside the host's body and are called endoparasites, e.g. plasmodium, tapeworm and polio virus. Some plants (e.g. cuscuta) also live as parasites: cuscuta has no green leaves, cannot manufacture food, grows on the surface of big plants (hosts), wraps itself around them and produces 'haustoria' (root) through which it inserts itself into the host and draws nourishment, weakening it. Parasites have a strong negative effect on the growth of the host's population, and epidemics of parasitic diseases can even cause the extinction of the host population. (ii) Mutualism: In this type of relationship, both the partners are mutually benefited and none of them is harmed. For example, the roots of leguminous plants (pea, bean etc.) have small nodules which contain nitrogen fixing bacteria; these bacteria get food from these plants and in return convert atmospheric nitrogen into nitrates and pass them on to the host plant. Other examples are termites and the protists living in their gut, which help them digest the cellulose of wood while the termite provides food and shelter, and the bacteria living in our intestine, which get food and a proper environment and in turn produce vitamin K, essential for blood clotting. (iii) Commensalism: In commensalism only one partner is benefited and the other is neither benefited nor harmed. For example, many epiphytes such as orchids grow on the branches of other trees, using the tree only for attachment while preparing their own food by photosynthesis, so the orchids are benefited but the tree is neither benefited nor harmed. Similarly, barnacles attach with the body of marine animals including whales; barnacles get a ride to better places but the large animals are not affected.

Q: 7. Enlist the causes of water pollution and also describe how water pollution can be controlled.

Ans: Water pollution is the contamination of water bodies (e.g. lakes, rivers, oceans and ground water), and occurs when pollutants are discharged directly or indirectly into water bodies without adequate treatment to remove harmful compounds. Causes: (a) Incomplete treatment of sewage - domestic sewage water from households is discharged into rivers and lakes; due to sewage pollution the concentration of ammonia, nitrates and phosphate increases and that of oxygen decreases, resulting in the death of aquatic life, and waterborne diseases such as typhoid, amoebiasis, hepatitis and diarrhoea spread. (b) Oil spills during the filling of oil tankers or due to accidents of tankers; oil spread over the water surface prevents the penetration of sunlight and mixing of oxygen with water, so marine plants and animals die because of suffocation. (c) Industrial effluent - industries generate a lot of waste materials, some containing very toxic compounds of mercury, cadmium, lead, chromium and arsenic. (d) Insecticides such as DDT, which decomposers cannot breakdown and rainwater may carry into streams, rivers and lakes, resulting in the poisoning of fish or other animals drinking such water. (e) Herbicides, some containing dioxin, washed by rainwater into streams or rivers, which can cause cancer. (f) Chemical fertilizers not absorbed by the crops, washed away into lakes or rivers, adversely affecting aquatic life. (g) Leakage from landfills, which pollutes underground water. (h) Animal wastes not disposed off properly, washed away into the rivers when it rains. (i) Leakage from underground petroleum storage pipes, mixing petroleum with underground water. Control of water pollution: 1. Waste water treatment is the most direct method - it is the removal of impurities from waste water before it reaches water bodies (lakes, rivers, sea). 2. Removal of pollutants from underground water - water supply agencies should apply techniques e.g. reverse osmosis and filtration for the removal of pollutants from water. 3. Reutilisation and recycling of wastes - various wastes may be recycled to produce beneficial products, e.g. urban wastes may be recycled to generate cheaper biogas and electricity. 4. Absorption by plants - certain plants can absorb pollutants from the water present in soil and accumulate such pollutants in their bodies without any harm.

Q: 8. Write a comprehensive note on land pollution.

Ans: Land pollution is the degradation of the Earth's land surfaces, often caused by human activities and misuse of land resources. It occurs when waste is not disposed off properly. The major causes of land pollution are: a. Municipal solid wastes - these are the solid materials added by homes, institutions and industry, of the following types: Garbage: moist and decomposable (biodegradable) food wastes; Rubbish: dry materials such as paper, glass, textiles and plastic objects; Trash: bulky waste materials (e.g. discarded mattresses, appliances, furniture); and Medical wastes: surgical gloves, body fluids (e.g. blood) and X-ray equipment. b. Agricultural activities - besides domestic waste, pesticides and herbicides used by farmers to increase crop yields also pollute the land when they are washed into the soil. c. Construction debris - this includes wood and metal objects, concrete rubble, asphalt and other materials produced when structures are built or demolished. d. Air and water pollutants - when polluted water enters the soil, it changes the quality of soil and causes land pollution; similarly, air pollutants can also lead to land pollution, for example acid rain dissolves away some of the important nutrients present in the soil and changes the composition of the soil. Control (from the book's control of land pollution): 1. Production of less wastes and recycling - people should produce less waste by using and re-using some products like plastic bags and towels; waste materials (plastics, glass, paper etc.) can be recycled to make new objects. 2. Proper disposal of wastes - if waste is properly disposed off, the chances of reducing land pollution increase significantly; throwing garbage on the roads and footpaths causes land pollution and huge inconvenience to passers-by. 3. Solid waste management - the government should construct standard landfills with an impermeable bottom that do not allow the leakage of pollutants to the underground water or the release of methane gas into the atmosphere; methane collected in the landfill can be used as biogas. 4. Disposal of dangerous waste - solid hazardous waste is buried in deep landfills while liquid hazardous wastes are disposed of in deep-wells, with impermeable bottoms and sealed layers at a safe distance from drinking-water supplies.

Q: 9. Explain, by making diagrams, the pyramids of number and biomass.

Ans: Diagram (in words): Pyramid of biomass (Fig. 16.9) - a stepped pyramid with the widest block at the bottom labelled Producer, 809 g/m2; above it a smaller block labelled Primary consumer, 37 g/m2; above it a still smaller block labelled Secondary consumer, 11 g/m2; and at the top the smallest block labelled Tertiary consumer, 1.5 g/m2. The pyramid of biomass represents the amount of biomass (total amount of living or organic matter of all organisms) in each trophic level in an ecosystem. Because biomass is lost in the transfer from one level to the next, there is successively less total biomass as you move up trophic levels, and in general higher trophic levels have less total biomass than those below. Diagram (in words): Pyramid of numbers (Fig. 16.10) - a triangle divided into horizontal layers: the broad base is labelled Primary Producers: Plants (1500000); the middle layer is labelled Primary Consumers: Ants (5000); and the small top layer is labelled Tertiary Consumers: Thorny Lizards (50). The pyramid of numbers represents the number of organisms at each trophic level in an ecosystem. In pyramids of numbers, each successive trophic level has fewer organisms: the number of producers is largest, at the next trophic level of primary consumers or herbivores the number of organisms is less than the previous level, at the third trophic level of secondary consumers or carnivores there are lesser numbers than primary consumers, and in all successive trophic levels the numbers of organisms go on decreasing.

Q: 10. Write a note on the causes and effects of air pollution.

Ans: Air pollution is defined as the presence of any substance in the atmosphere added by the activities of human beings, which can affect the comfort, safety and health of living organisms. Major causes of air pollution given in the book are: (a) Oxides of carbon - combustion of fuel processes produces oxides of carbon like carbon dioxide and carbon monoxides. (b) Oxides of nitrogen - the sources of oxides of nitrogen are chemical fertilizers, lightning and decay of organic matter. (c) Oxides of Sulphur - burning fuels in cars produces sulphur dioxide; it is also emitted from brick kilns and volcanic eruption. (d) Chlorofluorocarbons - CFCs emissions from refrigerators and air conditioners are major reasons for depletion of the ozone layer. (e) Lead compounds - compounds of lead cause air pollution, which can cause damage to the brain. (f) Particulates - these are the particles suspended in the air like dust particles, ethylene and acetylene. Factories and vehicles are major sources of air pollutants (Fig. 16.23). Effects of air pollution listed in the book are: reduced lung functioning; irritation of eyes, nose, mouth and throat; increased respiratory disease such as bronchitis and asthma; reduced energy levels; headaches and dizziness; disruption of endocrine, reproductive and immune systems; cardiovascular problems; and cancer.

mcqs.q: Why is most atmospheric nitrogen unavailable to organisms directly?
options: Because there is very little nitrogen in the air
Because the strong triple bond in N2 makes it relatively inert
Because nitrogen dissolves completely in rainwater
Because plants reject nitrogen gas through their roots
mcqs.why: Although most of the air is N2, its strong triple bond makes it relatively inert, so it must first be converted to ammonium, nitrate or organic nitrogen before use.

mcqs.q: Denitrification is described as the only nitrogen transformation that:
mcqs.why: Denitrification converts nitrate and nitrite to molecular nitrogen lost to the atmosphere; it is the only transformation that removes nitrogen and it roughly balances fixation.

mcqs.q: How do the flows of energy and materials in an ecosystem differ?
options: Energy flow is cyclic and material flow is non-cyclic
Energy flow is non-cyclic and material flow is cyclic
mcqs.why: Energy is finally lost as heat and does not recycle, while materials pass from organism to organism and decomposers return them as inorganic matter to be taken up again.

mcqs.q: What is the ultimate fate of all energy in an ecosystem?
options: It is stored forever in decomposers
It is recycled back to producers
It is lost as heat in the surroundings
It is converted into inorganic materials
mcqs.why: At respiration a portion of energy is used for metabolism and the rest is lost as heat, so the ultimate fate of all energy in ecosystems is to be lost as heat.

mcqs.q: Rabbits consume 1000 K Cal of plant energy. Using the 10% rule, how much new rabbit tissue energy can they form?
mcqs.why: Working: only 10% of energy at one level is available to the next. 10% of 1000 K Cal = 1000 x 10/100 = 100 K Cal, exactly the example given in the solved answer.

mcqs.q: In the energy diagram, 1000 J of sunlight reaches a plant and 10 J passes as food to a rabbit, which then passes food energy to an eagle. How much reaches the eagle?
mcqs.why: Working from Fig. 16.5: plant to rabbit passes 10 J, rabbit loses 9 J to the environment, so 10 - 9 = 1 J passes as food to the carnivore eagle; 990 J was lost at the plant stage.

mcqs.q: Lions and leopards competing for zebras is an example of:
mcqs.why: Lions and leopards are different species competing for the same limited resource, prey zebras, so this is inter-specific competition; competition within one species would be intraspecific.

mcqs.q: Rabbits introduced in Australia multiplied enormously mainly because:
options: They had no natural predator there
They lived in symbiosis with plants
mcqs.why: The solved answer explains that a prey in an area without its natural predator becomes a menace; rabbits in Australia multiplied enormously without a predator to control them.

mcqs.q: Which plants live as predators by capturing insects with modified leaves?
options: Pitcher plant, sundew and Venus flytrap
mcqs.why: Pitcher plant, sundew and Venus flytrap capture insects with modified leaves, secrete enzymes on them and absorb the digested food, so they live as predators.

mcqs.q: Some bacteria act as producers by chemosynthesis. This means they:
options: Use energy stored in inorganic molecules to produce food
Feed on dead animals and plants
Depend on other organisms for food
mcqs.why: Green plants and algae make food by photosynthesis using sunlight, but some bacteria are producers that carry out chemosynthesis, using energy stored in inorganic molecules.

mcqs.q: Decomposers are called cleaners of the ecosystem because they:
options: Help run biogeochemical cycles so nutrients are recycled for reuse
mcqs.why: Decomposers break down dead remains and help run cycles like the nitrogen and carbon cycles, so valuable nutrients are recycled for reuse by other organisms.

mcqs.q: Cuscuta harms its host plant by drawing nourishment through structures called:
mcqs.why: Cuscuta has no green leaves and cannot make food; it wraps around big host plants and produces haustoria through which it inserts itself into the host and draws nourishment, weakening it.

mcqs.q: Termites and the protists in their gut show mutualism because:
options: The protists help digest cellulose while the termite provides food and shelter
mcqs.why: Both partners benefit: protists in the termite gut help digest the cellulose of wood, and the termite in return provides them with food and shelter.

mcqs.q: Sewage pollution of water increases ammonia, nitrates and phosphate while it:
options: Decreases oxygen, causing death of aquatic life
mcqs.why: Due to sewage pollution the concentration of ammonia, nitrates and phosphate increases and that of oxygen decreases, resulting in the death of aquatic life and spread of diseases like typhoid and hepatitis.

mcqs.q: In the pyramid of biomass, the biomass values from producers to tertiary consumers are:
mcqs.why: Fig. 16.9 gives Producer 809 g/m2, Primary consumer 37 g/m2, Secondary consumer 11 g/m2 and Tertiary consumer 1.5 g/m2; biomass is lost at each transfer, so higher levels have less biomass.

lessons.title: Activities
lessons.notes_html:
Solved Exercises

Activities

Q: Visit a pond and compare the abiotic and biotic factors of a pond with that of an aquarium.

Ans: Model answer based on the book's components of an ecosystem. Abiotic factors of the pond: sunlight, water, temperature, soil (the sand/mud at the bottom, whose characteristics affect the types of plants and algae that can grow), air and humidity - the same kinds of abiotic components the book lists for any ecosystem. Its biotic factors form a community: all the fish, turtles, plants, algae and bacteria in the pond make up a community, with algae and water plants as producers, small animals and fishes as primary, secondary and tertiary consumers, and bacteria and fungi as decomposers; the book's own activity for the pond ecosystem is to identify and enlist producers and consumers in the pond and describe the interactions among biotic and abiotic factors involved. In an aquarium the same two kinds of factors are present but on a small, man-made scale: the abiotic factors are the water in the tank, the light provided, the temperature, and the sand or gravel at the bottom, while the biotic factors are the few plants or algae kept as producers, the fishes kept as consumers, and microbes as decomposers. Unlike the pond, which is a natural ecosystem where living organisms and their environment interact and exchange materials and maintain functional stability on their own, the aquarium depends on man for food, cleaning and the maintenance of its abiotic conditions.

lessons.title: Science, Technology and Society
lessons.notes_html:
Solved Exercises

Science, Technology and Society

Q: 1. State how your city or village is an ecosystem and describe your position and role in that ecosystem.

Ans: Model answer: An ecosystem is a natural area where the living organisms and their environment interact and exchange materials between them. A city or village is such an area: its abiotic components are sunlight, water, temperature, soil, air, humidity and the other physical and chemical characteristics of the environment, and its biotic components are the producers (trees, crops and other green plants), the consumers (human beings and animals) and the decomposers (bacteria and fungi) living there, all interacting with each other and with the non-living world. My position in this ecosystem is that of a consumer - human beings are omnivores, eating both producers and consumers. My role is therefore to use the resources the environment provides for my needs without disturbing the delicate balance of the environment, for example by conserving resources and controlling pollution, because in a balanced ecosystem the interactions and biogeochemical cycles run smoothly and all the species get natural resources.

Q: 2. Describe the possible consequences of competition (due to limited resources and overpopulation) in human society.

Ans: Model answer: Competition is an interaction between organisms for limited supply of at least one resource (such as food, water and space), and competition maintains a balance between the resources and the size of populations. In competition, one species is able to use a resource more efficiently than the other, so less of the resource is available to the weaker species, which results in a reduction in the size of the weaker population or its complete elimination. Applied to human society, overpopulation increases competition for the limited resources of food, water, land, education and employment. The book gives the reasons why population control is urgent: to reduce burden and stabilise our resources, to reduce the incidence of famine, to reduce threats to the already stressed ecosystem, to give current and future generations better education, and to provide chances for employment and better survival - so where competition is not controlled, the consequences are pressure on resources, famine, fewer chances of education and employment, and greater stress on the ecosystem.

Q: 3. Use data from the Internet and literature on Pakistan's population growth from 1998 to 2017 and interpret this population growth and the possible consequences on our society.

Ans: Model answer (interpretation based on the book; the 1998-2017 figures themselves are to be taken from the Internet and literature, as the activity directs): The book states that until the beginning of the 19th century the size of the human population was small in relation to environmental resources, so there was no immediate shortage, but with the increase in population at an unexpected rate humans are using environmental resources at an increasing rate, which has created degradation and depletion of resources and local effects like pollution and deforestation. Interpreting Pakistan's growth on this pattern: a fast-growing population requires an effective method for production of more food, resulting in extensive agriculture, with destruction of habitats, waterlogging and salinity from canals, pollution of soil and water by overuse of fertilizers, toxic water from over-use of pesticides and herbicides, destruction of forests, soil erosion and silting that decreases the life span of dams. Due to the tremendous increase in population, urbanisation and industrialisation, more sewerage enters the rivers and more gases are released into the atmosphere, so local problems of environmental pollution become global ones, and new industrial products, toxic chemicals and solid wastes make the land, air and water polluted.

Q: 4. Identify the environmental problems in your community. What are the causes and what should be done to solve these problems?

Ans: Model answer: The environmental problems named in the book that are found in a community are pollution of air, water and land, deforestation and the improper disposal of solid waste - Fig. 16.27 notes that if solid waste is not properly treated, such sights will keep on increasing in every nook and corner of Pakistan, and Fig. 16.24 notes that lack of proper treatment of sewage is a common sight in Pakistan. Their causes are the human activities described in the unit: discharge of untreated sewage and industrial effluent into water, oil spills, insecticides, herbicides and chemical fertilizers washed into water, municipal solid wastes (garbage, rubbish, trash and medical wastes) not disposed off properly, smoke and gases from factories and vehicles running on fossil fuels, and the unwise and unplanned removal of trees. What should be done is the book's control measures: treatment of industrial exhausts and waste water before release, use of public transportation, lead-free and low sulphur fuels, conservation of energy, use of clean energy resources, plantation of trees (afforestation), removal of pollutants from underground water by reverse osmosis and filtration, reutilisation and recycling of wastes, production of less waste, proper disposal of wastes, and standard landfills under solid waste management. The Pakistan Environmental Protection Agency (Pak-EPA), established under the Pakistan Environmental Protection Act (PEPA) 1997, ensures a clean environment by conducting scientific research for the prevention of pollution, providing information and guidance to the public on environmental matters, and specifying safeguards for the prevention of accidents and disasters.

Q: 5. How would you design a campaign against pollution in your area? What would the key messages be and what would you prioritise? Give reasons.

Ans: Model answer: The campaign would be built on the book's control measures and conservation methods, because pollution causes unexpected and sometimes serious and devastating changes in our land, river and sea environments, can kill animals and plants, and will harm us too. Key messages: treat industrial exhausts before their release into the atmosphere; use public transportation or car-pooling to save energy and money; use lead-free fuels in vehicles and low sulphur coal in industry; conserve energy - switch off fans and lights when not in the room and use energy saver lights/LED; use clean energy resources like solar, wind and geothermal; and plant trees, because trees absorb carbon dioxide from the air. For water and land the messages would be: treat waste water before it reaches water bodies, recycle wastes, produce less waste by reducing, reusing and recycling (the three R's responsible for a better environment), and dispose of waste properly instead of throwing garbage on roads and footpaths. Priority would be given first to the measures every person can practise at personal level - saving electricity, reducing, reusing and recycling waste, proper disposal of garbage and planting a tree - because the book shows that attempts are being made on personal, industrial and governmental levels, and personal habits (including not leaving electronic items on charge indefinitely overnight, but recharging them and then unplugging them so as not to waste energy) are the part the people of the area can start at once.

Q: 6. Organise a poster or picture exhibition at school on some environmental topic.

Ans: Model answer: A poster or picture exhibition can be organised at school on a topic taken from this unit, such as 'Control of Pollution' or 'Conservation of Nature'. Posters can be made from the book's own material and figures: factories and vehicles as major sources of air pollutants (Fig. 16.23), lack of proper treatment of sewage (Fig. 16.24), oil spills dangerous for marine life (Fig. 16.25), insecticides polluting water bodies (Fig. 16.26), improper and proper disposal of solid waste (Fig. 16.28), deforestation in tropical rainforests (Fig. 16.20), and slums alongside multi-storied skyscrapers in megacities (Fig. 16.19). The exhibition should carry the book's messages: conservation is the protection and preservation of natural resources; the three methods of conservation are Reduce, Reuse and Recycle; other ways include planting a tree, walking as much as you can, riding bikes for short distances, using carpooling, using energy-efficient light bulbs, using both sides of your paper, avoiding plastic water bottles, buying and eating local foods, growing your own vegetables, and unplugging electronics that aren't in use. One ton of waste paper recycled can save approximately 17 trees, which makes a strong poster message.

lessons.title: Multiple Choice Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Restriction endonucleases cut DNA at specific sequences.
  • Vector DNA carries the gene of interest to the target cell.
  • rDNA stands for recombinant DNA from two different organisms.
  • A plasmid can be used as a vector to insert a gene into bacteria.
  • Inserting a healthy gene for a defective one is gene therapy.
  • Lactobacillus bulgaricus is used in yogurt production.

Solved Exercises

Exercise A: Select the correct answer.

Q: 1. The enzymes which are used to cut the DNA in specified sequences is:

Options: (a) Ligase (b) Protease (c) DNAase (d) Endonuclease

Correct answer: Endonuclease

Q: 2. The DNA molecule in which the gene of interest is inserted for carrying to the target cell is:

Options: (a) Transforming DNA (b) Carrier DNA (c) Phage DNA (d) Vector DNA

Correct answer: Vector DNA

Q: 3. Endonucleases used in genetic engineering are naturally present in:

Options: (a) Bacteriophages (b) Bacterial cells (c) Plasmids (d) Blue green algae

Correct answer: Bacterial cells

Q: 4. Fermenter is a machine which is basically used for:

Options: (a) Increasing fermentation (b) Production of enzymes used in fermentation (c) Production of microorganisms (d) Making the conditions optimum

Correct answer: Production of microorganisms

Q: 5. Lactobacillus bulgaricus is a type of bacteria in the production of:

Options: (a) Alcohol (b) Cheese (c) Yogurt (d) All of the above

Correct answer: Yogurt

Q: 6. In a technique for genetic engineering, rDNA stands for:

Options: (a) Genetic makeup (b) Replicative DNA (c) Recombinant DNA (d) Retro DNA

Correct answer: Recombinant DNA

Q: 7. Interferons are chemical which are used to:

Options: (a) Kill viruses (b) Improve immunity (c) Work as vaccine (d) All of the above

Correct answer: Kill viruses

Q: 8. Which is a molecule containing DNA from two different organisms?

Options: (a) Vector DNA (b) DNA clone (c) Plasmid DNA (d) Recombinant DNA

Correct answer: Recombinant DNA

Q: 9. What term is used for inserting a healthy gene into a person who has a defective gene?

Options: (a) Cloning (b) Gene therapy (c) Vaccination (d) Fermentation

Correct answer: Gene therapy

Q: 10. Which of these can be used as a vector for inserting a gene into bacteria?

Options: (a) Plasmid (b) Algae (c) Yeast (d) E. coli

Correct answer: Plasmid

mcqs.why: Restriction endonucleases cut DNA at specific sites and sequences and are called molecular scissors; ligase does the opposite job of joining DNA fragments.

mcqs.q: 2. The DNA molecule in which the gene of interest is inserted for carrying to the target cell is:
mcqs.why: The gene of interest cannot travel by itself, so it is inserted into vector DNA, a cloning vehicle such as a plasmid, which carries it to the target host cell.

mcqs.q: 3. Endonucleases used in genetic engineering are naturally present in:
mcqs.why: The basic tools of recombinant DNA technology are enzymes of bacterial cells; restriction endonucleases occur naturally in bacterial cells.

mcqs.q: 4. Fermenter is a machine which is basically used for:
options: Production of enzymes used in fermentation
mcqs.why: A fermenter is a large container in which populations of microorganisms are grown on a large scale so that large quantities of their products can be obtained.

mcqs.q: 5. Lactobacillus bulgaricus is a type of bacteria in the production of:
mcqs.why: Lactobacillus bulgaricus is used in lactic acid fermentation of milk as a yogurt starter bacterium, converting lactose to lactic acid to make yogurt.

mcqs.why: rDNA stands for recombinant DNA, the DNA formed by combining genes from two different sources, a donor gene joined into vector DNA.

mcqs.q: 7. Interferons are chemical which are used to:
mcqs.why: Interferon is described in the unit as an anti-virus protein made in genetically modified bacteria and used against viruses; it is not a vaccine.

mcqs.q: 8. Which is a molecule containing DNA from two different organisms?
mcqs.why: Recombinant DNA is by definition a combination of DNA from two different sources, the donor organism and the recipient vector organism.

mcqs.q: 9. What term is used for inserting a healthy gene into a person who has a defective gene?
mcqs.why: Gene therapy treats genetic disorders by introducing a healthy gene into the cells of a person who has a defective gene, for example in blood disorders like thalassaemia.
