mcqs.why: The plasmid, the extra chromosomal circular DNA of Escherichia coli, is the most common vector; E. coli itself is the host bacterium, not the vector.

lessons.title: Short Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Yeast fermentation converts sugars into carbon dioxide and ethyl alcohol.
  • Yogurt starter contains Lactobacillus bulgaricus and Streptococcus thermophiles.
  • The E. coli plasmid is used as a vector for recombinant DNA.
  • Virus resistance was introduced into squashes, tomatoes, potatoes and tobacco.
  • Herbicide resistance was introduced into soybean, corn and cotton.
  • A vector is needed because a gene cannot reach the host by itself.

Solved Exercises

Exercise B: Write short answers to the following questions.

Q: 1. Write about any four products developed through fermentation.

Ans: 1. Alcohol: It is made by the fermentation of a natural source of sugar with a catalyst, which is usually yeast. The carbohydrates (starch and sugars) are converted into carbon dioxide and ethyl alcohol, and alcohol is widely used in medicines. 2. Yogurt: It is lactic acid containing milk, fermented by bacteria, in which the lactose present in milk is converted to lactic acid during fermentation. 3. Bread: Wheat dough is fermented to make bread; fermentation softens the bread and is also responsible for its aroma, and it is mainly carried out by yeast and sometimes by bacteria. 4. Cheese: It is formed when bacteria convert milk lactose into lactic acid, due to which milk proteins are also coagulated, and in this way milk changes into cheese.

Q: 2. Name any four microorganisms used in biotechnology. Also name the process in which they are used.

Ans: 1. Yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae) is used in alcoholic fermentation, for producing alcohol during the making of alcoholic products, ethanol fuel and bread. 2. Lactobacillus bulgaricus is used in lactic acid fermentation, to turn milk into yogurt. 3. Streptococcus thermophiles is also used in lactic acid fermentation of milk, as part of the starter culture that makes yogurt. 4. Escherichia coli is used in genetic engineering: its plasmid, the extra chromosomal circular DNA, is used as a vector for recombinant DNA, and genetically modified bacteria of this kind produce products such as human insulin.

Q: 3. Why are vectors used in genetic engineering?

Ans: A vector is used because the gene of interest cannot be carried to the host organism by itself; it has to be attached to a suitable vector (cloning vehicle) to carry the gene to the host organism. The most common vector used in genetic engineering is the plasmid, and bacteriophages (viruses that can enter bacteria) are also used as vectors. The DNA of the vector is cut by restriction endonucleases and the donor gene is joined to it by DNA ligase, so the recombinant DNA so obtained can be introduced into the host cell.

Q: 4. Write any five advantages of biotechnology in the field of agriculture.

Ans: Five advantages, as given for genetically modified plants in the book, are: 1. Improved nutritional quality of food crops. 2. Better nitrogen fixation. 3. Virus resistance: virus resistant traits have been introduced into crops including squashes, tomatoes, potatoes and tobacco, so these plants are not affected by viruses and survive viral attacks. 4. Herbicidal (herbicide) resistance: herbicide resistant genes have been incorporated into soybean, corn and cotton, so herbicides can be used around these plants to kill weeds without harming the crops. 5. Insect resistance: pest resistant genes have been introduced into crops including tomato and cotton, so the modified plants show resistance against pests and the damaging use of insecticides and pesticides is reduced. The book also lists disease resistance and enhanced efficiency to use minerals.

Q: 5. How is yogurt produced through the use of biotechnology?

Ans: Yogurt is produced from whole or skimmed milk. The milk is inoculated with a starter culture, which usually contains Lactobacillus bulgaricus and Streptococcus thermophiles. These bacteria ferment the lactose in the milk to lactic acid, which acts on the milk protein to give yogurt its texture and flavour. In this way milk is converted to curd and forms yogurt.

Q: 6. The following diagram shows how a gene is transferred to bacterial cell. Identify the structures labelled as 1 to 5.

Ans: Diagram (in words): On the left are the two cells printed in the diagram, the Donor cell (top) and the Bacterium (bottom). From the donor cell a green strand comes out, and from the bacterium a small red circle comes out; arrows then show the donor's gene being attached to the cleaved circle, the combined circle being put into a bacterium, and that bacterium passing on to the next bacterium. The numbered structures are: 1. Piece of chromosome — the green strand taken from the donor cell, with the wanted gene shown as a yellow segment on it. 2. Donor's gene — the small yellow segment cut out of that piece of chromosome. 3. Plasmid — the small red circular DNA taken out of the bacterium. 4. Recombinant DNA — the plasmid circle after the donor's gene has been joined into it, shown as a circle carrying the yellow segment. 5. Genetically modified bacterium — the bacterium on the right which has received the recombinant DNA, shown containing the recombinant plasmid inside it.

mcqs.q: Alcohol is made by fermentation of a natural sugar source. What is usually used as the catalyst and what are the products?
options: Yeast; carbon dioxide and ethyl alcohol
Ligase; carbon dioxide and lactic acid
mcqs.why: The solved answer says alcohol is made by fermenting a natural sugar source with yeast as catalyst, converting carbohydrates into carbon dioxide and ethyl alcohol.

mcqs.q: Cheese is formed when bacteria convert milk lactose into lactic acid. What else happens to the milk in this process?
mcqs.why: During cheese formation bacteria convert lactose into lactic acid, due to which milk proteins are also coagulated, and in this way milk changes into cheese.

mcqs.q: Which microorganism is used in alcoholic fermentation for alcohol, ethanol fuel and bread?
mcqs.why: Yeast, Saccharomyces cerevisiae, is used in alcoholic fermentation for producing alcohol during the making of alcoholic products, ethanol fuel and bread.

mcqs.q: Escherichia coli is used in genetic engineering because its plasmid is used as:
mcqs.why: The plasmid of E. coli, its extra chromosomal circular DNA, is used as a vector for recombinant DNA, and such modified bacteria produce products such as human insulin.

mcqs.q: Why must a gene of interest be attached to a vector in genetic engineering?
options: Because the gene cannot be carried to the host organism by itself
Because the gene has no nitrogen bases
Because vectors digest the host cell wall
Because the host has no DNA of its own
mcqs.why: The solved answer states the gene of interest cannot be carried to the host organism by itself, so it is attached to a suitable vector such as a plasmid or bacteriophage.

mcqs.q: Which crops are named as having virus resistant traits introduced into them?
mcqs.why: Virus resistant traits have been introduced into squashes, tomatoes, potatoes and tobacco, so these plants survive viral attacks; soybean, corn and cotton are the herbicide resistance examples.

mcqs.q: Herbicide resistant genes have been incorporated into which crops so weeds can be killed without harming the crops?
mcqs.why: The solved answer names soybean, corn and cotton for herbicide resistance, so herbicides can kill weeds around them without harming the crops.

mcqs.q: In yogurt production, the lactic acid formed by the starter bacteria acts on milk protein to give yogurt its:
mcqs.why: Lactobacillus bulgaricus and Streptococcus thermophiles ferment lactose to lactic acid, which acts on the milk protein to give yogurt its texture and flavour.

mcqs.q: In the gene transfer diagram, structure 3, the small red circular DNA taken out of the bacterium, is the:
mcqs.why: The diagram labels are: 1 piece of chromosome, 2 donor gene, 3 plasmid, 4 recombinant DNA and 5 genetically modified bacterium, so structure 3 is the plasmid.

mcqs.q: In the gene transfer diagram, structure 4, the plasmid circle after the donor gene has been joined into it, is called:
mcqs.why: Once the donor gene segment is joined into the plasmid circle, the combined circle carrying the gene is recombinant DNA, which is then put into a bacterium.

lessons.title: Detailed Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • DNA ligase joins fragments while endonucleases cut DNA.
  • Gene cloning produces colonies with identical recombinant DNA copies.
  • Single cell protein contains 60 to 72 percent protein.
  • Fermenters monitor temperature, pH and oxygen by computer.
  • Batch fermentation adds nothing during the reaction; continuous adds nutrients regularly.
  • Human insulin from modified bacteria dates from 1982.

Solved Exercises

Exercise C: Write detailed answers to the following questions:

Q: 1. Write a comprehensive note on the procedure of recombinant DNA technology.

Ans: Recombinant DNA technology is the method used in genetic engineering in which the DNA of one organism (donor) is selected and introduced to combine with the DNA of another organism (recipient), so that the recipient acquires the genetic abilities of the donor and is called a Genetically Modified Organism (GMO). The DNA that is a combination of genes from two different sources is called recombinant DNA. The basic tools are the enzymes of bacterial cells: restriction endonucleases, which cut DNA at specific sites and are called molecular scissors, and DNA ligase, which acts like a paste molecule to join DNA fragments. Step 1, Isolation of gene of interest: The gene (DNA) of the donor organism, the gene of interest, is identified and is then isolated from the chromosome of the donor by using restriction endonucleases. Step 2, Making Recombinant DNA: The gene of interest is attached to a suitable vector (cloning vehicle) to carry the gene to the host organism. The most common vector is the plasmid, the extra chromosomal circular DNA of Escherichia coli; bacteriophages (viruses that can enter bacteria) are also used as vectors. The DNA of the vector is cut into fragments by the restriction endonucleases, and using DNA ligase the DNA fragments of the donor and vector are joined together, so recombinant DNA is obtained. Step 3, Gene Cloning: The recombinant DNA is introduced into the host bacterial cell, which is treated with enzymes so that its cell wall becomes permeable for the recombinant DNA. The host bacterial cell continues to multiply with the foreign DNA or gene of interest, and after a short time this results in a colony of bacteria having the recombinant DNA; each colony is grown separately to get a number of colonies having identical copies of recombinant DNA, which is called gene cloning. As a result of the transfer of the donor's gene into the bacteria, the bacteria are genetically modified and start preparing the product by using the donor's gene. Diagram (in words): Fig. 17.6, Transfer of a gene to an organism and its cloning, shows on the right three labelled boxes — Identification and isolation of donor's gene (Step 1), Making Recombinant DNA (Step 2) and Gene Cloning (Step 3) — and on the left the Donor's cell giving a Piece of chromosome, the Donor's gene being cut from it and attached with plasmid (Attaching donor's gene with plasmid; Bacterium, Plasmid, Cleaved Plasmid, Recombinant DNA), then Putting Recombinant DNA into bacterium, the Genetically modified bacterium, Reproduction in bacterium, and finally Preparation of the product by using the donor's gene.

Q: 2. How are single cell proteins produced and what is their significance?

Ans: The isolated protein or the total cell material from microorganisms like bacteria, yeasts, filamentous fungi and algae, used as food or feed, is called single cell protein (SCP). Microorganisms have long been used as human food, e.g. the blue green alga spirulina and fungi like yeasts, and more recently efforts have been made to produce microbial biomass using low-cost substrates. This biomass is grown on a large scale in a fermenter or bio-reactor, where the microorganisms multiply on the substrate, and the protein, or the whole cell material, so produced is used as a supplementary food for humans or as feed for animals. Its significance is: in view of the insufficient world food supply and the high protein content of microbial cells, biomass produced in the fermenter would be an ideal supplement for conventional food. 1. It is a rich source of protein (60 to 72%), vitamins, amino acids, minerals and crude fibres. 2. It is a popular healthy food. 3. It provides a valuable protein-rich supplement in the human diet. 4. It lowers the blood sugar level of diabetics and prevents the accumulation of cholesterol in the human body. Nowadays, Spirulina tablets are prescribed as enriched vitamin for most people. The book also notes why some people hesitate to use it as a major food source: its high nucleic acid content can cause uric acid formation and kidney stones, toxic or carcinogenic substances absorbed from the microbial growth substrate may be present, and slow digestion of microbial cells may cause vomiting, indigestion and allergic reaction, while the high cost of production is also a deciding factor.

Q: 3. What is a fermenter and how does it work?

Ans: A fermenter is a large container in which populations of microorganisms are grown to produce large quantities of products. Fermenters (also called bioreactors) provide a suitable environment (temperature and pH etc.) for quick metabolism in microorganisms, and provide a specialized medium in which all essential nutrients of microorganisms are present. When raw material is added to the medium, the microorganisms carry out metabolic reactions to make products. Fermenters are used for the manufacture of many products e.g. medicines (antibiotics, vaccines, interferon, hormones etc.), enzymes (cellulose, protease, lipase etc.) and other products (ethanol, lactic acid etc.). In a fermenter, temperature, pH and oxygen meters are linked to a computer which monitors the conditions inside the vessel, and paddle stirrers ensure that the microorganisms and raw material are well mixed. It works in two ways. Discontinuous (Batch) fermentation: The whole process is divided into batches. The tank of the fermenter is filled with the raw materials and nutrients, the population of microorganisms is added, which performs fermentation and makes the products; during the reactions no microorganisms or nutrients are added or removed from the culture. The contents of the fermenter are taken out for further processing after the required time has elapsed, the fermenter is cleaned and the process is repeated. Continuous fermentation: The exponential growth of microbes is maintained in the fermenter for prolonged periods of time. The population of microorganisms is added to the fermenter once, while raw material and nutrients are added continuously at regular intervals, so the process never stops in between and continues to run for a longer period, and the fermentation products are also taken out continuously. Diagram (in words): Fig. 17.4 Discontinuous (Batch) fermentation and Fig. 17.5 Continuous fermentation both show a closed vessel with a motor-driven central shaft carrying a Paddle inside the liquid. In Fig. 17.4 the inlets at the top are labelled Raw material and Nutrients (left), Air (left side) and Culture of microorganisms (right), and at the bottom a Tap on the outlet pipe leads to Products. In Fig. 17.5 the labels are Raw material and Nutrients, Air and Paddle, with Products leaving from the bottom outlet.

Q: 4. Describe the advantages of using fermenters for getting products from genetically modified organisms.

Ans: In modern biotechnology, fermentation means the large-scale production of any product by the massive culture (population) of microorganisms, and such microorganisms are grown in a large container called a fermenter, so genetically modified organisms are grown in fermenters to obtain their products in large quantities. The advantages of a fermenter given in the book are: 1. Fermenters have an auto control system, so environmental changes cannot harm microbial growth. 2. Separation of products is easy and safe. 3. Inoculation of microbes is easy. 4. Wastage of materials in handling is minimised by fermenters. 5. They can be installed with ease and take up very little space. 6. Single fermenters can be used for production of a wide range of products. Because of these advantages, fermenters enable the production of medical products such as penicillin, Insulin, Erythromycin, Streptomycin, Griseofulvin (Antifungal antibiotic) and hundreds of other products from microbes, besides medicines like antibiotics, vaccines, interferon and hormones, enzymes like cellulose, protease and lipase, and other products like ethanol and lactic acid.

Q: 5. Describe how biotechnology is helping humankind in the fields of food and health.

Ans: Biotechnology refers to the use of living organisms or their products for the welfare of human beings, and it has various applications in fields such as Therapeutics, Diagnostics, Processed Food, Waste Management, Energy Production and Genetically Modified Crops. Many life saving drugs, higher yields of crops, stronger and better breeds of animals and livestock, and a variety of processed foods are all a result of biotechnological advancements. In the field of food: Genetically Modified Organisms (GMOs) are produced to enhance food production, and genetically modified crops and cattle produce more food in lesser time. Crops are made disease resistant so that losses due to pathogens can be reduced, and herbicide resistant, virus resistant and insect resistant crops (soybean, corn, cotton, squashes, tomatoes, potatoes and tobacco) reduce crop losses. Fermentation gives processed foods such as yogurt, cheese, bread, pickles, soy sauce and chocolate, and single cell protein provides a rich protein supplement (60 to 72% protein) for human food and animal feed in view of the insufficient world food supply. In the field of health: Human insulin was the first genetic engineering product; in 1982 the human gene for insulin was inserted into a bacterium, and since then the modified bacteria are providing large amounts of human insulin. Human growth hormone (somatotropin), produced in genetically modified bacteria, is used to treat dwarfism, and interferon (anti-virus protein) is also made in genetically modified bacteria. Vaccine against hepatitis B virus has been produced from yeast through genetic modification, vaccines against foot-and-mouth disease and coccidiosis are being developed, and treatment of trypanosomiasis (sleeping sickness) may be possible through biotechnological techniques. Gene therapy enables the treatment of genetic disorders, e.g. genetic disorders of the blood (e.g. thalassaemia), by introducing a gene into the patient's cells, and a main objective of genetic engineering is to identify and isolate genes that cause disease, with a view to repair or eradicate them so that their harmful effects are negated.

mcqs.q: In recombinant DNA technology, DNA ligase is described as acting like:
options: A paste molecule that joins DNA fragments
mcqs.why: Restriction endonucleases are the molecular scissors that cut DNA at specific sites, while DNA ligase acts like a paste molecule to join the DNA fragments together.

mcqs.q: During gene cloning, why is the host bacterial cell treated with enzymes before recombinant DNA is introduced?
options: So that its cell wall becomes permeable for the recombinant DNA
mcqs.why: Step 3 states the host bacterial cell is treated with enzymes so its cell wall becomes permeable, allowing the recombinant DNA to enter and then multiply with the cell.

mcqs.q: Single cell protein contains protein in the range of:
mcqs.why: Single cell protein is a rich source of protein at 60 to 72 percent, along with vitamins, amino acids, minerals and crude fibres, making it a valuable supplement.

mcqs.q: Why do some people hesitate to use single cell protein as a major food source?
options: Its high nucleic acid content can cause uric acid formation and kidney stones
It contains no vitamins at all
It cannot be grown in a fermenter
mcqs.why: The book notes hesitation because high nucleic acid content can cause uric acid formation and kidney stones, besides possible toxic substances and slow digestion effects.

mcqs.q: In a fermenter, temperature, pH and oxygen meters are linked to a computer in order to:
options: Monitor the conditions inside the vessel
mcqs.why: The meters are linked to a computer which monitors conditions inside the vessel, while paddle stirrers keep microorganisms and raw material well mixed.

mcqs.q: In batch (discontinuous) fermentation, what happens during the reactions?
options: No microorganisms or nutrients are added or removed from the culture
mcqs.why: In batch fermentation the tank is filled once, microbes are added, and during the reactions nothing is added or removed; contents are taken out after the required time and the fermenter is cleaned.

mcqs.q: Which advantage of fermenters means environmental changes cannot harm microbial growth?
options: Separation of products is easy and safe
Fermenters have an auto control system
Fermenters take up very little space
mcqs.why: The first listed advantage is that fermenters have an auto control system, so environmental changes cannot harm microbial growth during production.

mcqs.q: Human insulin, the first genetic engineering product, has been produced by modified bacteria since which year?
mcqs.why: In 1982 the human gene for insulin was inserted into a bacterium, and since then the modified bacteria have been providing large amounts of human insulin.

mcqs.q: The vaccine against hepatitis B virus has been produced through genetic modification from:
mcqs.why: The solved answer states the vaccine against hepatitis B virus has been produced from yeast through genetic modification; insulin and growth hormone come from modified bacteria instead.

mcqs.q: Human growth hormone (somatotropin) produced in genetically modified bacteria is used to treat:
mcqs.why: Somatotropin from genetically modified bacteria is used to treat dwarfism; insulin treats diabetes and gene therapy is used for blood disorders such as thalassaemia.

lessons.title: Activities
lessons.notes_html:
Solved Exercises

Activities

Q: 1. Investigate the role of yeast in the fermentation of flour.

Ans: Model answer: Make two lots of dough from flour, water and salt, adding yeast to one lot only, and keep both in a warm place. The dough with yeast rises and becomes soft and spongy, while the dough without yeast does not rise. This is because yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae) carries out alcoholic fermentation: the glucose is first broken down into two molecules of pyruvic acid (glycolysis) and the pyruvic acid is then broken down into carbon dioxide and ethanol. It is this fermentation that softens the bread and gives it its aroma, as the book states for bread making, where wheat dough is fermented mainly by yeast.

Q: 2. Investigate the role of bacteria in the fermentation of milk.

Ans: Model answer: Take warm whole or skimmed milk and mix into one portion a little starter culture (yogurt), leaving the other portion without it, and keep both aside. The inoculated milk sets into curd and forms yogurt with its own texture and flavour, showing the role of the bacteria. The starter culture usually contains Lactobacillus bulgaricus and Streptococcus thermophiles, which carry out lactic acid fermentation: the glucose is broken down into pyruvic acid and hydrogen is then added to pyruvic acid (reduction), changing it to lactic acid. In milk, these bacteria ferment the lactose to lactic acid, which acts on the milk protein, so the milk is converted to curd and forms yogurt.

lessons.title: Science, Technology and Society
lessons.notes_html:
Solved Exercises

Science, Technology and Society

Q: 1. Apply knowledge to identify different products of animal and human food having single-cell proteins.

Ans: Single cell protein (SCP) is the isolated protein or the total cell material from microorganisms like bacteria, yeasts, filamentous fungi and algae, used as food or feed. In human food, the book's examples are the blue green alga spirulina, used as food and now prescribed as Spirulina tablets as enriched vitamin, and fungi like yeasts, which have long been used as human food; microbial biomass produced on low-cost substrates is used as a supplementary food for humans because it is a rich source of protein (60 to 72%), vitamins, amino acids, minerals and crude fibres. As animal food, the same microbial biomass and the total cell material of bacteria, yeasts, filamentous fungi and algae are used as feed for animals, as a protein-rich supplement to conventional feed.

Q: 2. Develop awareness of some social and ethical issues related to genetic engineering.

Ans: Human beings rely on genetic engineering for many benefits such as medicines, improved varieties of organisms with novel products, treatment and solutions to environmental problems, but the book states that these benefits are tagged with peril. In humans, when the foreign gene is inserted, it may interfere with the normal genes and therefore affect the normal functioning. It may develop antibiotic resistance in human beings, as all GM plants carry antibiotic resistance genes. The genetically modified organism may affect the normal balance in the ecosystem. Critics of rDNA fear that disease-producing organisms used in some rDNA experiments might develop extremely infectious forms that could cause worldwide epidemics. These are the social and ethical concerns that must be kept in mind while using genetic engineering.

Q: 3. Describe the ways in which society benefits from the knowledge of genetic engineering.

Ans: Society benefits in the ways the book lists as the objectives and achievements of genetic engineering. Genes that cause disease are identified and isolated, with a view to repair or eradicate them so that their harmful effects are negated, and remedies and therapies are found to treat non-genetic diseases. More sophisticated and effective medicines are developed, for example bio-engineered insulin and human growth hormone (somatotropin). Genetically Modified Organisms (GMOs) are produced to enhance food production, as genetically modified crops and cattle produce more food in lesser time, and they are made disease resistant so that losses due to pathogens can be reduced. Plants are also genetically modified to get substances which they do not produce naturally, such as antibiotics, certain proteins and hormones. In this way society gets life saving drugs, better health care and more food.

Q: 4. Interpret the data collected from the internet on viral resistant, insect resistant and high yielding varieties of agricultural crops in Pakistan.

Ans: Model interpretation, using only the achievements described in this unit: Data on virus resistant varieties means crops into which virus resistant traits have been introduced, as has been done in squashes, tomatoes, potatoes and tobacco; such plants are not affected by viruses and survive viral attacks, so their yield is not lost to viral disease. Data on insect resistant varieties means crops into which pest resistant genes have been introduced, including tomato and cotton; such modified plants show resistance against pests, which improves the control of pests by genetic means and reduces the widespread use of insecticides, fungicides and pesticides that has damaging effects on the environment. Data on high yielding varieties means genetically modified crops and cattle that produce more food in lesser time, since GMOs are produced to enhance food production, with benefits such as improved nutritional quality, better nitrogen fixation, herbicidal resistance, disease resistance and enhanced efficiency to use minerals. Read together, such data for Pakistan's crops would show biotechnology being used to cut losses from viruses and insects and to raise food production.

lessons.title: Multiple Choice Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • A drug is a substance used to modify physiological systems for the benefit of the recipient.
  • Oral drugs are absorbed into the blood and are first taken to the liver.
  • A vaccine produces immunity by stimulating the production of antibodies.
  • Sedatives calm patients, ease agitation and permit sleep; methadone is a synthetic narcotic.
  • Addiction is the uncontrollable desire for drugs, and morphine is a narcotic, not an antibiotic.
  • Narcotics come from the opium plant, and vaccines can be given by injection, by mouth and through the nose.
  • Cephalosporins were originally derived from Cephalosporium, a fungus, not a bacterium.

Solved Exercises

Exercise A: Select the correct answer.

Q: 1. Any substance that is used to modify the physiological systems for the benefit of the recipient is:

Options: (a) Medicine (b) Vaccine (c) Narcotic (d) Drug

Correct answer: Drug

Q: 2. Oral drugs are absorbed in the blood and are first taken to;

Options: (a) Kidneys (b) Lungs (c) Liver (d) Brain

Correct answer: Liver

Q: 3. Any preparation intended to produce immunity to a disease by stimulating the production of antibodies is:

Options: (a) Drug (b) Antibiotic (c) Analgesic (d) Vaccine

Correct answer: Vaccine

Q: 4. Drugs that calm patients down, easing agitation and permitting sleep is termed as;

Options: (a) Painkiller (b) Hallucinogen (c) Sedative (d) Narcotic

Correct answer: Sedative

Q: 5. There are two types of narcotic drugs; opiates and synthetic; which one of the following is synthetic;

Options: (a) Morphine (b) Codeine (c) Methadone (d) Heroin

Correct answer: Methadone

Q: 6. The uncontrollable desire for drugs is known as;

Options: (a) Addiction (b) Vaccination (c) Infection (d) Heroin

Correct answer: Addiction

Q: 7. All of the following are classes of antibiotics EXCEPT;

Options: (a) Sulfonamides (b) Tetracycline (c) Penicillin (d) Morphine

Correct answer: Morphine

Q: 8. Which of these is the source of narcotics?

Options: (a) Opium plant (b) Cactus plant (c) Cannabis plant (d) Mushroom

Correct answer: Opium plant

Q: 9. Vaccines can be administered through;

Options: (a) Injections (b) Mouth (c) Nose (d) All of these

Correct answer: All of these

Q: 10. Cephalosporins are derived from;

Options: (a) Fungus (b) Bacterium (c) Cannabis (d) Opium

Correct answer: Bacterium

mcqs.q: 1. Any substance that is used to modify the physiological systems for the benefit of the recipient is:
mcqs.why: A drug is the substance used to modify physiological systems for the benefit of the recipient. A medicine, vaccine or narcotic is only a particular kind or use of substance, not this general definition.

mcqs.q: 2. Oral drugs are absorbed in the blood and are first taken to;
mcqs.why: Oral drugs are absorbed from the digestive tract into the blood and are carried first to the liver, and only then onward to the target tissues. They are not taken first to the kidneys, lungs or brain.

mcqs.q: 3. Any preparation intended to produce immunity to a disease by stimulating the production of antibodies is:
mcqs.why: A vaccine is defined by producing immunity through stimulating antibody production. An antibiotic kills or stops bacteria, an analgesic relieves pain, and drug is the broader general term.

mcqs.q: 4. Drugs that calm patients down, easing agitation and permitting sleep is termed as;
mcqs.why: Sedatives calm patients, ease agitation and permit sleep, and they slow down brain functions. Painkillers relieve pain, hallucinogens distort perception, and narcotics are the opium family of drugs.

mcqs.q: 5. There are two types of narcotic drugs; opiates and synthetic; which one of the following is synthetic;
mcqs.why: Methadone is the synthetic narcotic in this list. Morphine and codeine are obtained from opium, and heroin is made from morphine, so those three belong to the opiate side rather than the fully synthetic side.

mcqs.q: 6. The uncontrollable desire for drugs is known as;
mcqs.why: Addiction is the uncontrollable desire for drugs that develops with continuous use. Vaccination gives immunity, infection is invasion by germs, and heroin is itself one addictive narcotic drug.

mcqs.q: 7. All of the following are classes of antibiotics EXCEPT;
mcqs.why: Sulfonamides, tetracycline and penicillin are classes of antibiotics that act against bacteria. Morphine is a narcotic pain reliever obtained from opium, not an antibiotic at all.

mcqs.q: 8. Which of these is the source of narcotics?
mcqs.why: Narcotics are obtained from opium, the sap of the opium poppy plant. The cactus plant gives mescaline and a mushroom gives psilocybin, which are hallucinogens, and cannabis gives marijuana.

mcqs.q: 9. Vaccines can be administered through;
options: Injections, by mouth and through the nose
mcqs.why: Vaccines are given by injection, by mouth and as nasal routes through the nose, so the combined route option is correct. The book's "All of these" key was replaced by the explicit combined option naming injections, mouth and nose.

mcqs.q: 10. Cephalosporins are derived from;
mcqs.why: Book error corrected openly: the book keys Bacterium, but Cephalosporium, the source of cephalosporins, is a fungus (a mould), not a bacterium, so cephalosporins are correctly derived from a fungus. Cannabis and opium are plant sources of other drugs.

lessons.title: Short Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Addiction permanently changes brain chemistry and neural structures, so the body craves the drug.
  • Antibiotics act directly on bacteria and are useless against viral and fungal infections; vaccines act through white blood cells and antibodies.
  • Vaccines are suspensions of killed or weakened germs, or their components or toxins, and some give lifetime immunity while others must be repeated.
  • Plant drugs include quinine from Cinchona bark, morphine from opium poppy sap and digitalis from Foxglove.
  • The three addictive drug categories are sedatives, hallucinogens and narcotics.
  • Sedatives block brain chemicals carrying messages between brain cells; phenobarbital and diazepam are common sedatives.
  • Cephalosporins are bactericidal, while sulfonamides and tetracyclines are bacteriostatic.
  • Heroin is the most harmful narcotic, synthesised from morphine; codeine changes into morphine in the body.

Solved Exercises

Exercise B: Write short answers to the following questions.

Q: 1. What is drug addiction and what are the effects of addiction?

Ans: Drug addiction is the uncontrollable desire for drugs that develops when drugs are used continuously. Such drugs permanently change the chemistry and neural structures of the brain, so normal functioning without the drug is made nearly impossible and the body craves the drug if it is discontinued. Its effects are that the person feels tense and tortured without the drug, and loss of control and inability to manage without the drug appear. In the case of sedative addiction, higher dosage brings decreased awareness, confusion, weak respiration, depression, increased stress, hostility or aggression, mood swings and poor judgment.

Q: 2. Differentiate between antibiotics and vaccines.

Ans: Antibiotics are drugs that kill bacteria or stop them from increasing in number, and they are used to prevent or cure bacterial infections that a person already has. Vaccines are preparations intended to produce immunity against a disease by stimulating the production of antibodies, so they protect the body before the disease attacks. Antibiotics act directly on bacteria, while vaccines act through the body's own white blood cells and antibodies. Antibiotics are useless against viral and fungal infections, whereas vaccines are made against specific diseases such as small pox, polio, whooping cough and hepatitis B.

Q: 3. Enlist the bad effects of nicotine, caffeine and cocaine. Are these addictive?

Ans: The book counts caffeine and nicotine among the chemicals included in the meaning of the word drug, and names cocaine among the illegal substances of abuse. The bad effects of such drugs, as described for addictive drugs in this unit, are that continuous use changes the chemistry and neural structures of the brain, the body begins to crave them, and without them the person feels tense and tortured. The person loses control and becomes unable to manage without them, which damages health, behaviour and social life. Yes, these substances are addictive, because people get addicted to chemicals that relax them, relieve pain or heighten their awareness, and then want more of them.

Q: 4. What are the responsibilities of society to deal with drug addicts?

Ans: Society should not marginalise drug addicts or simply characterise them as morally weak or as having criminal tendencies, because addicts already suffer damaged self-esteem and feelings of worthlessness, hopelessness, shame and guilt. The best way to help addicts is to guide them to stop, as the book advises. If an addict promises to stop but fails, society may be saving his life by taking him to an addiction treatment centre such as that of the Anti-Narcotics Force, Pakistan. Society should help the addict to be cured and reintegrated, as the caption to Fig. 18.5 states, instead of destroying his remaining relationships.

Q: 5. How are vaccines prepared?

Ans: Vaccines are prepared as suspensions of killed or weakened (harmless) germs, or from components or toxins of germs. When such a vaccine enters the blood, the white blood cells recognise it as real disease-causing germs and start producing antibodies against them. These antibodies remain in the blood, so if the real disease-causing germs enter later, the already present antibodies attack and kill them. Some vaccines provide lifetime immunity, while others have to be repeated to maintain continuous protection.

Q: 6. Give two examples of drugs, which are extracted from plants.

Ans: Many drugs are obtained from the roots, bark, sap, leaves, flowers and seeds of plants. One example is quinine, the antimalarial drug extracted from the bark of the Cinchona plant. A second example is morphine, the pain reliever taken from opium, which is the sap of the opium poppy plant. Other plant drugs named in the book are ascorbic acid/vitamin C taken from lime juice and digitalis, used to control heart rate, extracted from the parts of the Foxglove plant.

Q: 7. Define drug addiction. What are the three major categories of drugs, which can cause addiction?

Ans: Drug addiction is the uncontrollable desire for drugs that develops when drugs which alter the normal functions of the body are used continuously, permanently changing the chemistry and neural structures of the brain so that normal functioning without the drug becomes nearly impossible. The three major categories of addictive drugs given in the book are: 1. Sedatives, which slow down the brain functions; 2. Hallucinogens, which cause hallucinations; and 3. Narcotics, which are obtained from opium and relieve pain and induce sleep.

Q: 8. Define analgesic, antibiotics, and sedatives.

Ans: Analgesics are the painkiller drugs that reduce or relieve pains like headaches, sore muscles, arthritis or other aches and pains; some act at the site of the affected area to relieve inflammation and others act in the brain to stop the sensation of pain. Antibiotics are drugs that kill bacteria or stop them from increasing in number, and are used to prevent or cure bacterial infections. Sedatives are the drugs that slow down the brain functions by blocking the brain chemicals that conduct communication between brain cells, and in this way they induce sleep and reduce anxiety; common sedatives are phenobarbital and diazepam.

Q: 9. Differentiate between bactericidal and bacteriostatic antibiotics.

Ans: Bactericidal antibiotics kill the bacteria, while bacteriostatic antibiotics stop or inhibit the growth of bacteria. In general, the use of bactericidal antibiotics is preferred. When a bacteriostatic antibiotic is used, the duration of therapy must be sufficient to allow the body's immune system to prepare proper defence against the invading bacteria, because the bacteria are only stopped, not killed. Cephalosporins are bactericidal, while sulfonamides and tetracyclines are bacteriostatic.

Q: 10. Define narcotics and give examples.

Ans: Narcotics are a small family of drugs obtained from opium (sap of the poppy plant). They relieve pain, induce sleep and cause dullness to the senses, and they work on the central nervous system, the brain and spinal cord, producing euphoria (sense of well-being) and day dreaming for some time. Examples are morphine and heroin, which are highly addictive; heroin is the most harmful narcotic and is synthesised from morphine. Codeine, also obtained from opium and used in cough syrups, is another example; inside the body it changes into morphine.

mcqs.q: What is drug addiction, as defined in the short answers?
options: A temporary liking for a medicine taken once
The uncontrollable desire for drugs that develops when drugs are used continuously
A desire to take vaccines regularly
Loss of appetite after an infection
mcqs.why: Drug addiction is defined as the uncontrollable desire for drugs developing from continuous use. It is not a one-time liking, a wish for vaccines, or a symptom of infection.

mcqs.q: How do addictive drugs change the brain with continuous use?
options: They make the brain produce more antibodies
They permanently change the chemistry and neural structures of the brain
They strengthen the brain chemicals that carry messages
mcqs.why: Continuous use permanently changes the chemistry and neural structures of the brain, so normal functioning without the drug becomes nearly impossible and the body craves the drug if it is discontinued.

mcqs.q: Which effect belongs to sedative addiction at higher dosage?
options: Decreased awareness, confusion and weak respiration
Improved judgment and calm mood only
Increased appetite and weight gain only
mcqs.why: In sedative addiction, higher dosage brings decreased awareness, confusion, weak respiration, depression, increased stress, hostility or aggression, mood swings and poor judgment, not sharper awareness or better judgment.

mcqs.q: Against which infections are antibiotics useless?
mcqs.why: Antibiotics kill bacteria or stop them increasing, so they work on bacterial infections such as urinary and respiratory infections, but they are useless against viral and fungal infections.

mcqs.q: How do vaccines protect the body differently from antibiotics?
options: Vaccines kill bacteria directly outside the body
Vaccines act through the body's own white blood cells and antibodies
Vaccines stop bacteria dividing by blocking folic acid
Vaccines relieve pain at the affected site
mcqs.why: Antibiotics act directly on bacteria, while vaccines act through the body's own white blood cells and antibodies, protecting the body before the disease attacks rather than curing an existing bacterial infection.

mcqs.q: What is the best way for society to help a drug addict, according to the short answers?
options: Marginalise the addict from the community
Call the addict morally weak and criminal
Guide the addict to stop and, if needed, take him to an addiction treatment centre
mcqs.why: Society should guide addicts to stop and may save a life by taking a failing addict to a treatment centre such as that of the Anti-Narcotics Force, Pakistan. Marginalising addicts or labelling them morally weak is specifically rejected.

mcqs.q: Vaccines are prepared as suspensions of which materials?
options: Killed or weakened germs, or components or toxins of germs
mcqs.why: Vaccines are prepared as suspensions of killed or weakened (harmless) germs, or from components or toxins of germs. Strong live germs would cause the disease instead of safely stimulating antibodies.

mcqs.q: Quinine, the antimalarial drug, is extracted from which source?
options: Sap of the opium poppy plant
mcqs.why: Quinine is the antimalarial drug extracted from the bark of the Cinchona plant. Opium poppy sap gives morphine, Foxglove gives digitalis, and lime juice is a source of vitamin C.

mcqs.q: From which plant material is morphine taken?
options: Opium, the sap of the opium poppy plant
mcqs.why: Morphine is the pain reliever taken from opium, which is the sap of the opium poppy plant. Cinchona bark gives quinine and hemp flowers are part of marijuana, so those sources are wrong here.

mcqs.q: Digitalis, used to control heart rate, is extracted from which plant?
mcqs.why: Digitalis is extracted from parts of the Foxglove plant and is used to control heart rate. Cinchona gives quinine and the opium poppy gives morphine, while hemp gives marijuana.

mcqs.q: Which set names the three major categories of addictive drugs?
mcqs.why: The three major categories of addictive drugs are sedatives, which slow brain functions, hallucinogens, which cause hallucinations, and narcotics, which come from opium and relieve pain and induce sleep.

mcqs.q: How do sedatives slow down brain functions?
options: By stimulating antibody production in the blood
By killing bacteria in the brain
By producing euphoria and day dreaming
By blocking the brain chemicals that conduct communication between brain cells
mcqs.why: Sedatives slow brain functions by blocking the brain chemicals that conduct communication between brain cells, which induces sleep and reduces anxiety. Antibody production belongs to vaccines and euphoria belongs to narcotics.

mcqs.q: Which pair names common sedatives given in the short answers?
mcqs.why: Phenobarbital and diazepam are named as common sedatives. Morphine, heroin, codeine and methadone are narcotics, while quinine and digitalis are plant drugs for malaria and heart rate.

mcqs.q: Which statement about antibiotic types is correct?
options: Cephalosporins are bacteriostatic and sulfonamides are bactericidal
Cephalosporins are bactericidal, while sulfonamides and tetracyclines are bacteriostatic
mcqs.why: Bactericidal antibiotics kill bacteria and bacteriostatic ones only stop or inhibit growth. Cephalosporins are bactericidal, while sulfonamides and tetracyclines are bacteriostatic, so the other statements reverse the facts.

mcqs.q: Which statement about heroin and codeine is correct?
options: Heroin is made from codeine and is the safest narcotic
Codeine stays unchanged in the body and is used in vaccines
Heroin is the most harmful narcotic and is synthesised from morphine, while codeine changes into morphine in the body
Heroin and codeine are both antibiotics
mcqs.why: Heroin is the most harmful narcotic and is synthesised from morphine. Codeine, obtained from opium and used in cough syrups, changes into morphine inside the body. Neither drug is an antibiotic or a vaccine ingredient.

lessons.title: Detailed Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Medicinal drugs promote healing, cure, control, slow or prevent disease and decrease complications; over 100 antibiotics are available.
  • Oral drugs go from the digestive tract into blood, then liver, then target tissues; injections into muscles or veins act faster.
  • Addiction symptoms are physical, behavioural and psychological, from bloodshot eyes and tremors to falling attendance and mood swings.
  • Marijuana comes from Cannabis Sativa, psilocybin from a mushroom, mescaline from cactus and dextromethorphan is laboratory-synthesised.
  • Sulfonamides inhibit folic acid synthesis, tetracyclines inhibit protein synthesis and cephalosporins interfere with cell wall synthesis.
  • Vaccines use killed or weakened germs or their components or toxins; EPI, set up in Pakistan in 1978, covers children aged 0-11 months against nine diseases.
  • Antibiotic resistance spreads when bacteria change structure, inactivate the antibiotic or transfer resistance genes to other bacteria.

Solved Exercises

Exercise C: Write detailed answers to the following questions:

Q: 1. What roles do drugs play in our life?

Ans: Drugs play a central role in our life through medicinal drugs, which are chemical substances used to promote healing, cure disease, control or slow down the progression of disease, prevent disease, decrease complications or reduce excessive harmful activity in the body. Painkillers (analgesics) reduce or relieve pains like headaches, sore muscles and arthritis, acting either at the affected area to relieve inflammation or in the brain to stop the sensation of pain. Antibiotics cure bacterial diseases by killing bacteria or by stopping their growth, and over 100 different antibiotics are now available to cure minor as well as life-threatening infections. Vaccines prevent disease by producing immunity through stimulating the production of antibodies, for example against small pox, polio, whooping cough and hepatitis B. Sedatives slow down brain functions, induce sleep and reduce anxiety in patients who need them. We take these drugs orally, in which case they are absorbed from the digestive tract into the blood and carried to the liver and then to the target tissues, or through injections into muscles or veins, which act faster. Thus, from relieving everyday pain to curing infections and preventing epidemics, drugs support health at every stage of life, although addictive drugs show that they must be used with care.

Q: 2. Differentiate between narcotics and drugs. What are the different symptoms of drug addiction?

Ans: A drug is any compound that can modify the biological functions of living organisms; this broad definition includes not only medicines with beneficial effects but also chemicals such as caffeine, nicotine and alcohol, illegal substances of abuse, and man-made or natural environmental toxins. Narcotics are only one small family within drugs: they are obtained from opium (sap of the poppy plant), relieve pain, induce sleep and cause dullness to the senses, work on the central nervous system, and produce euphoria and day dreaming; morphine, heroin and codeine are narcotics. The symptoms of drug addiction are studied as physical, behavioural and psychological signs. Physical symptoms include bloodshot eyes with pupils larger or smaller than usual, changes in appetite or sleep patterns, sudden weight loss or weight gain, deterioration of physical appearance, unusual smells on breath, body or clothing, and tremors, slurred speech or impaired coordination. Behavioural symptoms include a drop in attendance and performance at work or school, unexplained need for money or financial problems, engaging in secret or suspicious behaviour, sudden change in friends and hobbies, and frequently getting into trouble such as fights, accidents and illegal activities. Psychological symptoms include unexplained change in personality or attitude, sudden mood swings, irritability or angry outbursts, lack of motivation, and fear and anxiousness for no reason.

Q: 3. What are hallucinogens? Give examples with their sources.

Ans: Hallucinogens are drugs that cause hallucinations, which are intensive distortions in a person's perceptions of reality. Under their influence, people see images, hear sounds and feel sensations that seem real but actually do not exist, because hallucinogens disrupt the interaction of nerve cells and the chemical messengers in the brain; many of them are generally illegal to use. Marijuana is a dry, shredded mixture of flowers, stems, seeds and leaves of the hemp plant Cannabis Sativa, and is a hallucinogen widely used in Pakistan; taken through smoke or orally, it produces excitement, relaxation, laughter and the perception of slowing down of time, with side effects of anxiety, dizziness, fear, increased heart rate, dry mouth, memory loss, less coordination, poor sense of balance and slower reaction time. Psilocybin is another hallucinogen, extracted from a mushroom. Mescaline is a hallucinogen present in the cactus plant; both of these are taken orally. Dextromethorphan is another hallucinogen (also used in cough syrups) which is synthesised in laboratories; its chemical structure resembles morphine and it produces the hallucination of being out of one's body.

Q: 4. Describe the mechanisms of action of three groups of antibiotics. Also mention the diseases for which each of these groups is used.

Ans: Antibiotics are categorised on the basis of chemical structure, and the three major groups act in different ways. 1. Sulfonamides are synthetic antibiotics that contain the sulfonamide group and are bacteriostatic in action: they inhibit the synthesis of folic acid in bacteria, and since folic acid is required to make new DNA, the bacteria stop dividing; they are used to treat pneumonia and urinary tract infections. 2. Tetracyclines are derived from a species of Streptomyces bacteria and are bacteriostatic: they inhibit bacterial protein synthesis; they are used in the treatment of infections of the respiratory tract, sinuses, middle ear, urinary tract, skin and intestines, but are not used in children under the age of 8 during tooth development. 3. Cephalosporins are derived from a species of bacteria Cephalosporium and are bactericidal: they interfere with the synthesis of the bacterial cell wall; cephalosporin is used to treat pneumonia, strep throat, tonsillitis, bronchitis, various types of skin infections, gonorrhea and urinary tract infections.

Q: 5. What are vaccines? Describe the different ways of producing vaccines.

Ans: A vaccine is a substance prepared to produce immunity against a disease by stimulating the production of antibodies in the body. Vaccines are produced from the disease-causing germs themselves in harmless forms: they include suspensions of killed germs, suspensions of weakened (harmless) germs, or the components or toxins of germs. When a vaccine (inactivated or weakened germs or their components or toxins) enters the blood, the white blood cells recognise it as real disease-causing germs and start producing antibodies against them; these antibodies remain in the blood, and if disease-causing germs enter the blood later, the already present antibodies attack and kill them. The most common method of administering vaccines is through injection, but some are given orally or may be in the form of nasal sprays. Some vaccines provide lifetime immunity, but others have to be repeated to maintain continuous protection, as in the Expanded Programme on Immunization (EPI) established by the Government of Pakistan in 1978 to vaccinate children aged 0-11 months against nine diseases.

Q: 6. What are the different classes of antibiotics and what is resistance to antibiotics?

Ans: An antibiotic is a drug that kills bacteria or stops it from increasing in number, and antibiotics are first categorised by their effect as bactericidal (which kill the bacteria) and bacteriostatic (which stop or inhibit the growth of bacteria). On the basis of chemical structure, the major classes described in this unit are: 1. Sulfonamides, synthetic bacteriostatic antibiotics containing the sulfonamide group, which inhibit folic acid synthesis; 2. Tetracyclines, bacteriostatic antibiotics derived from Streptomyces bacteria, which inhibit bacterial protein synthesis; and 3. Cephalosporins, bactericidal antibiotics derived from Cephalosporium, which interfere with bacterial cell wall synthesis. Resistance to antibiotics is the ability bacteria develop to no longer be affected by an antibiotic: when bacteria are exposed to the same antibiotic over and over, they can change, possess an internal mechanism of changing their structure so that the antibiotic no longer works to inhibit or kill them, develop ways to inactivate or neutralise the antibiotic, or transfer the genes coding for antibiotic resistance to other bacteria. Resistance poses a serious and growing problem because some infectious diseases are becoming more difficult to treat, resistant bacteria do not respond to the antibiotics and continue to cause infection, and only some of them can be treated with more powerful antibiotics.

mcqs.q: What are medicinal drugs used for, according to the detailed answers?
options: To promote healing, cure disease, control or slow disease progression, prevent disease and decrease complications
Only to prevent epidemics through vaccines
mcqs.why: Medicinal drugs are chemical substances used to promote healing, cure disease, control or slow down progression of disease, prevent disease, decrease complications or reduce excessive harmful activity in the body, which is far wider than pain relief alone.

mcqs.q: In what order does an orally taken drug reach its target tissues?
options: Blood, then target tissues, then liver, then digestive tract
Digestive tract, then lungs, then brain
Digestive tract into the blood, then to the liver, then to the target tissues
Veins, then muscles, then digestive tract
mcqs.why: Oral drugs are absorbed from the digestive tract into the blood and carried to the liver and then to the target tissues. Injections into muscles or veins are a different, faster route and are not the oral sequence.

mcqs.q: Which sign is a physical symptom of drug addiction?
options: Bloodshot eyes with pupils larger or smaller than usual, with tremors and slurred speech
A drop in attendance at work or school
A sudden change in friends and hobbies
mcqs.why: Physical symptoms include bloodshot eyes with pupils larger or smaller than usual, changes in appetite or sleep, weight change, tremors, slurred speech and impaired coordination. Attendance, money problems and changed friends are behavioural symptoms.

mcqs.q: Which sign is a behavioural symptom of drug addiction?
options: Unusual smells on breath, body or clothing
Sudden mood swings and angry outbursts
A drop in attendance and performance at work or school, with secret or suspicious behaviour
mcqs.why: Behavioural symptoms include a drop in attendance and performance, unexplained need for money, secret or suspicious behaviour, sudden change in friends and hobbies, and frequently getting into trouble. Smells and appearance are physical, and mood swings are psychological.

mcqs.q: Marijuana is made from which plant material?
options: Sap of the opium poppy plant
A dry, shredded mixture of flowers, stems, seeds and leaves of the hemp plant Cannabis Sativa
Material present in the cactus plant
mcqs.why: Marijuana is a dry, shredded mixture of flowers, stems, seeds and leaves of the hemp plant Cannabis Sativa. The mushroom gives psilocybin, the cactus gives mescaline, and opium poppy sap is the source of narcotics.

mcqs.q: Dextromethorphan is described as a hallucinogen that is:
options: Extracted from a mushroom and taken through smoke
Present in the cactus plant and taken orally
Synthesised in laboratories, with a chemical structure resembling morphine, producing a feeling of being out of one's body
Made from flowers and leaves of the hemp plant
mcqs.why: Dextromethorphan is synthesised in laboratories, its chemical structure resembles morphine, and it produces the hallucination of being out of one's body. The mushroom, cactus and hemp descriptions belong to psilocybin, mescaline and marijuana.

mcqs.q: How do sulfonamides stop bacteria from dividing?
options: They interfere with synthesis of the bacterial cell wall
They inhibit synthesis of folic acid, which bacteria need to make new DNA
They stimulate production of antibodies against bacteria
mcqs.why: Sulfonamides are bacteriostatic synthetic antibiotics that inhibit folic acid synthesis. Since folic acid is required to make new DNA, the bacteria stop dividing. Protein synthesis inhibition is tetracyclines and cell wall interference is cephalosporins.

mcqs.q: Why are tetracyclines not used in children under the age of 8?
options: Because that is the period of tooth development
Because children cannot absorb oral drugs
Because tetracyclines cause hallucinations in children
Because children have no respiratory infections
mcqs.why: Tetracyclines inhibit bacterial protein synthesis and treat respiratory, sinus, middle ear, urinary, skin and intestinal infections, but they are not used in children under 8 during tooth development.

mcqs.q: What does the Expanded Programme on Immunization (EPI) state?
options: It was set up in 1998 to vaccinate adults against three diseases
It was established by the Government of Pakistan in 1978 to vaccinate children aged 0-11 months against nine diseases
It gives lifetime immunity with a single vaccine dose
It treats addicts at Anti-Narcotics Force centres
mcqs.why: The EPI was established by the Government of Pakistan in 1978 to vaccinate children aged 0-11 months against nine diseases. Some vaccines give lifetime immunity, but others must be repeated, so a single-dose claim is wrong.

mcqs.q: How can bacteria pass antibiotic resistance to other bacteria?
options: By producing antibodies against the antibiotic
By transferring the genes coding for antibiotic resistance to other bacteria
By stopping folic acid synthesis in other bacteria
mcqs.why: Resistant bacteria can change their structure so the antibiotic no longer works, inactivate or neutralise the antibiotic, or transfer the genes coding for antibiotic resistance to other bacteria, spreading the problem.

Q: 1. Compile a list of various painkillers, antibiotics and sedatives being used in your household.

Ans: Model answer (compile the actual names from the medicines present in your own household; examples below are the drugs named in this unit): Painkillers: aspirin-based painkillers used for headaches, sore muscles and arthritis (many painkillers are based on the naturally occurring drugs aspirin and opiates). Antibiotics: medicines of the groups named in the book, such as penicillin and other antibiotics from the sulfonamides, tetracyclines and cephalosporins groups, kept for bacterial infections. Sedatives: phenobarbital and diazepam, which slow down brain functions, induce sleep and reduce anxiety, and which must be used with special care because they can cause psychological dependence when taken for a longer period of time. The list should record the name of each medicine, the group it belongs to and the purpose for which it is used in the household.

Q: 2. Summarise the antisocial effects of the usage of hallucinogens and narcotics.

Ans: Hallucinogens and narcotics damage the user's place in society as well as his body. The self-esteem of drug addicts is damaged and sinks lower and lower, and they develop negative feelings of worthlessness, hopelessness, shame and guilt; they lose their ability to develop caring and honest relationships and destroy their existing relationships, and become less assertive with great difficulty expressing opinions or needs. Community members characterise drug addicts as morally weak or as having criminal tendencies, so they are generally marginalised. Drug abuse has led to an increase in the crime rate: drug abusers commit theft or robbery to steal money to pay for drugs, and in desperation they may steal household items and sell them to get money. Apart from leading to financial instability, addiction increases the occurrence of conflicts and causes emotional pain for every member of the family, and a person with sedative addiction may also display hostility or aggression, mood swings, poor judgment and inability to function appropriately in social settings or at the work place.

Q: 3. Analyse the effects of possible over-dosage, under-dosage and drug interactions when using antibiotics without a doctor's consultation.

Ans: The book stresses that a doctor can best determine if an antibiotic needs to be administered for a disease or not, so using antibiotics without consultation is risky in three ways. Over-dosage and repeated use expose bacteria to the same antibiotic over and over, so the bacteria can change and develop resistance; resistant bacteria do not respond to the antibiotic and continue to cause infection, and the World Health Organisation describes such antibiotic resistant bacteria as 'nightmare bacteria'. Under-dosage, or stopping the course early, is also harmful: when a bacteriostatic antibiotic is used, the duration of therapy must be sufficient to allow the body's immune system to prepare proper defence against the invading bacteria, so too little antibiotic leaves the infection uncured and helps resistance develop. Drug interactions are a further risk because a self-chosen antibiotic may be useless or wrong for the illness in the first place: antibiotics only treat bacterial infections and are useless against viral infections (for example, the common cold) and fungal infections (such as ringworm), and taking them together with other drugs without medical advice can disturb the treatment instead of curing the disease. Some resistant bacteria can then be treated only with more powerful antibiotics.
